    👋 Bienvenido al Libro del Desarrollador Web¶

    De cero a Silicon Valley

    Este libro nace con una idea simple: cualquiera puede aprender a programar si tiene una guía clara, ejemplos reales y ganas de practicar. No necesitas un título, ni un equipo caro, ni un curso de pago. Solo un navegador, un editor de texto y constancia.

    Te acompañaremos desde tu primera etiqueta HTML hasta las arquitecturas más avanzadas del desarrollo moderno: TypeScript, Web Components, PWA, Edge Computing, IA generativa y más.

    🎯 ¿Para quién es este libro?¶

    Este material está pensado para tres perfiles muy concretos:

    Perfil Lo que encontrarás aquí
    🌱 Principiante absoluto Explicaciones desde cero, sin asumir conocimientos previos. Cada concepto se introduce con ejemplos ejecutables.
    🎓 Estudiante o autodidacta Material de referencia estructurado en 7 niveles, con ejercicios resueltos y retos semanales.
    🔄 Profesional en transición Capítulos avanzados sobre arquitectura, testing, rendimiento y despliegue en producción.

    ¿No sabes por dónde empezar?

    Si es tu primera vez programando, ve directo al Nivel Principiante. Si ya tienes experiencia, salta al nivel que corresponda a tu conocimiento actual con el botón 🗂️ Explorar del menú superior.

    📚 ¿Qué vas a aprender?¶

    El libro está dividido en 7 niveles progresivos y 38 capítulos, diseñados para que avances sin perderte:

    • HTML5 semántico y accesible
    • CSS3 moderno: Flexbox, Grid, variables, animaciones
    • JavaScript esencial: variables, funciones, DOM, eventos
    • Diseño responsive con media queries y mobile-first
    • Formularios HTML y validación nativa
    • Git y GitHub: control de versiones y trabajo en equipo
    • APIs REST con fetch y async/await
    • Despliegue en Netlify, Vercel, GitHub Pages
    • Tu primer portfolio profesional
    • CSS moderno: container queries, :has(), subgrid
    • JavaScript asíncrono en profundidad: promesas, event loop
    • Módulos ES6 y bundlers (Vite, esbuild)
    • TypeScript desde cero
    • Testing con Vitest y Testing Library
    • Accesibilidad WCAG y ARIA
    • Full-stack con Node.js: Express, bases de datos, autenticación
    • DevOps para frontend: CI/CD, Docker, monitorización
    • Web Components nativos
    • PWA con service workers
    • WebSockets y tiempo real
    • Animaciones avanzadas con GSAP y Framer Motion
    • Design systems escalables
    • Seguridad web: XSS, CSRF, CSP, CORS
    • WebAssembly en el navegador
    • IA en el frontend con TensorFlow.js
    • WebXR para realidad aumentada y virtual
    • Web3 y blockchain
    • Testing E2E con Playwright
    • React Server Components
    • Edge Computing con Cloudflare Workers
    • Docker para frontend
    • GraphQL y micro-frontends
    • IA generativa aplicada al desarrollo

    🛠️ ¿Qué necesitas para empezar?¶

    Solo tres cosas, todas gratis:

    1. Un navegador moderno (Chrome, Firefox, Edge o Safari actualizado)
    2. Un editor de código: recomendamos VS Code o Zed
    3. Muchas ganas de practicar 💪

    No necesitas instalar nada para empezar

    Los primeros capítulos se pueden seguir directamente en el navegador, con los editores en vivo que encontrarás en cada página. Solo cuando llegues a Node.js necesitarás instalar cosas en tu equipo.

    📖 Cómo leer este libro¶

    Orden recomendado¶

    Sigue los capítulos en orden si estás empezando. Cada uno construye sobre el anterior:

    ```mermaid graph LR A[Fundamentos] --> B[Intermedio] B --> C[Avanzado] C --> D[Profesional] D --> E[Experto] E --> F[Élite] F --> G[Vanguardia]

    💭 Project Philosophy¶

    Why this book exists

    There is no shortage of tutorials on the internet. What is missing is structured material that does not leave you hanging halfway through. This book exists to fill that gap.

    It grew out of my own notes. When I was learning, I jotted everything down in a text file. When I was teaching, I reused those notes. Over the years, it became this.

    🎯 Principles¶

    Every decision in this book—what to include, what to leave out, how to explain it—is governed by these seven principles. If you ever spot something that contradicts them, it is a bug and you can report it.

    🛠 Practical over theoretical¶

    Every concept comes with code you can run. There are no filler chapters or abstract theory without application.

    Real example

    When we explain async/await, we do not stop at saying "it is used to wait for promises." We show a call to a real API, with try/catch, error handling, and an example of what happens if you do not use it.

    📈 Progressive and without jumps¶

    Chapters follow a smooth curve. There are no impossible "exercises for the reader" or advanced concepts shoehorned into an introductory chapter.

    Level What you know at the start What you know at the end
    🟢 Beginner Nothing Build static web pages with HTML, CSS, and JS
    🟡 Intermediate Basic HTML/CSS/JS Consume APIs, use Git, deploy to production
    🟠 Advanced Static frontend TypeScript, testing, frontend architecture
    🔴 Professional Frontend Full-stack with Node.js, basic DevOps
    🟣 Expert Full-stack Web Components, PWA, WebSockets, design systems
    🔵 Elite Expert Security, WebAssembly, AI, WebXR, Web3
    🚀 Cutting Edge Elite Edge computing, GraphQL, micro-frontends, generative AI

    🌍 Natural, clear English¶

    No robotic phrasing, no unnecessary buzzwords. Technical terms that are standard in the industry—such as callback, debounce, hoisting, or event loop—are explained, italicized, and used naturally.

    Terms we keep in standard form

    • callback: a function passed as an argument to another function
    • debounce: a technique to delay the execution of a function
    • hoisting: moving variable and function declarations to the top of their scope
    • event loop: the JavaScript engine's execution and event queue loop
    • closure: a function that remembers its lexical environment

    You can find definitions for each of these in the glossary.

    🧱 No trendy dependencies¶

    We do not depend on a specific framework that will go out of fashion in six months. The fundamentals—HTML, CSS, and JavaScript—are the same today as they were ten years ago. Frameworks come and go, while the browser keeps understanding the same core standards.

    What you will NOT find here

    • ❌ "Learn React in 24 hours"
    • ❌ "The ultimate framework that will replace everything else"
    • ❌ "This library will change your life"
    • ✅ "Here is how the DOM works, and how React, Vue, and Svelte use it underneath"
    • ✅ "Here are the fundamentals that do not change, and here are the frameworks you can learn next"

    ♿ Accessible by default¶

    Every example you see here is designed to be accessible. Because accessibility is not an extra: it is part of the job.

    • All examples use semantic HTML (<nav>, <main>, <article>, <button> instead of <div onclick>)
    • Forms include properly associated <label> elements
    • Colors meet WCAG AA contrast (4.5:1 minimum)
    • Images include descriptive alt text
    • Interactive components are keyboard-navigable

    Accessibility is not a checkbox

    It is not about "passing" a validator. It is about anyone, regardless of their abilities, being able to use what you build. And that starts with writing good HTML from day one.

    🔓 Open and free¶

    All source code is on GitHub. You can copy it, modify it, use it in your projects, or suggest improvements. The license is MIT: one of the most permissive licenses available.

    You can You cannot
    ✅ Use the content in your projects ❌ Remove attribution
    ✅ Modify and adapt it ❌ Sell it as if it were your own
    ✅ Share it with anyone ❌ Use it to cause harm
    ✅ Contribute improvements —

    🎓 Teach, do not show off¶

    I do not write to prove how much I know, but so that you learn. That means:

    • Explaining things twice if needed.
    • Avoiding unnecessary jargon.
    • Acknowledging when something is difficult.
    • Not showing off "clever code" if it makes the example more confusing.
    • Providing examples that work, rather than "elegant" examples that are hard to follow.

    ❌ What you will NOT find here¶

    It is just as important to say what is here as what is not. So you know what to expect:

    • ❌ Promises to "learn to code in 24 hours". This takes time. Months, not days. Anyone telling you otherwise is lying to you.
    • ❌ Courses in disguise. There is nothing paid behind the scenes. No hidden "pro version."
    • ❌ Ads or affiliate links. Nobody pays to appear in the recommended resources.
    • ❌ Opinions disguised as facts. When something is a matter of taste (like "React vs Vue"), it is stated clearly as a personal preference, not a technical fact.
    • ❌ Outdated tutorials. If something changes in the ecosystem and affects the book, it gets updated. You can check the history in the Changelog.
    • ❌ Content copied from elsewhere. All text is original, written from scratch, with custom examples.
    • ❌ Filler. Every paragraph is there because it adds value. If a chapter can be summarized in half the length, it gets summarized.

    🏗 How it is built¶

    The book is built with 100% open source and free tools. No paid services or expensive infrastructure.

    Tool Purpose Alternative if it did not exist
    MkDocs Generate the static site from Markdown Hugo, Jekyll, Astro
    Material for MkDocs The theme, which accounts for 80% of the design Docusaurus, Just the Docs
    Markdown Write content cleanly and simply Plain HTML (slower to write)
    GitHub Actions Deploy automatically on every push Netlify, Vercel, manual CI
    GitHub Pages Host the site for free Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare Pages
    Giscus Comments anchored to GitHub Discussions Disqus, Utterances
    Mermaid Architecture and flow diagrams Draw.io, Excalidraw, PlantUML

    All source code is public and lives in the repository. If you want to build your own book with the same structure, you can fork it and get started.

    🤝 A commitment¶

    This book will not lie to you. Nor will it sell you hype. When something is difficult, I will tell you. When something takes repeated practice, I will tell you that too. When something requires building projects on your own, I will not tell you that reading alone is enough.

    Learning to code is like learning to play an instrument

    It takes practice, making mistakes, and trying again. There are no shortcuts. No magic pills. No "tricks" that replace hours at the keyboard.

    What I can promise you¶

    • ✅ Every chapter will be written with clarity, without unnecessary jargon.
    • ✅ Every example will work when you copy and paste it.
    • ✅ If something changes in the ecosystem, it will be updated as soon as possible.
    • ✅ There will never be ads or paywalls.
    • ✅ Your progress is yours: it is not sent to any server or shared with anyone.
    • ✅ If I make a mistake, I will fix it and tell you.

    What I cannot promise you¶

    • ❌ That you will learn in a week. That is not realistic.
    • ❌ That reading alone will be enough. It does not work that way.
    • ❌ That you will not get frustrated. Frustration is part of the process.
    • ❌ That this book is perfect. It has bugs. If you find them, report them.
    • ❌ That you will know everything you need when you finish. Learning to code is a lifelong process.

    🧭 On the "best" language, framework, or tool¶

    One of the most common questions is: "Which framework is best?". The honest answer is: it depends.

    • React is great for dynamic interfaces, but is heavier than Svelte or Solid.
    • Vue is easier to learn, though it has fewer job openings in some regions.
    • Svelte compiles to vanilla JavaScript, though its ecosystem is smaller.
    • Angular is solid for large teams, though its learning curve is steeper.

    My advice

    Learn JavaScript well before picking a framework. 80% of what you will do with React, Vue, or Svelte is JavaScript. If you master the language, switching frameworks takes weeks, not months.

    The same applies to backend languages: Node.js is great for APIs, Python for data and AI, Go for microservices, Rust for extreme performance. There is no single "best" one overall—only the best one for each use case.

    🌱 Project sustainability¶

    This book is not a sprint: it is a marathon. Because of that:

    • There are no release deadlines. Chapters are published when they are ready, not on an artificial schedule.
    • There is no growth pressure. Whether 10 people or 10,000 read it, the project stays the same.
    • There is no team. It is just me, with help from the community. If you want to contribute, you are welcome.
    • There is no rush. I prefer one well-written chapter a month over a mediocre one every week.
    • No aggressive monetization. If the project ever generates revenue, it will be reinvested into the book itself.

    Want to help?

    There are many ways to contribute without writing code: reporting bugs, suggesting improvements, sharing the book, starring the repository on GitHub. Everything counts. You can read the details on the Contribute page.

    🔮 Future of the project¶

    These are the ideas I have in mind for the coming months. Not all of them will happen, and priorities may shift. Still, they give you a sense of where this is heading:

    • [ ] English translation with mkdocs-static-i18n (in progress).
    • [ ] More interactive labs with StackBlitz and CodeSandbox.
    • [ ] Verifiable certificates with QR codes.
    • [ ] Account system to sync achievements across devices.
    • [ ] "Read-only" mode for distraction-free printing.
    • [ ] Semantic search with embeddings (experimental).
    • [ ] Guest chapters by other community authors.

    Have an idea?

    If you think something important is missing, open an issue on GitHub with the enhancement label. Community ideas are reviewed every week.

    💬 Final reflection¶

    "The best way to learn is to teach."

    This book is my way of teaching. It is what I wish I had found when I started out. If it helps you, it has already been worth it.

    And if you ever write your own, let me know—I would love to read it.

    👋 Bienvenido al Libro del Desarrollador Web¶

    De cero a Silicon Valley

    Este libro nace con una idea simple: cualquiera puede aprender a programar si tiene una guía clara, ejemplos reales y ganas de practicar. No necesitas un título, ni un equipo caro, ni un curso de pago. Solo un navegador, un editor de texto y constancia.

    Te acompañaremos desde tu primera etiqueta HTML hasta las arquitecturas más avanzadas del desarrollo moderno: TypeScript, Web Components, PWA, Edge Computing, IA generativa y más.

    🎯 ¿Para quién es este libro?¶

    Este material está pensado para tres perfiles muy concretos:

    Perfil Lo que encontrarás aquí
    🌱 Principiante absoluto Explicaciones desde cero, sin asumir conocimientos previos. Cada concepto se introduce con ejemplos ejecutables.
    🎓 Estudiante o autodidacta Material de referencia estructurado en 7 niveles, con ejercicios resueltos y retos semanales.
    🔄 Profesional en transición Capítulos avanzados sobre arquitectura, testing, rendimiento y despliegue en producción.

    ¿No sabes por dónde empezar?

    Si es tu primera vez programando, ve directo al Nivel Principiante. Si ya tienes experiencia, salta al nivel que corresponda a tu conocimiento actual con el botón 🗂️ Explorar del menú superior.

    📚 ¿Qué vas a aprender?¶

    El libro está dividido en 7 niveles progresivos y 38 capítulos, diseñados para que avances sin perderte:

    • HTML5 semántico y accesible
    • CSS3 moderno: Flexbox, Grid, variables, animaciones
    • JavaScript esencial: variables, funciones, DOM, eventos
    • Diseño responsive con media queries y mobile-first
    • Formularios HTML y validación nativa
    • Git y GitHub: control de versiones y trabajo en equipo
    • APIs REST con fetch y async/await
    • Despliegue en Netlify, Vercel, GitHub Pages
    • Tu primer portfolio profesional
    • CSS moderno: container queries, :has(), subgrid
    • JavaScript asíncrono en profundidad: promesas, event loop
    • Módulos ES6 y bundlers (Vite, esbuild)
    • TypeScript desde cero
    • Testing con Vitest y Testing Library
    • Accesibilidad WCAG y ARIA
    • Full-stack con Node.js: Express, bases de datos, autenticación
    • DevOps para frontend: CI/CD, Docker, monitorización
    • Web Components nativos
    • PWA con service workers
    • WebSockets y tiempo real
    • Animaciones avanzadas con GSAP y Framer Motion
    • Design systems escalables
    • Seguridad web: XSS, CSRF, CSP, CORS
    • WebAssembly en el navegador
    • IA en el frontend con TensorFlow.js
    • WebXR para realidad aumentada y virtual
    • Web3 y blockchain
    • Testing E2E con Playwright
    • React Server Components
    • Edge Computing con Cloudflare Workers
    • Docker para frontend
    • GraphQL y micro-frontends
    • IA generativa aplicada al desarrollo

    🛠️ ¿Qué necesitas para empezar?¶

    Solo tres cosas, todas gratis:

    1. Un navegador moderno (Chrome, Firefox, Edge o Safari actualizado)
    2. Un editor de código: recomendamos VS Code o Zed
    3. Muchas ganas de practicar 💪

    No necesitas instalar nada para empezar

    Los primeros capítulos se pueden seguir directamente en el navegador, con los editores en vivo que encontrarás en cada página. Solo cuando llegues a Node.js necesitarás instalar cosas en tu equipo.

    📖 Cómo leer este libro¶

    Orden recomendado¶

    Sigue los capítulos en orden si estás empezando. Cada uno construye sobre el anterior:

    ```mermaid graph LR A[Fundamentos] --> B[Intermedio] B --> C[Avanzado] C --> D[Profesional] D --> E[Experto] E --> F[Élite] F --> G[Vanguardia]

    🟢 Nivel 1 — Principiante

    01 — Introduction to Web Development¶

    What you'll learn

    • What web development is and why it matters.
    • The three pillars: HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
    • The difference between frontend and backend.
    • How a web page works from the moment you request it until you see it.
    • The tools you need to get started.

    🌐 What is web development?¶

    Web development is the process of building sites and applications that run in a browser. It's one of the most in-demand disciplines in tech and one of the most accessible: all you need is a computer, a code editor and an internet connection.

    The web is the world's biggest showcase

    Every time you open a page, a team of developers has designed its structure, its style and its behavior. Learning web development means learning to build that showcase.

    🏛 The three fundamental pillars¶

    Every modern web page rests on three technologies:

    Pillar What it does Analogy
    HTML Defines the structure and content The skeleton
    CSS Defines the appearance (colors, typography, layout) The skin and clothes
    JavaScript Defines the behavior (interaction, logic) The muscles 
    graph LR
    A[Your code] --> B[HTML]
    A --> C[CSS]
    A --> D[JavaScript]
    B --> E[Browser]
    C --> E
    D --> E
    E --> F[Web page]

    Learn in this order

    First HTML (structure), then CSS (appearance), then JavaScript (behavior). Skipping the order is the #1 cause of frustration when starting out.

    ⚖️ Frontend vs Backend¶

    Frontend Backend
    Where it runs In the user's browser On the server
    Technologies HTML, CSS, JavaScript Node.js, Python, PHP, Java, Go…
    What it handles What you see and touch Data, logic, security, database
    Example A button that changes color Saving your password in the database

    Full-stack = knows how to do both.

    🔄 How a web page works¶

    When you type https://libro.urukais.com into the browser, this happens:

    sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant N as Browser
    participant D as DNS
    participant S as Server
    U->>N: Types the URL
    N->>D: What IP does libro.urukais.com have?
    D->>N: 185.x.x.x
    N->>S: GET /
    S->>N: HTML, CSS, JS
    N->>U: Renders the page
    1. DNS: translates the domain into an IP address.
    2. HTTP request: the browser asks the server for the files.
    3. Response: the server returns HTML, CSS and JS.
    4. Rendering: the browser interprets those files and paints the page.

    The browser doesn't run everything the same way

    HTML and CSS are interpreted (they're not programming languages). JavaScript is executed (it has logic: variables, loops, conditions).

    🧰 Tools you need¶

    Tool For what Recommendation
    Code editor Writing the code VS Code
    Modern browser Testing and debugging Chrome / Firefox
    Git Version control Git + GitHub
    Terminal Running commands Your system's default

    You don't need 20 tools

    With VS Code and a browser you can start. Everything else is added when you need it.

    👋 Your first "Hello, world"¶

    Create a file called index.html with this content:

    <!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>My first page</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Hello, world!</h1>
    <p>This is my first web page.</p>
</body>
</html>

    Open it with a double click. You'll see your first page in the browser. You're now a web developer. 😄

    🧪 Hands-on exercise¶

    Introduce yourself in HTML

    Create a file called presentation.html with:

    • An <h1> with your name.
    • A <p> with a sentence about you.
    • An <h2> with "My goals".
    • A <ul> list with 3 things you want to learn.

    Open it in the browser and check that it renders correctly.

    Solution 
    <!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>My presentation</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Urukais</h1>
    <p>I'm a web developer and I love teaching.</p>
    <h2>My goals</h2>
    <ul>
        <li>Mastering HTML and CSS</li>
        <li>Learning JavaScript in depth</li>
        <li>Building my own portfolio</li>
    </ul>
</body>
</html>

    🧠 Quiz¶

    Check what you've learned

    1. What are the three pillars of web development?

    HTML (structure), CSS (appearance) and JavaScript (behavior).

    2. What's the difference between frontend and backend?

    The frontend runs in the browser (what the user sees); the backend runs on the server (data, logic, security).

    3. Is HTML a programming language?

    No. It's a markup language. It has no variables, loops or conditions. JavaScript is a programming language.

    4. What does DNS do when you type a URL?

    It translates the domain name into the IP address of the server where the page is hosted.

    02 — Basic HTML¶

    What you will learn

    • The structure of an HTML document.
    • Tags, attributes, and nesting.
    • Essential tags: headings, paragraphs, lists, links, images.
    • What semantic HTML is and why it matters.
    • How to validate your HTML.

    🌐 What is HTML?¶

    HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the markup language that defines the structure of a web page. It is not a programming language: it has no variables, loops, or conditionals. It is a markup language—a system of tags that tells the browser what each element is.

    The skeleton analogy

    If a web page were a human body, HTML would be the skeleton (structure), CSS the skin and clothes (appearance), and JavaScript the muscles (movement and interaction).

    <h1>This is a heading</h1>
<p>This is a paragraph with <strong>bold text</strong>.</p>

    🏛 HTML Document Structure¶

    Every HTML document follows the same skeleton:

    <!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <title>My first page</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Hello, world!</h1>
  <p>My first web page.</p>
</body>
</html>

    What does each line do?¶

    Line Purpose
    <!DOCTYPE html> Tells the browser the document is HTML5.
    <html lang="en"> Root of the document. lang="en" sets the language (important for screen readers and SEO).
    <head> Metadata: not shown on the page itself, but configures the document.
    <meta charset="UTF-8"> Character encoding. Without it, accents and special characters can look broken.
    <meta name="viewport" ...> Makes the page adapt to mobile screens.
    <title> Text shown in the browser tab.
    <body> Everything visible on the page goes inside here. 
    graph TD
A[html] --> B[head]
A --> C[body]
B --> B1[meta charset]
B --> B2[title]
B --> B3[meta viewport]
C --> C1[h1]
C --> C2[p]
C --> C3[img]

    🏷 Tags, Attributes, and Nesting¶

    Tags¶

    A tag goes between < and >. Almost always they come in pairs:

    <p>Content</p>
    • <p> → opening tag.
    • </p> → closing tag (with /).
    • Content → what sits between them.

    Some are self-closing (no closing tag):

    <img src="photo.jpg" alt="A photo">
<br>
<hr>
<input type="text">

    Attributes¶

    Attributes add extra information to a tag. They go inside the opening tag:

    <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org">MDN Web Docs</a>
    • href is the attribute.
    • "https://developer.mozilla.org" is the value.

    Nesting¶

    Tags can be nested (one inside another). They must close in reverse order from how they opened:

    <p>This is <strong>very important</strong>.</p>   <!-- ✅ valid -->
<p>This is <strong>very important.</p></strong>   <!-- ❌ invalid -->

    Nesting errors

    A common beginner mistake is closing tags in the wrong order. If you open <strong> inside a <p>, close </strong> before </p>.

    📝 Essential Tags¶

    Headings: <h1> to <h6>¶

    There are 6 heading levels. <h1> is the most important and <h6> the least. Each page should have a single <h1>.

    <h1>Main title</h1>
<h2>Section</h2>
<h3>Subsection</h3>

    Hierarchy, not size

    Don't pick <h3> "because it looks smaller". Use the level that semantically matches the content structure. Size is controlled with CSS.

    Paragraphs: <p>¶

    <p>This is a normal paragraph.</p>
<p>This is another separate paragraph.</p>

    Lists¶

    Unordered (bullets):

    <ul>
  <li>HTML</li>
  <li>CSS</li>
  <li>JavaScript</li>
</ul>

    Ordered (numbers):

    <ol>
  <li>Install the editor</li>
  <li>Create the file</li>
  <li>Write the code</li>
</ol>

    Links: <a>¶

    <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org">Visit MDN</a>
<a href="contact.html">Contact page</a>
<a href="#section">Jump to a section</a>

    External links

    For links that open in a new tab (target="_blank"), always add rel="noopener noreferrer" for security.

    Images: <img>¶

    <img src="photo.jpg" alt="A sunset beach" width="400">
    • src → image path.
    • alt → alternative text (required for accessibility).

    alt is not optional

    The alt attribute describes the image for people who cannot see it (screen readers, broken images, SEO). If the image is purely decorative, use alt="" (empty).

    Emphasis: <strong> and <em>¶

    <p>This is <strong>important</strong> and this is <em>emphatic</em>.</p>
    • <strong> → importance (usually rendered bold).
    • <em> → emphasis (usually rendered italic).

    🧩 Semantic HTML¶

    Semantic tags describe the meaning of content, not just how it looks. They are key for accessibility and SEO:

    <header>
  <h1>My blog</h1>
  <nav>
    <a href="/">Home</a>
    <a href="/about">About</a>
  </nav>
</header>

<main>
  <article>
    <h2>My first post</h2>
    <p>Post content…</p>
  </article>
</main>

<footer>
  <p>© 2026 My blog</p>
</footer>
    Tag Meaning
    <header> Header (logo, title, navigation).
    <nav> Navigation block (menu).
    <main> Main content (one per page).
    <article> Standalone content (post, news item).
    <section> Thematic section with its own heading.
    <aside> Tangential content (sidebar).
    <footer> Footer.

    Rule of thumb

    When torn between a <div> and a semantic tag, pick the semantic one. Use <div> only when nothing else fits.

    🧪 Practical Exercise¶

    Your first complete page

    Create an index.html file with: - An <h1> with your name. - A <p> with a sentence about yourself. - A <ul> list with your 3 favorite languages. - A link to MDN. - An image (can be a URL).

    When you're done, open it in your browser (double click) and verify how it looks.

    Solution 
    <!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>My first page</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Urukais</h1>
  <p>I'm a web developer and love teaching.</p>
  <h2>My favorite languages</h2>
  <ul>
    <li>HTML</li>
    <li>CSS</li>
    <li>JavaScript</li>
  </ul>
  <p><a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/">Visit MDN</a></p>
  <img src="https://picsum.photos/400/200" alt="Random image" width="400">
</body>
</html>

    🧠 Quiz¶

    Check what you learned

    1. Which declaration indicates the document is HTML5?

    <!DOCTYPE html> at the very top of the file.

    2. What is the difference between <strong> and <b>?

    <strong> indicates semantic importance (for screen readers and SEO); <b> only applies visual bold. Whenever possible, use <strong>.

    3. What is the alt attribute on images for?

    It describes the image for people who cannot see it (accessibility), when the image fails to load, and for SEO.

    4. How many <h1> tags should a page have?

    Ideally one. It reflects the main heading of the document.

    03 — Basic CSS¶

    What you will learn

    • What CSS is and how it is applied.
    • Selectors, specificity, and the cascade.
    • The box model and box-sizing.
    • display, position, and z-index.
    • Flexbox and Grid in depth.
    • CSS variables, modern functions, and clamp().
    • Transitions, transforms, and prefers-reduced-motion.
    • Media queries and accessibility.

    🎨 What is CSS?¶

    CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) is the language that defines the presentation of a web page: colors, typography, layout, and animations.

    The human body analogy

    If HTML is the skeleton, CSS is the skin, clothes, and makeup. It defines how everything structured by HTML looks, feels, and moves.

    h1 {
  color: #6a5acd;
  font-size: 2rem;
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
}

    🔗 How to Apply CSS¶

    There are three ways:

    1. External CSS (recommended)¶

    <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">

    2. Internal CSS¶

    <style>
  h1 { color: red; }
</style>

    3. Inline CSS¶

    <h1 style="color: red;">Heading</h1>

    Always prefer external CSS

    External CSS separates structure from presentation, caches better, is reusable, and lets teams collaborate with fewer conflicts.

    🎯 Selectors¶

    p { color: #333; }
.boton { background: #6a5acd; }
#header { padding: 1rem; }
nav a { text-decoration: none; }
ul > li { margin: 0.5rem 0; }
a:hover { color: #00bcd4; }
input[type="text"] { border: 1px solid #ccc; }
    Selector Example Usage
    Tag p All paragraphs
    Class .boton Elements with class="boton"
    ID #header Element with id="header"
    Descendant nav a Links inside nav
    Direct child ul > li li direct children of ul
    Adjacent sibling h2 + p First p right after an h2
    Pseudo-class a:hover Link on mouse hover
    Attribute input[type="email"] Only email inputs

    :focus-visible is accessibility

    Never remove outline without replacing it. :focus-visible shows the focus ring only during keyboard navigation, not on mouse click.

    ⚖ Specificity and Cascade¶

    Type Weight Example
    Inline styles 1000 style="..."
    IDs 100 #header
    Classes / attributes / pseudo-classes 10 .boton, :hover
    Tags / pseudo-elements 1 p, ::before

    Avoid `!important

    !important breaks the cascade and makes CSS unpredictable.

    📦 The Box Model¶

    .caja {
  width: 200px;
  height: 100px;
  padding: 16px;
  border: 2px solid #333;
  margin: 8px;
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

    box-sizing: border-box

    By default, width does not include padding or border. With box-sizing: border-box, it does.

    🧱 display and position¶

    Value display position
    block Takes full width —
    inline Only what is needed —
    flex Flexbox container —
    grid Grid container —
    none Not rendered —
    static — Normal flow
    relative — Its original position
    absolute — Nearest positioned ancestor
    fixed — The viewport
    sticky — Scroll, up to a threshold 
    .header { position: fixed; top: 0; left: 0; right: 0; z-index: 100; }
.tooltip-wrap { position: relative; }
.tooltip { position: absolute; top: 100%; left: 50%; transform: translateX(-50%); }
.sidebar { position: sticky; top: 2rem; }

    z-index only works with `position

    It has no effect on static elements.

    🧩 Flexbox¶

    .contenedor {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: row;
  justify-content: space-between;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 1rem;
}
.hijo { flex: 1 1 auto; }

    🔲 Grid¶

    .grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}

    Named Grid Areas¶

    .layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr;
  grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto;
  grid-template-areas:
    "header header"
    "sidebar main"
    "footer footer";
  min-height: 100vh;
  gap: 1rem;
}

    🎨 CSS Variables¶

    :root {
  --primario: #6a5acd;
  --acento: #00bcd4;
  --radio: 8px;
}
.boton { background: var(--primario); border-radius: var(--radio); }

    ⚡ Modern Functions¶

    h1 { font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 5vw, 3rem); }
.contenedor { width: min(90%, 1200px); }
.layout { height: calc(100vh - 80px); }
.video { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; }
.avatar { object-fit: cover; border-radius: 50%; }
    ¶

    🎬 Transitions and Transforms¶

    .boton {
  transition: background 0.2s ease, transform 0.2s ease;
}
.boton:hover {
  background: #5a4abd;
  transform: translateY(-2px);
}

    📱 Media Queries and Preferences¶

    @media screen and (min-width: 640px) {
  .elemento { padding: 2rem; }
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  body { background: #1a1726; color: #fff; }
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  * { animation: none !important; transition: none !important; }
}

    ♿ CSS Accessibility¶

    • Never remove outline without replacing it. Use :focus-visible.
    • Minimum contrast 4.5:1 (WCAG AA).
    • Respect prefers-reduced-motion.
    • Minimum touch target size: 44×44 px.
    :root { color-scheme: light dark; }
button:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid #6a5acd; outline-offset: 2px; }

    🧠 Test Your Knowledge¶

    1. Which property enables Flexbox on a container?

    2. What does box-sizing: border-box do?

    3. Which layout model is two-dimensional?

    🧪 Practical Exercise¶

    Profile card with Flexbox

    Create a card with a circular avatar, name, description, and a "Follow" button. Use column Flexbox, gap: 12px, and a transition on button hover.

    Solution 
    .card {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 12px;
  padding: 24px;
  max-width: 280px;
  background: #fff;
  border-radius: 16px;
  box-shadow: 0 4px 16px rgba(0, 0, 0, .08);
}
.avatar {
  width: 80px;
  height: 80px;
  border-radius: 50%;
  object-fit: cover;
}
.btn {
  padding: 8px 20px;
  background: #6a5acd;
  color: #fff;
  border: none;
  border-radius: 8px;
  cursor: pointer;
  transition: background 0.2s ease, transform 0.2s ease;
}
.btn:hover {
  background: #5a4abd;
  transform: translateY(-1px);
}

    🧠 Review Quiz¶

    Check what you learned

    1. Difference between padding and margin?

    padding is inner space. margin is outer space.

    2. What does position: absolute do without a positioned ancestor?

    It positions relative to the viewport.

    3. Difference between :is() and :where()?

    :is() inherits specificity. :where() always has 0 specificity.

    4. Why use transform instead of top/left for animations?

    It animates on the GPU and avoids layout reflow.

    5. What does repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr)) do?

    Columns of at least 240px with equal distribution.

    05 — Responsive Design¶

    What you will learn

    • What responsive design is and why it is mandatory today.
    • The mobile-first philosophy.
    • meta viewport and why it is essential.
    • Media queries, relative units, and modern functions (clamp()).
    • Responsive images and container queries.

    📱 What is Responsive Design?¶

    Responsive design (or adaptive design) is the practice of building a website that looks and works well across any screen size: mobile, tablet, laptop, or 4K monitor.

    The water analogy

    Water adapts to the container that holds it. A responsive site should do the same: instead of "breaking" when resized, it reorganizes so it stays usable.

    graph LR
    A[Mobile 320px] --> B[Tablet 768px]
    B --> C[Laptop 1024px]
    C --> D[Desktop 1440px+]
    A -.-> E[Same HTML]
    B -.-> E
    C -.-> E
    D -.-> E

    🏛 Mobile-first¶

    Mobile-first means designing for mobile first and then expanding for larger screens. It is the opposite of "design for desktop and adapt it later".

    Approach Advantage Disadvantage
    Mobile-first Cleaner CSS, better mobile performance More upfront work on mobile
    Desktop-first Faster if you already have a desktop design CSS with more max-width, more tech debt

    Why mobile-first

    Mobile traffic exceeds 60% on most sites. Designing for mobile first forces you to prioritize content and simplify. In CSS, min-width (mobile-first) is cleaner than max-width (desktop-first).

    🖥 Meta Viewport (Essential)¶

    Without this tag in <head>, mobile browsers simulate a 980px width and zoom out. Result: tiny, unreadable text.

    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    • width=device-width → the viewport width matches the device's real width.
    • initial-scale=1.0 → no initial zoom.

    No viewport, no responsive

    It is the #1 beginner mistake. If your site looks "tiny" on mobile, check this tag.

    📐 Media Queries¶

    Media queries apply CSS only when a condition is met (screen width, orientation, preferences…).

    /* Base: mobile */
.container {
    padding: 1rem;
}

/* Tablet and up */
@media (min-width: 768px) {
    .container {
        padding: 2rem;
    }
}

/* Desktop and up */
@media (min-width: 1024px) {
    .container {
        padding: 3rem;
        max-width: 1200px;
        margin: 0 auto;
    }
}

    Common Breakpoints¶

    Name Width Typical use
    xs 0–479px Small mobile
    sm ≥ 480px Large mobile
    md ≥ 768px Tablet
    lg ≥ 1024px Laptop / desktop
    xl ≥ 1280px Large desktop
    2xl ≥ 1536px 4K monitor

    Don't chase devices

    Breakpoints should be based on where your layout breaks, not on "the width of an iPhone 15". Add media queries when content needs them.

    User Preferences¶

    /* System dark mode */
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
    body { background: #111; color: #eee; }
}

/* Reduce motion (accessibility) */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
    * { animation: none !important; transition: none !important; }
}

    📏 Relative Units¶

    Absolute units (px) don't scale. Relative units do:

    Unit Reference Example
    rem Root font size (16px by default) font-size: 1.5rem; = 24px
    em Parent element's font size padding: 1em;
    % Container's width/height width: 100%;
    vw / vh 1% of viewport height: 100vh; (full screen)
    svh / dvh Dynamic viewport (mobile with bar) height: 100dvh;

    Careful with vh on mobile

    100vh on mobile includes the browser bar → clipped content. Use 100svh (smallest) or 100dvh (dynamic) for full screen.

    clamp(): The Magic Function¶

    /* Fluid size: min 1rem, ideal 4vw, max 3rem */
h1 {
    font-size: clamp(1rem, 4vw, 3rem);
}

    clamp(min, preferred, max) scales smoothly between two values. Great for headings and spacing.

    /* Fluid spacing without media queries */
.section {
    padding: clamp(1rem, 5vw, 4rem);
}

    🖼 Responsive Images¶

    max-width: 100% (The Foundation)¶

    img {
    max-width: 100%;
    height: auto;
}

    Prevents images from overflowing their container.

    srcset and sizes¶

    To serve the right image for each screen (and save data):

    <img
    src="foto-800.jpg"
    srcset="foto-400.jpg 400w, foto-800.jpg 800w, foto-1600.jpg 1600w"
    sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw"
    alt="Responsive example"
>
    • srcset → list of images with their real width.
    • sizes → how much width it will take on each screen.
    • The browser picks the best option.

    <picture> (Alternative Formats)¶

    <picture>
    <source srcset="foto.avif" type="image/avif">
    <source srcset="foto.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="foto.jpg" alt="Example">
</picture>

    The browser uses the first format it supports (AVIF > WebP > JPG). Saves bandwidth in modern browsers.

    📦 Container Queries (Modern)¶

    Container queries apply CSS based on a parent container's size, not the viewport. They are the natural evolution of media queries.

    .card-wrapper {
    container-type: inline-size;
}

.card {
    padding: 1rem;
}

@container (min-width: 400px) {
    .card {
        display: grid;
        grid-template-columns: 120px 1fr;
        gap: 1rem;
    }
}

    Key difference: - Media query → "if the screen is wide…" - Container query → "if the container is wide…"

    The same component can look different depending on where it sits (sidebar, hero, grid). Support: 90%+ modern browsers (2024).

    Media vs Container

    Use media queries for global layout (header, footer, sidebar). Use container queries for reusable components (cards, widgets, buttons).

    🧩 Responsive Patterns¶

    1. Auto-Adaptive Grid (No Media Queries)¶

    .grid {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr));
    gap: 1rem;
}

    Creates as many columns as fit (minimum 250px). Zero media queries.

    2. Flexbox with Wrap¶

    .flex {
    display: flex;
    flex-wrap: wrap;
    gap: 1rem;
}

.flex > * {
    flex: 1 1 250px;
}

    3. Responsive Navigation¶

    .nav {
    display: flex;
    flex-wrap: wrap;
    gap: 1rem;
}

@media (max-width: 600px) {
    .nav {
        flex-direction: column;
    }
}

    🏗 Complete Example: Responsive Card¶

    <article class="card">
    <img src="foto.jpg" alt="Product">
    <div class="card-body">
        <h2>Mechanical keyboard</h2>
        <p>89 €</p>
        <button>Buy</button>
    </div>
</article>

    .card {
    display: flex;
    flex-direction: column;
    border-radius: 12px;
    overflow: hidden;
    background: #fff;
    box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.1);
}

.card img {
    width: 100%;
    height: auto;
}

.card-body {
    padding: clamp(1rem, 3vw, 2rem);
    display: flex;
    flex-direction: column;
    gap: .5rem;
}

/* On wide screens, image on the left */
@media (min-width: 768px) {
    .card {
        flex-direction: row;
    }
    .card img {
        width: 40%;
        object-fit: cover;
    }
}

    🧪 Practical Exercise¶

    Hero with fluid typography

    Create a "hero" section with:

    • An <h1> heading with a fluid size between 1.5rem and 4rem.
    • A <p> paragraph with a max width of 60ch.
    • Horizontally centered with fluid padding.

    Do not use media queries. Use clamp() and relative units.

    Solution 
    .hero {
    padding: clamp(2rem, 8vw, 6rem) clamp(1rem, 4vw, 3rem);
    text-align: center;
    background: linear-gradient(135deg, #6a5acd, #00bcd4);
    color: #fff;
}

.hero h1 {
    font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 5vw, 4rem);
    line-height: 1.2;
    margin: 0 auto 1rem;
    max-width: 20ch;
}

.hero p {
    font-size: clamp(1rem, 1.5vw, 1.25rem);
    max-width: 60ch;
    margin: 0 auto;
}

    Key points: clamp() for typography and spacing, max-width in ch (character width) for comfortable reading, margin: 0 auto to center.

    🧠 Quiz¶

    Check what you learned

    1. What is meta viewport for?

    Without it, mobile browsers simulate a 980px width and zoom out. With width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0, the browser uses the device's real width and applies no initial zoom.

    2. What is the difference between rem, em, and vw?

    rem → root font size (html). em → parent element's font size. vw → 1% of viewport width.

    3. What does clamp(1rem, 4vw, 3rem) do?

    Returns a fluid size: never less than 1rem, never more than 3rem, scaling with 4vw in between.

    4. When should you use container queries instead of media queries?

    For reusable components whose layout should adapt to the space available in their container, not the viewport size.

    5. Why can 100vh fail on mobile?

    Because it includes the browser navigation bar, which shows and hides. Use 100svh (smallest) or 100dvh (dynamic) for a safe full screen.

    07 — Git and Version Control¶

    🌳 What is Git?¶

    Git is a distributed version control system. It keeps a history of all changes in a project, lets you go back in time, work in parallel with others, and merge changes without losing anything.

    Without Git, you're lost

    If you've ever had files like final-project-v2-for-real-this-time.docx, Git is the solution. One single history, every change tracked, no duplicates.

    ⚙ Initial Setup¶

    ```bash git config --global user.name "Your Name" git config --global user.email "you@email.com" git config --global init.defaultBranch main git config --global core.editor "code --wait"

    08 — Consuming APIs with fetch¶

    What you will learn

    • What an API is and what it is used for.
    • How to make HTTP requests with fetch.
    • Handling JSON responses.
    • async/await and error handling.
    • Best practices when consuming APIs.

    🔌 What is an API?¶

    An API (Application Programming Interface) is a set of rules that allows two programs to communicate. In web development, it almost always refers to a REST API that returns data in JSON format.

    An API is like a waiter

    You (the client) order something from the menu (the request). The waiter (the API) goes to the kitchen (the server), picks up your order, and brings it to you (the response). You don't need to know how the kitchen works.

    🌐 Anatomy of an HTTP¶

    GET https://api.ejemplo.com/usuarios?limit=10
Headers:
  Authorization: Bearer token123
  Content-Type: application/json
    Verb Usage
    GET Fetch data
    POST Create a resource
    PUT / PATCH Update a resource
    DELETE Delete a resource
    Status Meaning
    200 OK
    201 Created
    400 Bad Request
    401 Unauthorized
    403 Forbidden
    404 Not Found
    500 Internal Server Error

    📡 Basic fetch¶

    fetch('https://api.ejemplo.com/usuarios')
  .then(res => {
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error('HTTP Error ' + res.status);
    return res.json();
  })
  .then(data => console.log(data))
  .catch(err => console.error(err));

    fetch does not reject on HTTP errors

    fetch only rejects the promise if there is a network error. If the server returns 404 or 500, the promise still resolves. That's why you must check res.ok manually.

    ⚡ async/await¶

    The modern and more readable way:

    async function cargarUsuarios() {
  try {
    const res = await fetch('https://api.ejemplo.com/usuarios');
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error('HTTP Error ' + res.status);
    const data = await res.json();
    console.log(data);
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('Something went wrong:', err);
  }
}

cargarUsuarios();

    📤 Sending Data (POST)¶

    async function crearUsuario(usuario) {
  const res = await fetch('https://api.ejemplo.com/usuarios', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': 'application/json',
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(usuario),
  });

  if (!res.ok) throw new Error('Failed to create user');
  return res.json();
}

crearUsuario({ nombre: 'Ana', email: 'ana@ejemplo.com' })
  .then(data => console.log('Created:', data))
  .catch(err => console.error(err));

    🔑 Token Authentication¶

    const res = await fetch('https://api.ejemplo.com/perfil', {
  headers: {
    'Authorization': 'Bearer ' + token,
  },
});

    Never store tokens in source code

    Tokens belong in environment variables or in localStorage (with care). Never in the source code you push to GitHub.

    🔄 Parallel Requests¶

    const [usuarios, posts] = await Promise.all([
  fetch('/api/usuarios').then(r => r.json()),
  fetch('/api/posts').then(r => r.json()),
]);

    Promise.all waits for all promises to settle. If one fails, the whole thing fails.

    const resultados = await Promise.allSettled([
  fetch('/api/a').then(r => r.json()),
  fetch('/api/b').then(r => r.json()),
]);
// resultados[0].status === 'fulfilled' or 'rejected'

    Promise.allSettled waits for all of them, but does not fail if any one rejects.

    🚨 Error Handling¶

    async function cargarDatos() {
  try {
    const res = await fetch('/api/datos');
    if (!res.ok) {
      if (res.status === 401) throw new Error('Unauthorized');
      if (res.status === 404) throw new Error('Not found');
      throw new Error('HTTP Error ' + res.status);
    }
    return await res.json();
  } catch (err) {
    console.error(err.message);
    return null;
  }
}

    1. Which HTTP verb is used to fetch data?

    2. What must you check after a fetch to know if an HTTP error occurred?

    3. Which method waits for all promises to complete?

    09 — Deployment¶

    What you will learn

    • What it means to "deploy" a web application.
    • Static hosting vs. dynamic hosting.
    • Recommended platforms: Vercel, Netlify, GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages.
    • CI/CD with GitHub Actions.
    • Environment variables, custom domains, and HTTPS.
    • Rollbacks and basic monitoring.

    🚀 What is Deployment?¶

    Deploying means publishing your application to a server accessible from the internet. Until then, your site only exists on your computer (localhost). When you deploy, it gets a public URL and anyone can visit it.

    The storefront analogy

    Your local project is the workshop where you build the display. Deploying is opening the shop to the public: setting up the window display on the street, turning on the lights, and hanging the sign.

    graph LR
    A[Your code] --> B[Git repository]
    B --> C[CI/CD]
    C --> D[Server]
    D --> E[Public URL]

    🏛 Hosting Types¶

    Type What it serves Examples Typical cost
    Static HTML, CSS, JS, images (no backend) GitHub Pages, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages Free
    Serverless / JAMstack Static + on-demand functions Vercel, Netlify Functions Free within limits
    PaaS Node.js, Python, etc. with managed server Railway, Render, Fly.io €0–5/month
    IaaS / VPS Full server (you manage everything) DigitalOcean, Hetzner, AWS EC2 €5–20/month
    Containers Orchestrated Docker AWS ECS, Google Cloud Run, Fly.io Pay as you go

    Start with static

    If your project is HTML + CSS + JS, static hosting is free, fast, and includes automatic HTTPS. Step up only when you need a backend.

    🎯 Recommended Platforms¶

    GitHub Pages (static, free)¶

    Great for documentation, portfolios, and personal projects.

    # .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: Deploy to GitHub Pages
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run build
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: dist/
      - uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4

    No backend

    GitHub Pages only serves static files. It does not run Node.js, Python, or databases.

    Vercel (Next.js, React, static + functions)¶

    npm i -g vercel
vercel
    • Automatic framework detection (Next.js, Vite, Astro…).
    • Preview deployments for every PR (temporary URL).
    • Serverless functions included.
    • Free HTTPS and domain.
    • Generous free tier for personal projects.

    Netlify (static + functions)¶

    • Similar to Vercel, very popular for JAMstack.
    • Built-in forms (<form netlify>).
    • Serverless functions in netlify/functions/.
    • Built-in A/B split testing.

    Cloudflare Pages + Workers¶

    • Global CDN (300+ PoPs).
    • Very generous free tier.
    • Workers for edge logic (see Chapter 33).
    • Ideal when combining static assets + edge functions.

    Railway / Render / Fly.io (backend)¶

    • Railway: deploy from Git, PostgreSQL included.
    • Render: similar, free tier spins down when idle.
    • Fly.io: global Docker containers, very fast.
    I need… Platform
    Just HTML/CSS/JS GitHub Pages / Netlify
    Next.js / React Vercel
    Edge functions Cloudflare Pages
    Node/Python backend Railway / Render / Fly.io
    Database + API Railway / Supabase / Neon

    🔁 CI/CD with GitHub Actions¶

    CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment) automates the workflow: every git push builds, tests, and deploys.

    # .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
          cache: "npm"
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build

    One workflow per responsibility

    Keep one workflow for tests (ci.yml) and another for deploy (deploy.yml). That way you can tell at a glance whether code or deployment failed.

    🔐 Environment Variables and Secrets¶

    Never commit keys to the repository. Use environment variables:

    // ❌ Bad
const API_KEY = "sk-abc123...";

// ✅ Good
const API_KEY = process.env.API_KEY;

    In GitHub Actions¶

    1. Repo → Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions.
    2. Add API_KEY with its value.
    3. Use it in the workflow:
    - run: npm run build
  env:
    API_KEY: ${{ secrets.API_KEY }}

    In Vercel / Netlify¶

    Configure them in the web dashboard (Settings → Environment Variables). They are injected at build time and runtime.

    .env never goes into the repo

    Add .env, .env.local, .env.*.local to .gitignore. If you accidentally push one, rotate the keys right away: even if you delete the commit, they remain in Git history.

    🌐 Custom Domain and HTTPS¶

    Custom Domain¶

    1. Buy the domain (Namecheap, Cloudflare Registrar, etc.).
    2. In your platform (Vercel/Netlify), add the domain.
    3. Configure DNS records:
    4. A record → server IP (or ALIAS/ANAME with some providers).
    5. CNAME → www.tudominio.com pointing to the platform host.

    HTTPS¶

    All modern platforms (Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare, GitHub Pages) issue Let's Encrypt certificates automatically. You don't have to do anything.

    If you manage your own server:

    # Install certbot
sudo apt install certbot python3-certbot-nginx

# Issue certificate
sudo certbot --nginx -d tudominio.com -d www.tudominio.com

# Automatic renewal test (cron)
sudo certbot renew --dry-run

    HTTPS is mandatory

    Beyond security, Google penalizes sites without HTTPS in search rankings. Modern browsers also flag them as "Not secure".

    📊 Basic Monitoring¶

    What to Measure?¶

    Metric Tool Threshold
    Uptime UptimeRobot, BetterStack >99.9%
    JS Errors Sentry <0.1% sessions
    Performance Lighthouse, WebPageTest LCP <2.5s
    Traffic Google Analytics, Plausible —
    Logs Platform (Vercel Logs, etc.) —

    Example with Sentry (production errors)¶

    import * as Sentry from "@sentry/browser";

Sentry.init({
    dsn: "https://...@sentry.io/...",
    tracesSampleRate: 0.1,
});

    Automatically captures JS errors in the browser and alerts you via email/Slack.

    🔄 Rollback¶

    If a deploy breaks production, you need to revert to the previous version in seconds.

    Platform Rollback
    Vercel Dashboard → Deployments → Promote previous
    Netlify Deploys → Rollback to this deploy
    GitHub Pages git revert + push (rebuild)
    Cloudflare Pages Deployments → Rollback
    VPS Docker tag / git checkout <tag>

    Version with tags

    Before each major deploy: git tag v1.2.0 && git push --tags. If something breaks, git checkout v1.2.0 and redeploy. It will save you more than once.

    🏗 Typical Full Pipeline¶

    graph LR
    A[git push] --> B[GitHub Actions]
    B --> C[npm test]
    C --> D[npm run build]
    D --> E[Deploy Vercel]
    E --> F[Preview URL]
    F --> G{OK?}
    G -->|Yes| H[Merge to main]
    G -->|No| I[Fix]
    H --> J[Production deploy]
    1. Develop on a branch.
    2. git push → triggers CI.
    3. If it passes, a preview URL is generated.
    4. Review the preview.
    5. Merge into main → deploy to production.

    🧪 Practical Exercise¶

    Deploy a static site to GitHub Pages

    Deploy a static site (HTML + CSS) to GitHub Pages using GitHub Actions.

    Steps: 1. Create a repo with index.html and styles.css. 2. Create .github/workflows/deploy.yml that: - Runs on push to main. - Uses actions/upload-pages-artifact to upload the site folder. - Uses actions/deploy-pages to publish. 3. Enable GitHub Pages in Settings → Pages → Source: GitHub Actions. 4. Push and verify the URL https://tu-usuario.github.io/tu-repo/.

    Solution 
    name: Deploy Pages
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/configure-pages@v5
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: "."
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4

    Note: if your site is at the root of the repo, use path: ".". If it is built into dist/, use path: "dist".

    🧠 Quiz¶

    Check what you learned

    1. What is the difference between static and dynamic hosting?

    Static hosting only serves files (HTML, CSS, JS, images). Dynamic hosting runs server-side code (Node, Python, etc.) and accesses databases.

    2. What is CI/CD?

    Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment. CI: every push builds and tests automatically. CD: if it passes, it deploys automatically.

    3. Why shouldn't you commit .env to the repository?

    Because it contains secrets (API keys, passwords). In Git history they stay forever. Use environment variables on the platform and .gitignore.

    4. How does automatic HTTPS work on Vercel/Netlify?

    The platform issues Let's Encrypt certificates automatically when you add the domain. You don't have to manage anything.

    5. What is a rollback and when do you need it?

    Reverting to the previously deployed version. You need it when a deploy breaks production and you can't fix it in minutes.

    10 — Final Project: Portfolio¶

    What you will learn

    • Plan a real project from start to finish.
    • Structure a professional portfolio.
    • Apply everything learned in previous chapters.
    • Deploy it to production.

    🎯 The Project¶

    You are going to build your personal portfolio: a website that shows who you are, what you know how to do, and what you have built. It is the most important project of the Intermediate Level because it is your introduction to the world.

    Your portfolio is your living résumé

    Recruiters don't read résumés: they look at portfolios. A good portfolio is worth more than 10 certificates.

    📋 Requirements¶

    Your portfolio should include:

    • Hero with your name, role, and a call to action.
    • About me: who you are, what you do, what excites you.
    • Projects: at least 3, with a screenshot, description, and link.
    • Skills: technologies you know well.
    • Contact: email, GitHub, LinkedIn.
    • Responsive design: looks good on mobile and desktop.
    • Dark/light mode (optional, but highly valued).

    ⚡ Step 3: JavaScript (Dark Mode)¶

    const btnTema = document.getElementById('tema');
const temaGuardado = localStorage.getItem('tema');

if (temaGuardado === 'dark') {
  document.documentElement.setAttribute('data-theme', 'dark');
  btnTema.textContent = '☀';
}

btnTema.addEventListener('click', () => {
  const actual = document.documentElement.getAttribute('data-theme');
  const nuevo = actual === 'dark' ? 'light' : 'dark';
  document.documentElement.setAttribute('data-theme', nuevo);
  localStorage.setItem('tema', nuevo);
  btnTema.textContent = nuevo === 'dark' ? '☀' : '🌙';
});

    11 — Modern CSS¶

    What you will learn

    • CSS variables and modern functions.
    • Advanced selectors: :has(), :is(), :where().
    • Container queries.
    • Advanced Grid and subgrid.
    • Animations and transitions.

    🎨 CSS Is Not What It Used to Be¶

    CSS has evolved enormously in recent years. What used to require JavaScript or preprocessors is now native: variables, nesting, math functions, container queries…

    CSS is a programming language (almost)

    Even without loops or functions like JavaScript, modern CSS has variables, conditionals (with @supports and media queries), and functions. It is much more powerful than it looks.

    🔤 CSS Variables¶

    :root {
  --primario: #6a5acd;
  --acento: #00bcd4;
  --espaciado: 1rem;
  --radio: 8px;
}

.boton {
  background: var(--primario);
  padding: var(--espaciado);
  border-radius: var(--radio);
}

    Benefits¶

    • Theming: change one variable and everything updates.
    • Dark mode: redefine variables inside [data-theme="dark"].
    • Readability: descriptive names instead of magic values.
    [data-theme="dark"] {
  --primario: #a78bfa;
  --acento: #22d3ee;
}

    🧮 Modern Functions¶

    calc()¶

    .elemento {
  width: calc(100% - 2rem);
  padding: calc(var(--espaciado) * 2);
}

    clamp()¶

    h1 {
  font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 4vw, 3rem);
}

    clamp(min, ideal, max) is ideal for fluid typography.

    min() and max()¶

    .contenedor {
  width: min(90%, 1200px);
  padding: max(1rem, 2vw);
}

    color-mix()¶

    .boton {
  background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--primario) 80%, white);
}

    🎯 Advanced Selectors¶

    :is()¶

    :is(h1, h2, h3) {
  line-height: 1.2;
}

    :where()¶

    Just like :is(), but with 0 specificity:

    :where(h1, h2, h3) {
  margin: 0;
}

    :has()¶

    Selects an element that contains another:

    .card:has(img) {
  grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr;
}

.form:has(input:invalid) {
  border-color: red;
}

    :has() is a game changer

    Previously you needed JavaScript to style a parent based on its children. With :has() it's pure CSS. It is now supported across all modern browsers.

    :not()¶

    .boton:not(.boton--disabled) {
  cursor: pointer;
}

    📐 Container Queries¶

    Container queries let you apply styles based on the size of the container, not the viewport.

    .card-container {
  container-type: inline-size;
  container-name: card;
}

@container card (min-width: 400px) {
  .card {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr;
  }
}

    The end of media queries for components

    Media queries are still useful for page layouts. But for reusable components, container queries are far more powerful: the same component can look different depending on the space available.

    🔲 Advanced Grid¶

    Grid template areas¶

    .layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-areas:
    "header header"
    "sidebar main"
    "footer footer";
  grid-template-columns: 250px 1fr;
  grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto;
}

.header { grid-area: header; }
.sidebar { grid-area: sidebar; }
.main { grid-area: main; }
.footer { grid-area: footer; }

    Subgrid¶

    .padre {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
}

.hijo {
  display: grid;
  grid-column: span 2;
  grid-template-columns: subgrid;
}

    auto-fit vs auto-fill¶

    /* auto-fit: empty tracks collapse */
.grid { grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr)); }

/* auto-fill: empty tracks stay */
.grid { grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr)); }

    ✨ Animations and Transitions¶

    Transitions¶

    .boton {
  transition: background-color .2s ease, transform .15s ease;
}

.boton:hover {
  background-color: var(--acento);
  transform: translateY(-2px);
}

    Keyframe animations¶

    @keyframes fadeIn {
  from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(10px); }
  to   { opacity: 1; transform: translateY(0); }
}

.animado {
  animation: fadeIn .4s ease forwards;
}

    Respect prefers-reduced-motion¶

    @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after {
    animation-duration: .01ms !important;
    transition-duration: .01ms !important;
  }
}

    Accessibility in animations

    Some people experience motion sickness from animations. Respect prefers-reduced-motion whenever possible.

    2. Which selector styles a parent that contains a specific child?

    3. Which function clamps a value between a minimum and a maximum?

    12 — Asynchronous JavaScript¶

    What you will learn

    • Why asynchrony exists in JavaScript.
    • Callbacks, promises, and async/await.
    • The event loop in depth.
    • Asynchronous error handling.
    • Patterns: Promise.all, Promise.race, Promise.allSettled.

    ⏳ Why Asynchrony?¶

    JavaScript is single-threaded: it can only execute one thing at a time. If an operation takes time (an HTTP request, reading a file, a timer), it would block everything. Asynchrony lets you avoid blocking while waiting.

    // Synchronous: blocks
console.log('1');
console.log('2');
console.log('3');
// Output: 1, 2, 3

// Asynchronous: non-blocking
console.log('1');
setTimeout(() => console.log('2'), 0);
console.log('3');
// Output: 1, 3, 2

    JavaScript waits for no one

    When an asynchronous operation starts, JavaScript keeps running the rest of the code. The operation finishes later and its result is handled with callbacks, promises, or async/await.

    🕰 Callbacks (The Old Way)¶

    function cargarDatos(callback) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    callback({ nombre: 'Ana' });
  }, 1000);
}

cargarDatos(function (datos) {
  console.log(datos); // { nombre: 'Ana' }
});

    The Problem: Callback Hell¶

    cargarUsuario(id, function (usuario) {
  cargarPosts(usuario.id, function (posts) {
    cargarComentarios(posts[0].id, function (comentarios) {
      console.log(comentarios);
    });
  });
});

    This is hard to read and hard to handle errors in. That is why promises were created.

    🤝 Promises¶

    A promise represents a value that will be available in the future. It has three states:

    • Pending: still in progress.
    • Fulfilled: resolved with a value.
    • Rejected: rejected with an error.
    const promesa = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  const exito = true;
  if (exito) resolve('¡Funcionó!');
  else reject(new Error('Algo salió mal'));
});

promesa
  .then(valor => console.log(valor))
  .catch(err => console.error(err));

    Chaining Promises¶

    fetch('/api/usuario')
  .then(res => res.json())
  .then(usuario => fetch('/api/posts/' + usuario.id))
  .then(res => res.json())
  .then(posts => console.log(posts))
  .catch(err => console.error(err));

    Much easier to read than nested callbacks.

    ⚡ async/await¶

    The modern way, syntactic sugar over promises:

    async function cargarDatos() {
  try {
    const res = await fetch('/api/usuario');
    const usuario = await res.json();
    const res2 = await fetch('/api/posts/' + usuario.id);
    const posts = await res2.json();
    console.log(posts);
  } catch (err) {
    console.error(err);
  }
}
    • async marks the function as asynchronous (it always returns a promise).
    • await pauses execution until the promise resolves.

    async/await does not block

    Even though await looks like it blocks, it doesn't: it only pauses that function. The rest of the program keeps running.

    🧠 The Event Loop in Depth¶

    console.log('1');

setTimeout(() => console.log('2'), 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3'));

console.log('4');

// Output: 1, 4, 3, 2

    Why This Order?¶

    1. 1 and 4 are synchronous → they run first.
    2. 3 is a microtask (promise) → it runs before macrotasks.
    3. 2 is a macrotask (setTimeout) → it runs at the end.
    Type Examples Priority
    Call stack Synchronous code 1
    Microtasks Promises, queueMicrotask 2
    Macrotasks setTimeout, setInterval, events 3

    The event loop in one sentence

    The event loop drains the call stack, then all microtasks, then one macrotask. And repeats.

    🎯 Promise Patterns¶

    Promise.all¶

    Waits for all promises to resolve. If one fails, everything fails.

    const [usuarios, posts] = await Promise.all([
  fetch('/api/usuarios').then(r => r.json()),
  fetch('/api/posts').then(r => r.json()),
]);

    Promise.allSettled¶

    Waits for all promises, even if some fail. Returns an array with status and value/reason.

    const resultados = await Promise.allSettled([p1, p2, p3]);
resultados.forEach(r => {
  if (r.status === 'fulfilled') console.log('OK:', r.value);
  else console.error('Error:', r.reason);
});

    Promise.race¶

    Returns the first promise to settle (resolve or reject).

    const resultado = await Promise.race([
  fetch('/api/a'),
  new Promise((_, reject) => setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('Timeout')), 5000)),
]);

    Promise.any¶

    Returns the first promise that fulfills. If all reject, it rejects.

    const primero = await Promise.any([p1, p2, p3]);

    🚨 Error Handling¶

    async function cargar() {
  try {
    const res = await fetch('/api/datos');
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error('HTTP ' + res.status);
    return await res.json();
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('Error:', err.message);
    return null;
  } finally {
    console.log('Terminado');
  }
}

    Don't forget catch

    If you don't catch promise errors, they become unhandled rejections and can crash the app. Always add .catch() or try/catch.

    🧠 Test Your Knowledge¶

    1. Which keyword marks a function as asynchronous?

    2. Which method waits for all promises to finish, even if some fail?

    3. What runs first: a promise or a setTimeout?

    13 — Modules and Bundlers¶

    What you will learn

    • Why modules exist in JavaScript.
    • Differences between CommonJS, ESM, UMD, and AMD.
    • What a bundler is and what problem it solves.
    • Modern bundlers: Vite, esbuild, Rollup, webpack.
    • When to use a bundler and when not to.

    📦 The Module Problem¶

    In 1995, JavaScript didn't have modules. All code lived in the global scope, and any variable could collide with another.

    <script src="a.js"></script>
<script src="b.js"></script>
<!-- If a.js and b.js both define "contador", they overwrite each other -->

    Modules solve this: each file has its own scope, exports what it chooses, and another file explicitly imports it.

    The labeled boxes analogy

    Without modules, all your code is scattered on the living room floor: anyone can step on it, move it, or mix it up. With modules, each piece has its own labeled box, and you only open the box you need.

    graph LR
    A[main.js] -->|imports| B[math.js]
    A -->|imports| C[ui.js]
    C -->|imports| D[api.js]
    B -.exports.-> A
    C -.exports.-> A
    D -.exports.-> C

    🏛 Module Systems¶

    System When Syntax Environment
    CommonJS (CJS) 2009 require / module.exports Classic Node.js
    ES Modules (ESM) 2015 (ES6) import / export Modern Node.js, browsers
    UMD 2011 define(...) or global Universal libraries
    AMD 2010 define(...) Legacy (RequireJS)

    CommonJS (Classic Node)¶

    // math.js
function sumar(a, b) {
    return a + b;
}
module.exports = { sumar };

// main.js
const { sumar } = require("./math.js");
console.log(sumar(2, 3));

    ES Modules (Modern Standard)¶

    // math.js
export function sumar(a, b) {
    return a + b;
}
export const PI = 3.1416;

// main.js
import { sumar, PI } from "./math.js";
console.log(sumar(2, 3), PI);

    ESM is the future (and the present)

    All modern browsers support ESM natively (<script type="module">). Node.js does too since v12+. Use ESM in new projects.

    Key Differences¶

    Aspect CommonJS ESM
    Loading Synchronous Asynchronous
    import Evaluated when require runs Hoisted (resolved beforehand)
    Top-level this module.exports undefined
    Top-level await ❌ No ✅ Yes (Node 14+, browsers)
    __dirname ✅ Yes ❌ No (use import.meta.url)
    Tree-shaking ❌ Hard ✅ Yes (static)

    🛠 What is a Bundler?¶

    A bundler takes all your modules and dependencies and packages them into one or a few files that the browser can load.

    What Does It Do Exactly?¶

    1. Resolves imports: knows where ./utils or react lives.
    2. Transpiles: converts TS, JSX, SCSS into JS/CSS.
    3. Optimizes: minifies, removes dead code (tree-shaking).
    4. Bundles: generates dist/main.js ready for production.
    5. Emits assets: copies images, fonts, etc.
    6. HMR (optional): hot module replacement on save.
    graph LR
    A[main.js] --> B[Bundler]
    C[utils.js] --> B
    D[styles.css] --> B
    E[imagen.png] --> B
    B --> F[dist/main.hash.js]
    B --> G[dist/style.hash.css]
    B --> H[dist/imagen.hash.png]

    What about no bundler?

    You can use native ESM with <script type="module"> and skip a bundler. However: - Every file is an extra HTTP request. - No tree-shaking. - You can't use TypeScript, JSX, or SCSS without transpiling. - No minification.

    For small projects it works fine. For large apps, a bundler is almost mandatory.

    🚀 Modern Bundlers¶

    Bundler Speed Config Best for
    Vite ⚡ Very fast (esbuild + Rollup) Minimal SPAs, React, Vue, Svelte, Vanilla
    esbuild ⚡ Fastest (Go) Minimal Libraries, CLIs, fast builds
    Rollup 🚀 Fast Medium Libraries (best tree-shaking)
    webpack 🐢 Slow High Legacy, very specific cases
    Parcel 🚀 Fast Zero config Prototypes, simple projects
    Rspack / Turbopack ⚡ Very fast Low Modern webpack alternatives

    2026 Recommendation

    • New app → Vite (or whichever bundler your framework ships with).
    • Library → Rollup or tsup (powered by esbuild).
    • Legacy webpack → only if required by the project.

    Vite in 30 Seconds¶

    npm create vite@latest mi-app -- --template react
cd mi-app
npm install
npm run dev

    # vite.config.js — minimal
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react";

export default defineConfig({
    plugins: [react()],
});

    Why Vite is fast: - Dev: serves modules unbundled (using native browser ESM). Millisecond startup. - Build: uses Rollup for production (optimal tree-shaking). - HMR: only reloads the changed module, not the whole page.

    📦 Tree-shaking¶

    Tree-shaking = removing unused code. The bundler analyzes which imports are actually used and drops the rest.

    // utils.js
export function sumar(a, b) { return a + b; }
export function restar(a, b) { return a - b; }
export function multiplicar(a, b) { return a * b; }

// main.js
import { sumar } from "./utils.js";
console.log(sumar(2, 3));
// restar and multiplicar are removed from the bundle

    Requirements: - ESM (bundlers cannot tree-shake CommonJS). - No side effects (sideEffects: false in package.json). - Pure functions (without mutating global state).

    The enemy of tree-shaking

    import * as utils from "./utils" prevents tree-shaking (it imports everything). Use import { sumar } from "./utils". And avoid hidden side effects (such as modifying window on import).

    🧩 Code Splitting¶

    Code splitting = splitting the bundle into chunks loaded on demand.

    // ❌ Everything in the main bundle
import { Chart } from "chart.js";

// ✅ Load only when needed
button.addEventListener("click", async () => {
    const { Chart } = await import("chart.js");
    new Chart(ctx, config);
});

    When to split: - Routes (lazy loading per page). - Heavy modals and components. - Large libraries (chart.js, monaco, mapbox). - Features not every user uses.

    Vite/Rollup does this automatically with dynamic import() and generates separate chunks.

    // React.lazy (React)
import { lazy, Suspense } from "react";

const Dashboard = lazy(() => import("./pages/Dashboard"));

function App() {
    return (
        <Suspense fallback={<p>Cargando…</p>}>
            <Dashboard />
        </Suspense>
    );
}

    🌐 ESM in the Browser (No Bundler)¶

    <script type="module" src="/main.js"></script>

    // main.js
import { sumar } from "./utils.js";
console.log(sumar(2, 3));

    Pros: - Zero configuration. - Works in all modern browsers. - Great for small projects or prototypes.

    Cons: - Each file = 1 HTTP request. - No tree-shaking or minification. - No transpilation (TS, JSX don't run directly).

    The middle ground

    For a 3-page site, native ESM is enough. For an SPA with 50 components and TypeScript, you need a bundler.

    🏗 Example: Comparing Bundles¶

    Project Without bundler With Vite (build)
    10 JS files, 50 KB total 10 requests, unminified 1 file, ~20 KB minified
    50 React components Impossible without transpiling 1 bundle + chunks, tree-shaking
    100 npm libraries Impossible (no node_modules in browser) 1 bundle with everything resolved

    🧪 Practical Exercise¶

    Create a project with Vite

    Create a vanilla project with Vite that:

    • Displays "Hola, Vite" in the DOM.
    • Imports a saludar(nombre) function from ./saludar.js.
    • Has HMR working (when you change the text, it updates).

    Follow these steps: 1. npm create vite@latest mi-vite -- --template vanilla 2. cd mi-vite && npm install 3. Create saludar.js with export function saludar(n) { return "Hola, " + n; } 4. Import it in main.js and display the result. 5. Run npm run dev and test HMR.

    Solution 
    // saludar.js
export function saludar(nombre) {
    return `Hola, ${nombre}`;
}

    // main.js
import "./style.css";
import { saludar } from "./saludar.js";

document.querySelector("#app").innerHTML = `
    <h1>${saludar("Vite")}</h1>
`;

    HMR: with npm run dev, when you edit saludar.js or main.js, the browser updates without reloading the page.

    🧠 Quiz¶

    Check what you learned

    1. What is the difference between CommonJS and ESM?

    CommonJS uses require and module.exports, is synchronous, and belongs to classic Node.js. ESM uses import and export, is asynchronous, hoists imports, and supports top-level await and tree-shaking.

    2. What does a bundler do?

    Resolves imports, transpiles (TS, JSX, SCSS), minifies, performs tree-shaking, bundles into one or a few files, and copies assets.

    3. Why is Vite so fast in development?

    Because it serves modules unbundled using native browser ESM. It only bundles for production builds (with Rollup).

    4. What is tree-shaking?

    Removing unused code from the final bundle. It requires ESM and pure functions without side effects.

    5. What is code splitting?

    Splitting the bundle into chunks loaded on demand (via dynamic import()), reducing initial load time.

    • Vite — Docs
    • Rollup — Docs
    • esbuild — Docs
    • webpack — Docs
    • Node.js — ESM
    • web.dev — Reduce JavaScript payloads
