    14 — Web Accessibility¶

    What you will learn

    • What accessibility is and why it is mandatory.
    • The WCAG guidelines.
    • Semantic HTML and ARIA.
    • Keyboard navigation.
    • Contrast and auditing tools.

    ♿ What is Accessibility?¶

    Web accessibility (a11y) is the practice of designing websites that anyone can use, including people with visual, auditory, motor, or cognitive disabilities.

    Not an extra, it is part of the job

    Accessibility is not a checkbox you tick at the end. It is a way of thinking about development from the very first div.

    📜 The WCAG Guidelines¶

    WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) are the international standard. They have three levels:

    Level Description
    A Minimum level. Legally required in many countries.
    AA Recommended level. The standard target.
    AAA Maximum level. Very hard to meet at 100%.

    The four principles of WCAG (POUR):

    1. Perceivable: information must be presented in ways everyone can perceive.
    2. Operable: the interface must be usable with a keyboard or other devices.
    3. Understandable: content and interface must be easy to understand.
    4. Robust: must work reliably with different assistive technologies.

    🏗 Semantic HTML¶

    Semantic HTML is the foundation of accessibility. Screen readers understand it.

    <!-- Correct -->
<button onclick="enviar()">Send</button>
<nav><a href="/inicio">Home</a></nav>
<main><h1>Title</h1></main>

<!-- Incorrect -->
<div onclick="enviar()">Send</div>
<div class="nav"><a href="/inicio">Home</a></div>

    A div is not a button

    A div with onclick is not accessible: it cannot be focused with Tab, cannot be activated with Enter, and screen readers don't announce it as a button. Use button.

    🏷 ARIA: When and How to Use It¶

    ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) are attributes that add semantics to elements that HTML doesn't cover on its own.

    <div role="alert">Error: incorrect password</div>
<button aria-label="Close menu">✕</button>
<nav aria-label="Main navigation">...</nav>

    Golden rule of ARIA

    Don't use ARIA if you can use native HTML. A button already has an implicit role=button. Use ARIA only when there is no other option.

    ⌨ Keyboard Navigation¶

    Every website must be usable with the keyboard alone. Test navigating with Tab, Enter, Escape, and the arrow keys.

    /* Never remove outline without replacing it */
:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid #6a5acd;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

    Test with Tab

    Open your site and press Tab repeatedly. Can you see where focus is? Can you reach all buttons and links? If not, you have an accessibility issue.

    🎨 Color Contrast¶

    Contrast between text and background must meet WCAG AA:

    Element Minimum ratio
    Normal text 4.5:1
    Large text (18pt+ or 14pt+ bold) 3:1
    UI components (borders, icons) 3:1

    Tools to check it:

    • WebAIM Contrast Checker
    • Coolors Contrast Checker
    • Lighthouse (in Chrome DevTools)

    📝 Accessible Forms¶

    <label for="email">Email:</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email" required
       aria-describedby="email-error">
<small id="email-error" class="error">Enter a valid email</small>

    Best practices:

    • ✅ Associate every input with a <label>.
    • ✅ Use aria-describedby for error messages.
    • ✅ Mark required fields with required.
    • ✅ Group related fields with <fieldset> and <legend>.
    • ✅ Give clear feedback when something fails.

    Placeholder is not a label

    Placeholders disappear when typing and aren't read by all screen readers. Always use a visible label.

    🖼 Images and Media¶

    <!-- Informative image -->
<img src="grafico.png" alt="Quarterly sales: 40% in January, 35% in February, 25% in March">

<!-- Decorative image -->
<img src="decoracion.png" alt="">

<!-- Video with captions -->
<video controls>
  <source src="video.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  <track kind="captions" src="subtitulos.vtt" srclang="es" label="Español">
</video>

    The right alt

    • If the image conveys information, describe what information it conveys.
    • If it is decorative, use alt="" (empty).
    • Don't start with "Image of..." (screen readers already announce it).

    🔍 Auditing Tools¶

    Tool What it measures
    Lighthouse (Chrome DevTools) Accessibility, performance, SEO, PWA
    axe DevTools Detailed accessibility errors
    WAVE Visual accessibility evaluation
    Pa11y Command-line auditing
    Screen Reader (NVDA, VoiceOver) How a blind person perceives it

    Test with a screen reader

    Nothing replaces testing your site with a real screen reader. On Linux you can use Orca, on Windows NVDA (free), and on macOS VoiceOver (built-in).

    🧠 Test Your Knowledge¶

    1. What does WCAG stand for?

    2. What minimum contrast ratio does WCAG AA require for normal text?

    3. When should you use aria-label?

    15 — TypeScript from Scratch¶

    What you will learn

    • What TypeScript is and why to use it.
    • Basic types and annotations.
    • Interfaces and custom types.
    • Generics.
    • Configuring tsconfig.json.

    🔷 What is TypeScript?¶

    TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript that adds static types. The code compiles to plain JavaScript before running in the browser or in Node.js.

    function sumar(a: number, b: number): number {
  return a + b;
}

sumar(2, 3);      // OK
sumar("2", "3");  // Type error

    Types are documentation that doesn't lie

    A mistyped value never reaches production: the compiler warns you first. That saves hours of debugging.

    🎯 Why Use TypeScript?¶

    Benefit Description
    Early error detection The compiler warns before execution.
    Autocomplete The editor knows what properties each object has.
    Safe refactoring Changing a type flags every affected spot.
    Living documentation Types document the intent of the code.
    Better teamwork Contracts between modules are explicit.

    📦 Basic Types¶

    // Primitives
let nombre: string = "Ana";
let edad: number = 30;
let activo: boolean = true;

// Arrays
let numeros: number[] = [1, 2, 3];
let nombres: Array<string> = ["Ana", "Luis"];

// Tuples
let coordenadas: [number, number] = [40.4, -3.7];

// Any (avoid)
let cualquiera: any = "can be anything";

// Unknown (safer than any)
let desconocido: unknown = obtenerAlgo();

// Void (functions with no return)
function log(mensaje: string): void {
  console.log(mensaje);
}

// Null and undefined
let nulo: null = null;
let indefinido: undefined = undefined;

    🏗 Interfaces and Types¶

    interface Usuario {
  id: number;
  nombre: string;
  email: string;
  edad?: number; // optional
}

const usuario: Usuario = {
  id: 1,
  nombre: "Ana",
  email: "ana@ejemplo.com"
};

    Type vs. interface¶

    // With type
type Punto = {
  x: number;
  y: number;
};

// With interface (extensible)
interface PuntoConZ extends Punto {
  z: number;
}

    type or interface

    Use interface for objects that can be extended. Use type for unions, intersections, and primitive type aliases.

    🔀 Unions and Intersections¶

    // Union: can be one or the other
type Estado = "pendiente" | "en-progreso" | "completado";

let tarea: Estado = "pendiente";
tarea = "completado"; // OK
tarea = "cancelado"; // Error

// Intersection: must have both
type Persona = { nombre: string };
type Trabajador = { empresa: string };
type Empleado = Persona & Trabajador;

    🧬 Generics¶

    Generics let you write functions and types that work with any type while preserving type safety.

    function identidad<T>(valor: T): T {
  return valor;
}

identidad<string>("hola");  // string
identidad<number>(42);      // number
identidad(true);            // boolean (inferred)

    Generics in Interfaces¶

    interface Respuesta<T> {
  data: T;
  error: string | null;
}

const respuesta: Respuesta<Usuario> = {
  data: { id: 1, nombre: "Ana", email: "ana@ejemplo.com" },
  error: null
};

    ⚙ tsconfig.json¶

    {
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "ESNext",
    "strict": true,
    "esModuleInterop": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "forceConsistentCasingInFileNames": true,
    "outDir": "./dist",
    "rootDir": "./src"
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*"]
}

    strict: true

    Turn on strict: true from day one. It's stricter, but it saves you from bugs. You can relax it later if needed.

cd mi-app
npm install
npm run dev

    With Node.js¶

    npm install -D typescript @types/node tsx
npx tsc --init
npx tsx src/index.ts

    🔵 Nivel 4 — Testing y Arquitectura

    16 — Frontend Testing¶

    What you will learn

    • Why testing matters.
    • Test types: unit, integration, E2E.
    • Vitest: the modern testing framework.
    • Testing Library: testing like a user.
    • Testing best practices.

    🧪 Why Test?¶

    Automated tests let you change code without fear. If something breaks, the test warns you before it reaches production.

    Tests are your safety net

    Without tests, every change is a gamble. With tests, every change is a verification.

    📊 The Testing Pyramid¶

            /\
       /E2E\      <- few, slow, brittle
      /------\
     /Integrat.\  <- some, faster
    /------------\
   /     Unit     \ <- many, fast, isolated
  /----------------\
    Type What it tests Speed Volume
    Unit A single function or isolated component ⚡ Very fast Many
    Integration Multiple modules working together 🚀 Fast Some
    E2E The full app in a real browser 🐢 Slow Few

    ⚡ Vitest¶

    Vitest is the modern testing framework built on Vite. It is blazing fast and compatible with the Jest API.

    npm install -D vitest

    Your First Test¶

    // sumar.js
export function sumar(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}

// sumar.test.js
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { sumar } from "./sumar.js";

describe("sumar", () => {
  it("adds two positive numbers", () => {
    expect(sumar(2, 3)).toBe(5);
  });

  it("adds negative numbers", () => {
    expect(sumar(-2, -3)).toBe(-5);
  });

  it("adds zero", () => {
    expect(sumar(0, 5)).toBe(5);
  });
});

    Running Tests¶

    npx vitest          # watch mode
npx vitest run      # single run
npx vitest --coverage # with coverage

    🎯 Most Used Matchers¶

    Matcher What it checks
    toBe(value) Strict equality (===)
    toEqual(value) Deep equality (objects, arrays)
    toBeTruthy() Truthy value
    toBeFalsy() Falsy value
    toContain(item) Array or string contains item
    toThrow() Function throws an error
    toHaveLength(n) Length
    toMatch(regex) Matches regex

    🧩 Testing Library¶

    Testing Library helps you test components like a real user, not like a programmer.

    npm install -D @testing-library/dom @testing-library/user-event

    import { screen } from "@testing-library/dom";
import userEvent from "@testing-library/user-event";

// Your component HTML
document.body.innerHTML = `
  <button id="btn">Click me</button>
  <p id="resultado">0</p>
`;

let clicks = 0;
document.getElementById("btn").addEventListener("click", () => {
  clicks++;
  document.getElementById("resultado").textContent = clicks;
});

// Test
const btn = screen.getByText("Click me");
await userEvent.click(btn);
expect(screen.getByText("1")).toBeTruthy();

    Test like a user

    Don't test implementation details (variable names, DOM structure). Test what the user sees and does: text, roles, clicks.

    🎭 E2E Testing with Playwright¶

    Playwright lets you automate a real browser: open pages, click, fill forms, and verify results.

    npm install -D @playwright/test
npx playwright install

    // tests/ejemplo.spec.js
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("login flow", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("[https://mi-app.com/login](https://mi-app.com/login)");
  await page.fill("#email", "ana@ejemplo.com");
  await page.fill("#password", "12345678");
  await page.click("button[type=submit]");
  await expect(page).toHaveURL("[https://mi-app.com/dashboard](https://mi-app.com/dashboard)");
  await expect(page.locator("h1")).toContainText("Welcome");
});

    Running Tests¶

    npx playwright test
npx playwright test --ui
npx playwright show-report

    Playwright vs. Cypress

    Both are great. Playwright supports more browsers (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit), is faster, and has a better API for parallel testing. Cypress has a nicer DX for visual debugging.

    ✅ Testing Best Practices¶

    • ✅ Test behavior, not implementation. If you refactor and tests fail, they are poorly written.
    • ✅ One test, one thing. If a test checks 5 things, when it fails you won't know what broke.
    • ✅ Descriptive names. "should add two positive numbers" is better than "test 1".
    • ✅ Follow the AAA pattern: Arrange, Act, Assert.
    • ✅ Test edge cases: empty, null, undefined, negative, very large.
    • ✅ Don't test the library. Don't test that Array.push works.
    • ❌ Don't chase 100% coverage. 80% done well is worth more than 100% done poorly.

    📊 Test Coverage¶

    npx vitest run --coverage
    Metric What it measures
    Statements Executed statements
    Branches Covered if/else branches
    Functions Called functions
    Lines Covered lines

    Coverage isn't everything

    100% coverage does not mean good tests. You can have a test that runs a line without asserting its result.

    ⚡ Modern Testing with Vitest¶

    Vitest is the testing framework that has become the standard for Vite projects. It is fast, compatible with the Jest API, and works with zero configuration.

    Installation¶

    npm install -D vitest @testing-library/dom @testing-library/user-event jsdom

    Basic Configuration (vite.config.js)¶

    import { defineConfig } from "vite";

export default defineConfig({
    test: {
        environment: "jsdom",   // simulates browser DOM
        globals: true,          // describe, it, expect without importing
        coverage: {
            provider: "v8",
            reporter: ["text", "html"],
        },
    },
});

    Your First Test with Vitest¶

    // sumar.js
export function sumar(a, b) {
    return a + b;
}

// sumar.test.js
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { sumar } from "./sumar.js";

describe("sumar", () => {
    it("adds two positive numbers", () => {
        expect(sumar(2, 3)).toBe(5);
    });

    it("adds negative numbers", () => {
        expect(sumar(-1, -2)).toBe(-3);
    });

    it("adds zero", () => {
        expect(sumar(0, 5)).toBe(5);
    });
});

    Run it:

    npx vitest          # watch mode
npx vitest run      # single run (CI)
npx vitest --ui     # graphical UI

    Vitest vs. Jest

    Vitest is much faster than Jest in Vite projects (it doesn't transpile with Babel). The API is nearly identical, so migrating is trivial. If you start a new project with Vite, use Vitest.

    🧪 Component Testing with Testing Library¶

    Testing Library is the standard library for testing components from the user's perspective. It doesn't test implementation, it tests behavior.

    Plain DOM Example¶

    // contador.js
export function crearContador(container) {
    let n = 0;
    const boton = document.createElement("button");
    const display = document.createElement("span");

    boton.textContent = "Increment";
    display.textContent = n;
    boton.addEventListener("click", () => {
        n++;
        display.textContent = n;
    });

    container.appendChild(boton);
    container.appendChild(display);
}

// contador.test.js
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { screen } from "@testing-library/dom";
import userEvent from "@testing-library/user-event";
import { crearContador } from "./contador.js";

describe("contador", () => {
    it("increments on click", async () => {
        const container = document.createElement("div");
        crearContador(container);
        document.body.appendChild(container);

        const boton = screen.getByRole("button", { name: /increment/i });
        expect(screen.getByText("0")).toBeTruthy();

        await userEvent.click(boton);
        expect(screen.getByText("1")).toBeTruthy();
    });
});

    Recommended Queries (By Priority)¶

    Query When to use it
    getByRole ✅ First (buttons, links, headings)
    getByLabelText Forms with labels
    getByPlaceholderText Inputs without labels (less accessible)
    getByText Visible text
    getByTestId When there is no other option (last resort)

    Don't test implementation

    ❌ expect(component.state.count).toBe(1) — tests internal state. ✅ expect(screen.getByText("1")).toBeTruthy() — tests what the user sees. If you change internal state but behavior stays the same, the test shouldn't break.

    🎭 Mocking: Simulating Dependencies¶

    Mocking means replacing a real dependency (API, database, module) with a controlled fake. It is key for testing without relying on external services.

    Mocking Functions with vi.fn()¶

    import { vi, describe, it, expect } from "vitest";

const enviarEmail = vi.fn(() => Promise.resolve({ ok: true }));

describe("registro", () => {
    it("sends email when registering a user", async () => {
        await registrarUsuario({ email: "ana@example.com" }, enviarEmail);

        expect(enviarEmail).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
        expect(enviarEmail).toHaveBeenCalledWith("ana@example.com");
    });
});

    Mocking Modules with vi.mock()¶

    import { vi, describe, it, expect } from "vitest";

// Mock the full module before importing the consumer
vi.mock("./api.js", () => ({
    obtenerUsuario: vi.fn(() => Promise.resolve({ id: 1, nombre: "Ana" })),
}));

import { obtenerUsuario } from "./api.js";
import { cargarPerfil } from "./perfil.js";

describe("perfil", () => {
    it("loads user profile", async () => {
        const perfil = await cargarPerfil(1);
        expect(perfil.nombre).toBe("Ana");
        expect(obtenerUsuario).toHaveBeenCalledWith(1);
    });
});

    Mocking fetch (Real API)¶

    import { vi, describe, it, expect, beforeEach } from "vitest";

beforeEach(() => {
    global.fetch = vi.fn(() =>
        Promise.resolve({
            ok: true,
            json: () => Promise.resolve({ id: 1, nombre: "Ana" }),
        })
    );
});

it("fetches user from API", async () => {
    const user = await fetchUsuario(1);
    expect(user.nombre).toBe("Ana");
    expect(fetch).toHaveBeenCalledWith("/api/usuarios/1");
});

    Mock the minimum necessary

    Mocking everything makes tests brittle. Mock only what is slow, expensive, or non-deterministic (APIs, dates, Math.random, localStorage).

    📊 Test Coverage¶

    Coverage measures what percentage of code your tests execute. It isn't a perfect metric (100% coverage doesn't mean 0 bugs), but it helps spot untested areas.

    npx vitest run --coverage

    Typical output:

    Recommended Thresholds¶

    Project Minimum coverage
    Prototype 30-50%
    Personal project 60-70%
    Production 80%+
    Library 90%+

    Coverage isn't everything

    A test can run a line without asserting anything. Coverage measures execution, not quality. Combine it with tests that verify real behavior.

    🧠 Review Quiz¶

    Check what you learned

    1. What advantage does Vitest have over Jest?

    It is much faster in Vite projects (no Babel transpilation) and its API is nearly identical to Jest, so migrating is trivial.

    2. Why is getByRole the recommended query?

    Because it tests from the user's perspective and verifies accessibility. If a button has role="button" and an accessible name, screen readers can use it.

    3. What is mocking and when should you do it?

    Replacing a real dependency with a controlled fake. Use it for slow dependencies (APIs), expensive ones (payment services), or non-deterministic ones (dates, Math.random).

    4. What does 100% coverage mean?

    That your tests execute every line of code. It doesn't mean there are no bugs: a test can execute a line without checking its result.

    17 — Web Performance¶

    What you will learn

    • Why performance matters (business, UX, SEO).
    • Core Web Vitals: LCP, INP, CLS.
    • How to measure performance.
    • Optimizing images, fonts, CSS, and JS.
    • Advanced techniques: lazy loading, code splitting, critical CSS.

    ⚡ Why Does Performance Matter?¶

    Web performance is not a technical luxury: it is money. A one-second delay can cut conversions by 7%. Google penalizes slow sites in search rankings.

    Every millisecond counts

    Amazon calculated that 100 ms of latency cost them 1% in sales. Performance is not optional.

    📊 Core Web Vitals¶

    Google measures three key metrics for SEO:

    Metric What it measures Target
    LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) When the largest visible element loads less than 2.5 s
    INP (Interaction to Next Paint) Interaction latency less than 200 ms
    CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) Unexpected layout shifts less than 0.1

    How to Measure Them¶

    # Lighthouse (Chrome DevTools)
F12 -> Lighthouse -> Analyze page load

# PageSpeed Insights
[https://pagespeed.web.dev/](https://pagespeed.web.dev/)

    🖼 Image Optimization¶

    Images make up 60% of the weight of a typical website. Optimizing them has the biggest impact.

    <img
  src="foto-800.webp"
  srcset="foto-400.webp 400w, foto-800.webp 800w, foto-1600.webp 1600w"
  sizes="(max-width: 600px) 400px, (max-width: 1200px) 800px, 1600px"
  alt="Description"
  loading="lazy"
  decoding="async"
  width="800"
  height="600"
>

    Modern Formats¶

    Format Advantage
    WebP 25-35% lighter than JPG/PNG
    AVIF 50% lighter than JPG, better quality
    SVG Vector-based, ideal for icons and logos

    Compression tools

    • Squoosh — compress images in the browser.
    • TinyPNG — PNG/JPG compression.
    • SVGOMG — optimize SVGs.

    🔤 Font Optimization¶

    @font-face {
  font-family: "Inter";
  src: url("/fonts/inter.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-display: swap;
  font-weight: 100 900;
}
    • font-display: swap: shows text with the fallback font while the custom font loads.
    • WOFF2: lightest format, supported by all modern browsers.
    • Preload the critical font with link rel=preload.

    Every font weighs

    Each custom font weighs between 20 and 200 KB. Limit the number of font families and weights to what is strictly necessary.

    🎨 CSS Optimization¶

    • Minify CSS in production.
    • Critical CSS: inline critical CSS (above the fold) and load the rest with loadCSS.
    • Remove unused CSS: tools like PurgeCSS.
    • Avoid @import in CSS: it blocks loading in a waterfall.
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles.css" media="print" onload="this.media='all'">
<noscript><link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles.css"></noscript>

    ⚡ JavaScript Optimization¶

    • Minify and compress (gzip/brotli).
    • Code splitting: load only the JS needed for each page.
    • Tree shaking: remove unused code.
    • Defer scripts: <script defer> or <script async>.
    • Avoid huge libraries for small tasks (moment.js → date-fns, lodash → lodash-es).
    <script src="/app.js" defer></script>
    • defer: downloads in parallel and runs after HTML parsing (in order).
    • async: downloads in parallel and runs as soon as ready (out of order).

    🚀 Lazy Loading¶

    Load resources only when needed, not beforehand.

    <!-- Images -->
<img src="foto.jpg" alt="Description" loading="lazy">

<!-- Iframes (videos, maps) -->
<iframe src="[https://youtube.com/embed/](https://youtube.com/embed/)..." loading="lazy"></iframe>

<!-- JS components -->
<script>
  document.getElementById("btn").addEventListener("click", async () => {
    const { abrirModal } = await import("./modal.js");
    abrirModal();
  });
</script>

    🏎 Advanced Techniques¶

    Technique What it does
    Preload Downloads a high-priority resource before it is needed
    Prefetch Downloads a resource likely needed for the next navigation
    Preconnect Opens a connection to an external domain before needing it
    Service Worker Caches resources for offline and instant loading
    CDN Serves assets from the server closest to the user 
    <link rel="preconnect" href="[https://fonts.googleapis.com](https://fonts.googleapis.com)">
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>
<link rel="prefetch" href="/proxima-pagina.html">

    18 — Frontend Architecture¶

    What you will learn

    • What frontend architecture is and why it matters.
    • Folder structures: feature-first vs. layer-first.
    • Component patterns.
    • State management.
    • Best practices for scalable projects.

    🏗 What is Frontend Architecture?¶

    Frontend architecture is how you organize an application's code so it stays maintainable, scalable, and easy to understand. It isn't about adding more libraries—it's about making decisions that let the project grow without collapsing.

    Code is read many more times than it is written

    Good architecture makes code easy to read, change, and test. Bad architecture makes every change a nightmare.

    📁 Folder Structure¶

    Layer-first (By Layer)¶

    src/
├── components/
├── hooks/
├── services/
├── utils/
├── pages/
└── styles/

    Pros: easy to find things by type. Cons: each feature is spread across 5 folders.

    Feature-first (By Feature)¶

    src/
├── features/
│   ├── auth/
│   │   ├── components/
│   │   ├── hooks/
│   │   ├── api.js
│   │   └── auth.test.js
│   ├── carrito/
│   └── productos/
├── shared/
│   ├── components/
│   └── utils/
└── app/
    ├── routes.js
    └── layout.js

    Pros: each feature lives together. Cons: more folders at the start.

    Feature-first for large projects

    If the project will grow, use feature-first. If it's small, layer-first is enough. You can start with layer-first and migrate as the project grows.

    🧩 Component Patterns¶

    Presentational Components¶

    Only receive props and render UI. They have no business logic.

    function Boton({ texto, onClick }) {
  return <button onClick={onClick}>{texto}</button>;
}

    Container Components¶

    Manage state and logic, and pass props to presentational components.

    function ListaTareas() {
  const [tareas, setTareas] = useState([]);

  const añadir = (texto) => {
    setTareas([...tareas, { id: Date.now(), texto }]);
  };

  return <ListaTareasUI onAñadir="{añadir}" tareas="{tareas}"/>;
}

    Separate logic and presentation

    Separating presentation and logic makes components easier to test, reuse, and understand.

    🗃 State Management¶

    Local State¶

    For things that only affect one component (an input, a toggle).

    const [abierto, setAbierto] = useState(false);

    Shared State¶

    For things that affect several nearby components: lift state up to their common parent.

    Global State¶

    For things that affect the whole app: theme, authenticated user, cart.

    Tool When to use it
    Context API Simple state, low update frequency
    Zustand Simple global state without boilerplate
    Redux Toolkit Complex state with many actions
    TanStack Query Server state (fetch, cache, refetch)

    ✅ Architecture Best Practices¶

    • ✅ Small components: if a component exceeds 200 lines, split it up.
    • ✅ One responsibility per file: one component, one hook, one function.
    • ✅ Descriptive names: BotonPrimario is better than Btn1.
    • ✅ Avoid logic inside JSX: extract helper functions.
    • ✅ Use TypeScript: types document the architecture.
    • ✅ Tests near the code: Boton.test.jsx right next to Boton.jsx.
    • ✅ Use barrel files sparingly: index.js re-exports can slow down builds.
    • ❌ Don't overuse global state: if only one component uses it, keep it local.
    • ❌ Don't mix business logic with UI: use hooks or services.

    🧱 Complete Architecture Example¶

    src/
├── app/
│   ├── App.jsx
│   ├── routes.jsx
│   └── providers.jsx
├── features/
│   ├── auth/
│   │   ├── components/
│   │   │   ├── LoginForm.jsx
│   │   │   └── LoginForm.test.jsx
│   │   ├── hooks/
│   │   │   └── useAuth.js
│   │   ├── api.js
│   │   └── index.js
│   └── carrito/
│       ├── components/
│       ├── hooks/
│       └── api.js
├── shared/
│   ├── components/
│   │   ├── Button.jsx
│   │   └── Modal.jsx
│   ├── hooks/
│   └── utils/
└── styles/
    └── global.css

    19 — Full-Stack with Node.js¶

    What you will learn

    • What Node.js is and why it is used on the server.
    • Creating an HTTP server with Express.
    • Routes, middlewares, and controllers.
    • Databases with PostgreSQL and Prisma.
    • Authentication with JWT.

    🟢 What is Node.js?¶

    Node.js is a runtime environment that lets you run JavaScript outside the browser, on the server. It uses Chrome's V8 engine and a non-blocking I/O model.

    node --version   # v20.x or higher
npm --version

    JavaScript everywhere

    With Node.js you can use the same language on the frontend and backend. That reduces cognitive load and makes sharing code easier.

    ⚡ Your First Server with Express¶

    mkdir mi-api && cd mi-api
npm init -y
npm install express

    // index.js
import express from "express";

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

app.get("/", (req, res) => {
  res.json({ mensaje: "Hola, mundo" });
});

app.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log("Servidor en http://localhost:3000");
});

    node index.js

    🛣 Routes and Middlewares¶

    app.get("/usuarios", (req, res) => {
  res.json([{ id: 1, nombre: "Ana" }]);
});

app.get("/usuarios/:id", (req, res) => {
  const { id } = req.params;
  res.json({ id, nombre: "Ana" });
});

app.post("/usuarios", (req, res) => {
  const { nombre } = req.body;
  res.status(201).json({ id: Date.now(), nombre });
});

app.delete("/usuarios/:id", (req, res) => {
  res.status(204).end();
});

    Logging Middleware¶

    app.use((req, res, next) => {
  console.log(`${req.method} ${req.url}`);
  next();
});

    Error Middleware¶

    app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  console.error(err);
  res.status(500).json({ error: "Algo salió mal" });
});

    🗄 Database with Prisma¶

    npm install prisma @prisma/client
npx prisma init

    // prisma/schema.prisma
model Usuario {
  id        Int      @id @default(autoincrement())
  nombre    String
  email     String   @unique
  password  String
  creadoEn  DateTime @default(now())
}

    npx prisma migrate dev --name init
npx prisma generate

    import { PrismaClient } from "@prisma/client";
const prisma = new PrismaClient();

app.get("/usuarios", async (req, res) => {
  const usuarios = await prisma.usuario.findMany();
  res.json(usuarios);
});

    🔐 Authentication with JWT¶

    npm install jsonwebtoken bcryptjs

    import jwt from "jsonwebtoken";
import bcrypt from "bcryptjs";

const SECRET = process.env.JWT_SECRET;

// Register
app.post("/registro", async (req, res) => {
  const { nombre, email, password } = req.body;
  const hash = await bcrypt.hash(password, 10);
  const usuario = await prisma.usuario.create({
    data: { nombre, email, password: hash }
  });
  res.status(201).json({ id: usuario.id });
});

// Login
app.post("/login", async (req, res) => {
  const { email, password } = req.body;
  const usuario = await prisma.usuario.findUnique({ where: { email } });
  if (!usuario) return res.status(401).json({ error: "Credenciales inválidas" });

  const valido = await bcrypt.compare(password, usuario.password);
  if (!valido) return res.status(401).json({ error: "Credenciales inválidas" });

  const token = jwt.sign({ id: usuario.id }, SECRET, { expiresIn: "7d" });
  res.json({ token });
});

    Authentication Middleware¶

    function auth(req, res, next) {
  const header = req.headers.authorization;
  if (!header) return res.status(401).json({ error: "Sin token" });

  const token = header.split(" ")[1];
  try {
    req.usuario = jwt.verify(token, SECRET);
    next();
  } catch {
    res.status(401).json({ error: "Token inválido" });
  }
}

// Protected route
app.get("/perfil", auth, async (req, res) => {
  const usuario = await prisma.usuario.findUnique({
    where: { id: req.usuario.id },
    select: { id: true, nombre: true, email: true }
  });
  res.json(usuario);
});

    Never store JWT_SECRET in code

    Use environment variables (.env) and never push them to GitHub. Add .env to .gitignore.

    🔐 Authentication with JWT¶

    JWT (JSON Web Token) is the standard for authenticating users in APIs. The server signs a token that the client sends on every request.

    Installation¶

    npm install jsonwebtoken bcrypt

    Register User (Password Hashing)¶

    import bcrypt from "bcrypt";
import jwt from "jsonwebtoken";

const SECRET = process.env.JWT_SECRET; // never in code

app.post("/api/registro", async (req, res) => {
    const { email, password } = req.body;

    // Check if it already exists
    const existe = await db.usuarios.findOne({ email });
    if (existe) return res.status(409).json({ error: "Email ya registrado" });

    // Hash password (10 rounds)
    const hash = await bcrypt.hash(password, 10);

    const usuario = await db.usuarios.create({ email, password: hash });

    // Create token (expires in 7 days)
    const token = jwt.sign({ id: usuario.id, email }, SECRET, { expiresIn: "7d" });

    res.status(201).json({ token, usuario: { id: usuario.id, email } });
});

    Login¶

    app.post("/api/login", async (req, res) => {
    const { email, password } = req.body;

    const usuario = await db.usuarios.findOne({ email });
    if (!usuario) return res.status(401).json({ error: "Credenciales inválidas" });

    const valida = await bcrypt.compare(password, usuario.password);
    if (!valida) return res.status(401).json({ error: "Credenciales inválidas" });

    const token = jwt.sign({ id: usuario.id, email }, SECRET, { expiresIn: "7d" });
    res.json({ token });
});

    Authentication Middleware¶

    function autenticar(req, res, next) {
    const auth = req.headers.authorization || "";
    const token = auth.replace("Bearer ", "");

    if (!token) return res.status(401).json({ error: "Token requerido" });

    try {
        req.usuario = jwt.verify(token, SECRET);
        next();
    } catch (err) {
        res.status(401).json({ error: "Token inválido o expirado" });
    }
}

// Protected route
app.get("/api/perfil", autenticar, (req, res) => {
    res.json({ usuario: req.usuario });
});

    Never store passwords in plain text

    Always hash with bcrypt (or argon2). Never store the raw password. And never return the hash in the API response.

    Keep the JWT secret in an environment variable

    JWT_SECRET must be a long, random string stored in .env (never in code). If it leaks, anyone can sign valid tokens.

    ✅ Validation with Zod¶

    Zod validates input data using a declarative schema. Essential for APIs: never trust data coming from the client.

    Installation¶

    npm install zod

    Registration Schema¶

    import { z } from "zod";

const registroSchema = z.object({
    email: z.string().email("Email inválido"),
    password: z.string().min(8, "Mínimo 8 caracteres").max(100),
    nombre: z.string().min(2, "Mínimo 2 caracteres").optional(),
});

app.post("/api/registro", async (req, res) => {
    const resultado = registroSchema.safeParse(req.body);

    if (!resultado.success) {
        return res.status(400).json({ errores: resultado.error.errors });
    }

    const { email, password, nombre } = resultado.data;
    // ... continue with registration
});

    Query Params Validation¶

    const listadoSchema = z.object({
    page: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).default(1),
    limit: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(100).default(20),
    q: z.string().optional(),
});

app.get("/api/usuarios", (req, res) => {
    const { page, limit, q } = listadoSchema.parse(req.query);
    // page and limit are numbers, q is string or undefined
});

    Validate at the boundary of the application

    Validate in the controller (when receiving the request), not inside business logic. That way the rest of the code can assume valid data without filling up with if checks.

    🏗 Scalable Project Structure¶

    A growing full-stack project needs a clear structure. This is the one I use:

    mi-app/
├── src/
│   ├── config/
│   │   └── env.js            # validated environment variables
│   ├── db/
│   │   ├── schema.js         # tables / models
│   │   └── index.js          # DB connection
│   ├── middlewares/
│   │   ├── auth.js           # JWT authentication
│   │   └── error.js          # error handling
│   ├── routes/
│   │   ├── auth.routes.js
│   │   └── usuarios.routes.js
│   ├── controllers/
│   │   └── usuarios.controller.js
│   ├── services/
│   │   └── usuarios.service.js
│   ├── schemas/
│   │   └── usuarios.schema.js # Zod
│   └── app.js                # Express setup
├── tests/
├── .env
├── package.json
└── server.js

    Separation of Concerns¶

    Layer Responsibility
    routes Define URLs and HTTP methods
    controllers Validate input, call services, return response
    services Business logic (reusable, testable)
    db Data access (queries, ORM) 
    // routes/usuarios.routes.js
import { Router } from "express";
import { autenticar } from "../middlewares/auth.js";
import * as ctrl from "../controllers/usuarios.controller.js";

const router = Router();
router.get("/", autenticar, ctrl.listar);
router.get("/:id", autenticar, ctrl.obtener);
router.post("/", ctrl.crear);

export default router;

    // controllers/usuarios.controller.js
import * as service from "../services/usuarios.service.js";
import { registroSchema } from "../schemas/usuarios.schema.js";

export async function listar(req, res, next) {
    try {
        const usuarios = await service.listar();
        res.json(usuarios);
    } catch (err) {
        next(err);
    }
}

export async function crear(req, res, next) {
    try {
        const datos = registroSchema.parse(req.body);
        const usuario = await service.crear(datos);
        res.status(201).json(usuario);
    } catch (err) {
        next(err);
    }
}

    Services don't know about HTTP

    A service receives data, does its work, and returns the result. It doesn't touch req or res. That lets you reuse it from a CLI, a job, or a test without starting the server.

    🚨 Centralized Error Handling¶

    // middlewares/error.js
export function errorHandler(err, req, res, next) {
    console.error(err);

    if (err.name === "ZodError") {
        return res.status(400).json({ errores: err.errors });
    }

    if (err.code === "P2002") {
        return res.status(409).json({ error: "Recurso duplicado" });
    }

    res.status(err.status || 500).json({
        error: err.message || "Error interno del servidor",
    });
}

// app.js
app.use(errorHandler); // always at the end

    Never return stack traces in production

    In development it's fine for debugging, but in production it exposes sensitive info (paths, versions, internal logic). Return a generic message and log details on the server.

    🧠 Review Quiz¶

    Check what you learned

    1. Why hash passwords with bcrypt instead of storing them as-is?

    Because if the database leaks, passwords aren't exposed. bcrypt adds a unique salt per password and is intentionally slow, making brute-force attacks harder.

    2. Where should the JWT secret be stored?

    In an environment variable (.env), never in code. If it leaks, anyone can sign valid tokens and impersonate any user.

    3. What is the advantage of validating with Zod in the controller?

    The rest of the application can assume valid data. When you validate at the boundary (the controller), services and business logic don't fill up with type-checking if statements.

    4. Why shouldn't services touch req or res?

    Because that keeps them reusable anywhere (tests, CLI, jobs) without depending on HTTP. Business logic stays isolated from Express.

    20 — Frontend DevOps¶

    What you will learn

    • What DevOps is and why it matters for frontend.
    • CI/CD with GitHub Actions.

    • Monitoring and logs.

    🚀 What is DevOps?¶

    DevOps is the culture and set of practices that bring development and operations together to deliver software faster and with fewer errors. For a frontend developer, it means automating builds, tests, and deployments.

    If you do it more than twice, automate it

    DevOps isn't a tool—it's a way of working: if a manual process repeats, turn it into a script or a workflow.

    🔄 CI/CD¶

    Concept What it means
    CI (Continuous Integration) Integrating changes frequently, running automated tests
    CD (Continuous Delivery) Code is always ready to deploy
    CD (Continuous Deployment) Every change is deployed automatically

    ⚙ GitHub Actions¶

    # .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: Deploy

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build-and-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
          cache: "npm"

      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run test
      - run: npm run build

      - uses: peaceiris/actions-gh-pages@v3
        with:
          github_token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          publish_dir: ./dist

    What this workflow does

    1. Runs on every push to main.
    2. Installs Node.js 20 and dependencies.
    3. Runs the tests.
    4. Builds the project.
    5. Publishes it to GitHub Pages.

    🐳 Docker for Frontend¶

    Docker packages your app with all its dependencies so it runs the same way in any environment.

    # Dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM nginx:alpine
COPY --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
EXPOSE 80
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]

    docker build -t mi-frontend .
docker run -p 8080:80 mi-frontend

    Multi-stage build

    The Dockerfile above uses two stages: one to build and one to serve. That keeps the final image much smaller (only Nginx + static files).

    Tool What it measures
    Sentry Production errors with stack traces
    LogRocket User sessions (screen recording)
    Google Analytics 4 Traffic and behavior
    Vercel Analytics Real-world Core Web Vitals
    UptimeRobot Site availability

import * as Sentry from "@sentry/browser";

    ✅ Deployment Best Practices¶

    • ✅ Deploy from main: don't deploy manually from your local machine.
    • ✅ Run tests before deploying: if a test fails, don't deploy.
    • ✅ Use environment variables: never put secrets in code.
    • ✅ Version releases: use Git tags (v1.0.0).
    • ✅ Easy rollback: be able to revert to the previous version in minutes.
    • ✅ Monitor after deploying: errors don't report themselves.
    • ✅ Notify the team: Slack, Discord, or email after each deployment.
    • ❌ Don't deploy on Fridays: if something breaks, nobody is around to fix it.

    # .env (never push it to GitHub)
VITE_API_URL=[https://api.miapp.com](https://api.miapp.com)
VITE_ANALYTICS_ID=G-XXXXXXX

    // In code
const apiUrl = import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL;

.env
.env.local
.env.*.local

    If you push a .env file with secrets to GitHub, consider them compromised. Rotate them immediately.

    21 — Web Components¶

    What you will learn

    • What Web Components are and why they exist.
    • Custom Elements: creating your own tags.
    • Shadow DOM: encapsulating styles and markup.
    • Templates and slots.
    • Component lifecycle.

    🧩 What are Web Components?¶

    Web Components are a set of native browser standards that let you create reusable components without needing frameworks. They work in all modern browsers.

    class MiBoton extends HTMLElement {
  connectedCallback() {
    this.innerHTML = `<button>${this.textContent}</button>`;
  }
}
customElements.define("mi-boton", MiBoton);

    <mi-boton>Haz clic</mi-boton>

    Components without a framework

    Web Components are the foundation of what React, Vue, or Svelte do, but native. They don't need a build step, dependencies, or updates.

    🏷 Custom Elements¶

    Custom Elements let you define custom HTML tags. The name must include a hyphen (mi-componente, mi-boton, user-card).

    class UserCard extends HTMLElement {
  connectedCallback() {
    const nombre = this.getAttribute("nombre") || "Anónimo";
    this.innerHTML = `
      <div class="card">
        <h3>${nombre}</h3>
        <p>Usuario</p>
      </div>
    `;
  }
}

customElements.define("user-card", UserCard);

    <user-card nombre="Ana"></user-card>
<user-card nombre="Luis"></user-card>

    🌑 Shadow DOM¶

    Shadow DOM encapsulates a component's markup and styles. What happens inside doesn't affect outside, and vice versa.

    class MiTarjeta extends HTMLElement {
  constructor() {
    super();
    const shadow = this.attachShadow({ mode: "open" });
    shadow.innerHTML = `
      <style>
        .card {
          background: #6a5acd;
          color: white;
          padding: 1rem;
          border-radius: 8px;
        }
      </style>
      <div class="card">
        <slot></slot>
      </div>
    `;
  }
}

customElements.define("mi-tarjeta", MiTarjeta);

    <mi-tarjeta>Contenido dentro del slot</mi-tarjeta>

    Benefits of Shadow DOM

    • Styles don't leak out.
    • Outside styles don't affect the inside.
    • The component is completely encapsulated and reusable.

    🔄 Lifecycle¶

    Method When it runs
    constructor() When the element is created
    connectedCallback() When added to the DOM
    disconnectedCallback() When removed from the DOM
    attributeChangedCallback() When an attribute changes
    adoptedCallback() When moved to another document 
    class MiComponente extends HTMLElement {
  static get observedAttributes() {
    return ["nombre"];
  }

  connectedCallback() {
    console.log("Montado");
  }

  disconnectedCallback() {
    console.log("Desmontado");
  }

  attributeChangedCallback(nombre, viejo, nuevo) {
    console.log(`Atributo ${nombre}: ${viejo} -> ${nuevo}`);
  }
}

    📄 Templates¶

    Templates let you define markup that is not rendered until cloned.

    <template id="mi-template">
  <style>
    .card { padding: 1rem; background: #6a5acd; color: white; }
  </style>
  <div class="card">
    <h3>Tarjeta</h3>
  </div>
</template>

    class MiTarjeta extends HTMLElement {
  constructor() {
    super();
    const template = document.getElementById("mi-template");
    const clone = template.content.cloneNode(true);
    this.attachShadow({ mode: "open" }).appendChild(clone);
  }
}
customElements.define("mi-tarjeta", MiTarjeta);

    🕳 Slots¶

    Slots let you inject content from outside the component.

    <template id="card-template">
  <div class="card">
    <header><slot name="titulo">Título por defecto</slot></header>
    <main><slot>Contenido por defecto</slot></main>
  </div>
</template>

<mi-card>
  <span slot="titulo">Mi título</span>
  <p>Contenido personalizado</p>
</mi-card>

    ✅ Best Practices¶

    • ✅ Use Shadow DOM to encapsulate styles.
    • ✅ Define observed attributes only for the ones you need.
    • ✅ Use slots to allow customization.
    • ✅ Document the component's attributes and events.
    • ✅ Test the component in isolation.
    • ❌ Don't overuse Web Components for everything: if it's simple, use native HTML.

    22 — Progressive Web Apps (PWA)¶

    What you will learn

    • What a PWA is and why it is the future of the web.
    • The manifest: installable on mobile.
    • Service Workers: offline and caching.
    • Push notifications.
    • Auditing with Lighthouse.

    📱 What is a PWA?¶

    A PWA (Progressive Web App) is a website that behaves like a native app: it can be installed, works offline, and sends push notifications. All with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

    Normal website + manifest + service worker = PWA

    PWAs are the future of the web

    Twitter, Spotify, Pinterest, Starbucks... they all have PWAs. And they work just as well (or better) than their native apps, without going through app stores.

    📄 The Manifest¶

    The manifest is a JSON file that tells the browser how to install the app.

    // manifest.json
{
  "name": "Mi App",
  "short_name": "MiApp",
  "start_url": "/",
  "display": "standalone",
  "background_color": "#ffffff",
  "theme_color": "#6a5acd",
  "icons": [
    { "src": "/icon-192.png", "sizes": "192x192", "type": "image/png" },
    { "src": "/icon-512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png" }
  ]
}

    <link rel="manifest" href="/manifest.json">
<meta name="theme-color" content="#6a5acd">

    Key Properties¶

    Property What it does
    name Full name of the app
    short_name Short name (for the icon)
    start_url Startup URL when opened
    display standalone, fullscreen, minimal-ui, browser
    theme_color Status bar color
    icons Icons in multiple sizes

    ⚙ The Service Worker¶

    The Service Worker is a script that runs in the background and acts as a proxy between the app and the network. It lets you cache resources and serve the app offline.

    // sw.js
const CACHE = "mi-app-v1";
const ASSETS = [
  "/",
  "/index.html",
  "/styles.css",
  "/app.js",
  "/icon-192.png"
];

self.addEventListener("install", (event) => {
  event.waitUntil(
    caches.open(CACHE).then((cache) => cache.addAll(ASSETS))
  );
});

self.addEventListener("fetch", (event) => {
  event.respondWith(
    caches.match(event.request).then((res) => {
      return res || fetch(event.request);
    })
  );
});

    Registering the Service Worker¶

    if ("serviceWorker" in navigator) {
  navigator.serviceWorker.register("/sw.js")
    .then((reg) => console.log("SW registrado", reg))
    .catch((err) => console.error("Error", err));
}

    Production only

    Service Workers require HTTPS (or localhost). Make sure your site uses HTTPS before registering one.

    🔄 Caching Strategies¶

    Strategy What it does
    Cache first Checks cache first; if missing, goes to the network
    Network first Goes to the network first; if it fails, checks cache
    Stale while revalidate Returns cached response and updates in the background
    Cache only Cache only (fully offline)
    Network only Network only (no cache) 
    // Network first
self.addEventListener("fetch", (event) => {
  event.respondWith(
    fetch(event.request)
      .then((res) => {
        const clone = res.clone();
        caches.open(CACHE).then((cache) => cache.put(event.request, clone));
        return res;
      })
      .catch(() => caches.match(event.request))
  );
});

    🔔 Push Notifications¶

    // Request permission
const permiso = await Notification.requestPermission();
if (permiso === "granted") {
  new Notification("¡Hola!", {
    body: "Bienvenido a Mi App",
    icon: "/icon-192.png"
  });
}

    Push from the Server¶

    // In the service worker
self.addEventListener("push", (event) => {
  const data = event.data.json();
  self.registration.showNotification(data.title, {
    body: data.body,
    icon: "/icon-192.png"
  });
});

    Don't ask for permission on load

    Ask for notification permission after the user takes a meaningful action (buying, signing up, etc.). If you ask on page load, most users will deny it.

    🔍 Auditing with Lighthouse¶

    # In Chrome DevTools
F12 -> Lighthouse -> Analyze
# Categories to check: PWA, Performance, Accessibility
    PWA Requirement How to meet it
    HTTPS SSL certificate (free Let's Encrypt)
    Manifest Linked manifest.json file
    Service Worker Registered and caching
    Icons 192x192 and 512x512
    start_url Defined in the manifest

    ✅ Best Practices¶

    • ✅ HTTPS is mandatory: without it there is no PWA.
    • ✅ Cache only what you need: don't bloat the cache.
    • ✅ Update the cache when deploying a new version.
    • ✅ Ask for notification permission with context.
    • ✅ Test offline: disconnect the network and verify it works.
    • ✅ Use Workbox if the project is large.
    • ❌ Don't cache HTML forever: users won't see updates.

    23 — WebSockets and Real Time¶

    What you will learn

    • Rooms and broadcasting.
    • Reconnection and error handling.

    🔌 What is a WebSocket?¶

    A WebSocket is a bidirectional and persistent communication protocol between client and server. Unlike HTTP, the connection does not close after each request: it stays open to send and receive messages in real time.

    HTTP:      request → response → close
WebSocket: persistent connection ↔ messages in both directions

    True real time

    WebSockets power chats, live notifications, real-time collaboration, and multiplayer games.

    🎯 When to Use WebSockets?¶

    Use Case WebSocket HTTP Polling
    Chat ✅ ❌
    Live notifications ✅ ❌
    Collaborative editing ✅ ❌
    Multiplayer games ✅ ❌
    Rarely changing data ❌ ✅
    Traditional REST APIs ❌ ✅

    💻 Client: The WebSocket API¶

    const ws = new WebSocket("wss://mi-servidor.com");

ws.addEventListener("open", () => {
  console.log("Conectado");
  ws.send(JSON.stringify({ tipo: "saludo", nombre: "Ana" }));
});

ws.addEventListener("message", (event) => {
  const data = JSON.parse(event.data);
  console.log("Mensaje recibido:", data);
});

ws.addEventListener("close", () => {
  console.log("Desconectado");
});

ws.addEventListener("error", (err) => {
  console.error("Error:", err);
});

    Use wss:// in production

    Always use wss:// (secure WebSocket) in production. Only use ws:// for local development.

    🖥 Server with Node.js and ws¶

    npm install ws

    // server.js
import { WebSocketServer } from "ws";

const wss = new WebSocketServer({ port: 8080 });

wss.on("connection", (ws) => {
  console.log("Cliente conectado");

  ws.on("message", (data) => {
    const mensaje = JSON.parse(data);
    console.log("Recibido:", mensaje);

    // Broadcast to all clients
    wss.clients.forEach((client) => {
      if (client.readyState === 1) {
        client.send(JSON.stringify({ tipo: "mensaje", texto: mensaje.texto }));
      }
    });
  });

  ws.on("close", () => {
    console.log("Cliente desconectado");
  });
});

    🏠 Rooms and Broadcasting¶

    const salas = new Map();

wss.on("connection", (ws) => {
  ws.on("message", (data) => {
    const { tipo, sala, texto } = JSON.parse(data);

    if (tipo === "entrar") {
      if (!salas.has(sala)) salas.set(sala, new Set());
      salas.get(sala).add(ws);
      ws.sala = sala;
    }

    if (tipo === "mensaje" && ws.sala) {
      salas.get(ws.sala).forEach((client) => {
        if (client.readyState === 1) {
          client.send(JSON.stringify({ texto }));
        }
      });
    }
  });

  ws.on("close", () => {
    if (ws.sala && salas.has(ws.sala)) {
      salas.get(ws.sala).delete(ws);
    }
  });
});

    🔄 Automatic Reconnection¶

    WebSockets can drop due to network issues, server restarts, or timeouts. Implement reconnection:

    let ws;
let reintentos = 0;

function conectar() {
  ws = new WebSocket("wss://mi-servidor.com");

  ws.addEventListener("open", () => {
    console.log("Conectado");
    reintentos = 0;
  });

  ws.addEventListener("close", () => {
    console.log("Desconectado, reconectando...");
    reintentos++;
    const delay = Math.min(1000 * 2 ** reintentos, 30000);
    setTimeout(conectar, delay);
  });

  ws.addEventListener("error", () => ws.close());
}

conectar();

    ✅ Best Practices¶

    • ✅ Use wss:// in production (secure WebSocket).
    • ✅ Reconnect with exponential backoff: 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s...
    • ✅ Heartbeat: send periodic pings to detect dead connections.
    • ✅ Authentication: validate the token on connection, not just at login.
    • ✅ Limit message size: huge messages block the event loop.
    • ✅ Validate incoming data from the client.
    • ❌ Don't use WebSockets for everything: for simple CRUD, HTTP is enough.

    3. Which technique prevents reconnecting too fast?

    24 — Advanced Animations¶

    What you will learn

    • CSS transitions and animations.
    • The Web Animations API.
    • Scroll animations.
    • GSAP and Framer Motion.
    • Animation performance.

    🎬 Why Do Animations Matter?¶

    Well-crafted animations improve UX: they guide attention, give feedback, and make the web feel alive. Poorly made ones distract, cause motion sickness, and slow things down.

    Animation is communication

    An animation isn't decoration—it's a way to tell the user what is happening and what they can do.

    ✨ CSS Transitions¶

    .boton {
  background: #6a5acd;
  transition: background-color .2s ease, transform .15s ease;
}

.boton:hover {
  background: #7d6ce0;
  transform: translateY(-2px);
}
    Timing function Behavior
    ease Smooth start and end (default)
    linear Constant speed
    ease-in Slow start
    ease-out Slow end
    ease-in-out Slow at both ends
    cubic-bezier() Custom curve

    🎞 Keyframes¶

    @keyframes fadeInUp {
  from {
    opacity: 0;
    transform: translateY(20px);
  }
  to {
    opacity: 1;
    transform: translateY(0);
  }
}

.animado {
  animation: fadeInUp .5s ease forwards;
}

    Stagger¶

    .lista > * {
  animation: fadeInUp .4s ease forwards;
  opacity: 0;
}

.lista > *:nth-child(1) { animation-delay: .05s; }
.lista > *:nth-child(2) { animation-delay: .1s; }
.lista > *:nth-child(3) { animation-delay: .15s; }

    ⚡ Web Animations API¶

    The Web Animations API lets you animate with JavaScript in a more powerful and controllable way.

    const elemento = document.querySelector(".caja");

elemento.animate([
  { transform: "translateX(0)", opacity: 1 },
  { transform: "translateX(200px)", opacity: 0.5 }
], {
  duration: 500,
  easing: "ease-in-out",
  iterations: 1,
  fill: "forwards"
});

    Advantages of WAAPI

    • Full control from JavaScript (play, pause, reverse, cancel).
    • Better performance than animating properties manually with JS.
    • Can be combined with CSS.

    📜 Scroll Animations¶

    Scroll-Driven Animations (Native)¶

    @keyframes aparecer {
  from { opacity: 0; transform: scale(.9); }
  to { opacity: 1; transform: scale(1); }
}

.elemento {
  animation: aparecer linear;
  animation-timeline: view();
  animation-range: entry 0% entry 50%;
}

    Intersection Observer (Broader Support)¶

    const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
  entries.forEach((entry) => {
    if (entry.isIntersecting) {
      entry.target.classList.add("visible");
      observer.unobserve(entry.target);
    }
  });
});

document.querySelectorAll(".animar").forEach((el) => observer.observe(el));

    .animar {
  opacity: 0;
  transform: translateY(20px);
  transition: opacity .5s, transform .5s;
}

.animar.visible {
  opacity: 1;
  transform: translateY(0);
}

    🎬 GSAP¶

    GSAP (GreenSock Animation Platform) is one of the most powerful animation libraries available. Used by Google, Apple, Netflix…

    npm install gsap

    import gsap from "gsap";

gsap.to(".caja", {
  x: 200,
  rotation: 360,
  duration: 1,
  ease: "power2.out"
});

    Timeline¶

    const tl = gsap.timeline({ repeat: -1, yoyo: true });

tl.to(".caja", { x: 100, duration: .5 })
  .to(".caja", { y: 100, duration: .5 })
  .to(".caja", { x: 0, duration: .5 })
  .to(".caja", { y: 0, duration: .5 });

    ⚛ Framer Motion (React)¶

    Framer Motion is the most popular animation library for React.

    npm install framer-motion

    import { motion } from "framer-motion";

function MiComponente() {
  return (
    <motion.div
      initial={{ opacity: 0, y: 20 }}
      animate={{ opacity: 1, y: 0 }}
      exit={{ opacity: 0 }}
      transition={{ duration: .3 }}
    >
      Hola
    </motion.div>
  );
}

    ⚡ Animation Performance¶

    Not all CSS properties animate at the same speed:

    Property Performance
    transform ⚡ Excellent (GPU)
    opacity ⚡ Excellent (GPU)
    filter 🚀 Good (GPU)
    width, height 🐢 Poor (repaint + layout)
    top, left 🐢 Poor (repaint + layout)
    background 🐢 Poor (repaint)

    Animate only transform and opacity

    For smooth 60fps animations, animate only transform and opacity. Everything else triggers repaint and layout, which are much more expensive.

    /* Bad */
.caja:hover { left: 10px; }

/* Good */
.caja:hover { transform: translateX(10px); }

    Respecting prefers-reduced-motion¶

    @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after {
    animation-duration: .01ms !important;
    transition-duration: .01ms !important;
  }
}

    ✅ Best Practices¶

    • ✅ Animate with purpose: guide attention, give feedback.
    • ✅ Short duration: 200-500ms for most interactions.
    • ✅ Natural easing: avoid linear for motion.
    • ✅ Respect prefers-reduced-motion.
    • ✅ Use GPU: transform and opacity.
    • ✅ Don't overdo it: less is more.
    • ❌ Don't animate width/height if you can avoid it.
    • ❌ Don't make interactions last longer than 1s.

    1. Which CSS properties are most efficient to animate?

    2. Which library is most powerful for animations?

    3. Which native API lets you animate with JavaScript?

    🎬 @keyframes in Depth¶

    @keyframes define multi-step animations. Unlike transition (which animates between two states), @keyframes lets you control every frame.

    Basic Syntax¶

    @keyframes rebotar {
    0%   { transform: translateY(0); }
    50%  { transform: translateY(-30px); }
    100% { transform: translateY(0); }
}

.pelota {
    animation: rebotar 1s ease-in-out infinite;
}

    animation Properties¶

    Property What it does Example
    animation-name Name of the @keyframes rebotar
    animation-duration Duration of one cycle 1s, 500ms
    animation-timing-function Speed curve ease, linear, cubic-bezier(...)
    animation-delay Initial delay 200ms
    animation-iteration-count Repetitions 1, infinite, 3
    animation-direction Direction normal, reverse, alternate
    animation-fill-mode State before/after none, forwards, backwards, both
    animation-play-state Pause/resume running, paused

    animation Shorthand¶

    .pelota {
    animation: rebotar 1s ease-in-out 0s infinite alternate both;
    /* name duration timing delay iteration direction fill-mode */
}

    animation-fill-mode: both is very useful

    Keeps the first keyframe's state before the animation starts, and the last keyframe's state after it ends. Prevents visual "snapping" when the animation finishes.

    🔄 View Transitions API (Modern CSS)¶

    The View Transitions API lets you animate transitions between pages (or between states in an SPA) with very little code. The browser captures "before" and "after" snapshots and morphs between them automatically.

    Basic Usage in an SPA¶

    document.startViewTransition(() => {
    // Update the DOM here
    document.querySelector("#app").innerHTML = nuevaVista();
});

    Customizing the Transition with CSS¶

    ::view-transition-old(root) {
    animation: fade-out 0.3s ease;
}

::view-transition-new(root) {
    animation: fade-in 0.3s ease;
}

@keyframes fade-out {
    to { opacity: 0; }
}

@keyframes fade-in {
    from { opacity: 0; }
}

    Transitioning a Specific Element¶

    /* Element moves smoothly across views */
.card {
    view-transition-name: card-principal;
}

    ::view-transition-group(card-principal) {
    animation-duration: 0.5s;
    animation-timing-function: cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1);
}

    Limited support

    The View Transitions API works in Chrome/Edge 111+ and Safari 18+. Firefox does not support it yet (2026). Use it with @supports or as progressive enhancement:

    @supports (view-transition-name: none) {
    /* styles only if supported by the browser */
}

    ♿ prefers-reduced-motion (Accessibility)¶

    Some users have motion sensitivity (vertigo, epilepsy, migraines). Respect their system preference with a media query.

    Disabling Animations When Requested¶

    @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
    *,
    *::before,
    *::after {
        animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
        animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
        transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
        scroll-behavior: auto !important;
    }
}

    Alternative: Softer Animations¶

    @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
    .hero {
        animation: entrada 0.8s ease-out;
    }
}

/* If the user prefers reduced motion, no animation */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
    .hero {
        opacity: 1;
        transform: none;
    }
}

    It's a requirement, not an extra

    WCAG 2.2 includes prefers-reduced-motion as a conformance criterion (2.3.3). If your site has animations, you must respect this preference.

    ⚡ Performant Animations¶

    Not all CSS properties animate the same way. Some force the browser to recalculate layout (slow), others only repaint, and others animate on the GPU (fast).

    Property Cost Why
    transform ⚡ GPU Animated on the graphics card
    opacity ⚡ GPU Also animated on the GPU
    background-color 🚀 Repaint Repaints the element
    width, height 🐢 Reflow Recalculates layout
    top, left 🐢 Reflow Recalculates layout
    margin, padding 🐢 Reflow Recalculates layout

    Golden Rule: Animate Only transform and opacity¶

    /* ✅ Good: GPU, no reflow */
.boton:hover {
    transform: scale(1.05);
    opacity: 0.9;
}

/* ❌ Bad: reflow on every frame */
.boton:hover {
    width: 110%;
    height: 110%;
    top: -5px;
}

    will-change (In Moderation)¶

    .elemento-que-va-a-animarse {
    will-change: transform;
}

    Don't overuse will-change

    Creates a compositing layer on the GPU. Putting it on many elements consumes video memory and hurts performance. Use it only on elements about to animate, and remove it once the animation finishes.

    📜 scroll-driven animations (Modern CSS)¶

    Lets you animate elements based on scroll, without JavaScript. There are two types:

    1. animation-timeline: scroll() — Based on a Container's Scroll¶

    .barra-progreso {
    position: fixed;
    top: 0;
    left: 0;
    height: 4px;
    background: #6a5acd;
    transform-origin: left;
    animation: crecer linear;
    animation-timeline: scroll(root);
}

@keyframes crecer {
    from { transform: scaleX(0); }
    to   { transform: scaleX(1); }
}

    2. animation-timeline: view() — Based on an Element's Visibility¶

    .tarjeta {
    animation: aparecer linear both;
    animation-timeline: view();
    animation-range: entry 0% entry 100%;
}

@keyframes aparecer {
    from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(40px); }
    to   { opacity: 1; transform: translateY(0); }
}

    Less JavaScript, more CSS

    Scroll-driven animations replace most "reveal on scroll" libraries (AOS, ScrollReveal). They work in Chrome/Edge 115+ and Safari 26+ (2026). Firefox not yet.

    🧪 Hands-On Exercise¶

    Entrance animation respecting prefers-reduced-motion

    Create a card that:

    • Appears with a fade-in + translateY on page load.
    • Uses @keyframes with a 0.6s duration.
    • Disables the animation if the user has prefers-reduced-motion: reduce.
    Solution 
    .tarjeta {
    opacity: 0;
    transform: translateY(20px);
    animation: entrada 0.6s ease-out forwards;
}

@keyframes entrada {
    to {
        opacity: 1;
        transform: translateY(0);
    }
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
    .tarjeta {
        animation: none;
        opacity: 1;
        transform: none;
    }
}

    🧠 Review Quiz¶

    Check what you learned

    1. What is the difference between transition and animation?

    transition animates between two states (start and end) when a property changes. animation uses @keyframes and allows multiple steps, repetition, direction, and full control.

    2. Which CSS properties are animated on the GPU?

    transform and opacity. They are the only ones that don't cause reflow or repaint. Animating width, top, or margin forces the browser to recalculate layout on every frame.

    3. What is prefers-reduced-motion for?

    To respect users with motion sensitivity (vertigo, epilepsy). When enabled, animations should be disabled or reduced. It is a WCAG accessibility criterion.

    4. What does animation-fill-mode: both do?

    Keeps the first keyframe's state before the animation starts and the last keyframe's state after it ends. Prevents visual jumps.

    5. What advantage do scroll-driven animations have?

    They let you animate based on scroll without JavaScript, replacing libraries like AOS. They are declared with animation-timeline: scroll() or view().

    25 — Design Systems¶

    What you will learn

    • What a design system is and why it matters.
    • Design tokens: colors, typography, spacing.
    • Reusable components.
    • Documentation with Storybook.
    • Governance and maintenance.

    🎨 What is a Design System?¶

    A design system is a collection of reusable components, style guides, and rules that guarantee visual and behavioral consistency across a product. It isn't just a component library—it's a shared language between design and development.

    A design system is a product, not a project

    You don't build it once and forget it. You maintain it, document it, and version it like any other product.

    🎯 Why Use a Design System?¶

    Benefit Description
    Consistency Every button looks and behaves the same way
    Speed Teams don't reinvent the wheel
    Scalability Adding a feature is faster
    Maintainability Changing a color happens in one place
    Communication Design and engineering speak the same language

    🎨 Design Tokens¶

    Design tokens are the atomic values of the system: colors, typography, spacing, shadows, radii… You define them once and use them everywhere.

    :root {
  /* Colors */
  --color-primary: #6a5acd;
  --color-primary-hover: #7d6ce0;
  --color-success: #28a745;
  --color-danger: #dc3545;

  /* Typography */
  --font-sans: "Inter", system-ui, sans-serif;
  --font-mono: "JetBrains Mono", monospace;
  --text-sm: .875rem;
  --text-base: 1rem;
  --text-lg: 1.25rem;
  --text-xl: 1.5rem;

  /* Spacing */
  --space-1: .25rem;
  --space-2: .5rem;
  --space-3: 1rem;
  --space-4: 1.5rem;
  --space-5: 2rem;

  /* Radii */
  --radius-sm: 4px;
  --radius-md: 8px;
  --radius-lg: 16px;

  /* Shadows */
  --shadow-sm: 0 1px 2px rgba(0,0,0,.05);
  --shadow-md: 0 4px 12px rgba(0,0,0,.1);
  --shadow-lg: 0 12px 32px rgba(0,0,0,.15);
}

    Token naming

    Use semantic names, not visual ones: --color-primary is better than --color-purple. If the color changes, the name still makes sense.

    🧩 Components¶

    Every component should:

    1. Have a clear API (props/attributes).
    2. Be accessible (keyboard, ARIA, contrast).
    3. Be testable (unit + visual).
    4. Be documented (props, examples, when to use it).
    5. Be versioned (compatible changes vs. breaking).
    // Button.jsx
export function Button({
  children,
  variant = "primary",
  size = "md",
  disabled = false,
  onClick
}) {
  return (
    <button
      className={`btn btn--${variant} btn--${size}`}
      disabled={disabled}
      onClick={onClick}
    >
      {children}
    </button>
  );
}

    📚 Storybook¶

    Storybook is the standard tool for documenting and testing components in isolation.

    npx storybook@latest init
npm run storybook

    // Button.stories.jsx
import { Button } from "./Button";

export default {
  title: "Components/Button",
  component: Button,
  argTypes: {
    variant: { control: "select", options: ["primary", "secondary"] },
    size: { control: "select", options: ["sm", "md", "lg"] }
  }
};

export const Primary = {
  args: { children: "Haz clic", variant: "primary" }
};

export const Secondary = {
  args: { children: "Cancelar", variant: "secondary" }
};

    Storybook is living documentation

    Each component has its "stories": real use cases that serve as documentation, visual tests, and a playground for designers.

    🏛 Governance¶

    A design system without governance dies in 6 months. You need:

    • Owner: someone accountable for the system.
    • Contribution process: how new components are added.
    • Semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.
    • Changelog: what changes in each release.
    • Deprecation policy: when and how components are removed.
    • Communication: Slack/Discord channel, internal newsletter.

    ✅ Best Practices¶

    • ✅ Start small: 5-10 well-built components beat 50 half-baked ones.
    • ✅ Document every component: props, examples, when to use it and when not to.
    • ✅ Version with semver: breaking changes should be rare and announced.
    • ✅ Test visually: Chromatic, Percy, or reg-suit.
    • ✅ Involve design: the system belongs to both teams.
    • ✅ Measure adoption: how many teams use it? How many components are reused?
    • ❌ Don't build everything at once: start with the most-used components.

    26 — Web Security¶

    What you will learn

    • Most common attacks: XSS, CSRF, SQL Injection.
    • How to prevent them.
    • HTTPS, CORS, and CSP.
    • Authentication best practices.
    • Security auditing.

    🔒 Why Does Security Matter?¶

    A vulnerability can cost millions of euros, destroy a company's reputation, and expose users' personal data. Security isn't optional—it's part of the job.

    Security is a process, not a product

    It's not about installing a plugin and forgetting about it. It's about thinking about security in every design, code, and deployment decision.

    🚨 Most Common Attacks¶

    Attack What it does Impact
    XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) Injects malicious code into the page Session hijacking, redirects
    CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) Forces an authenticated user to run actions Password changes, transfers
    SQL Injection Injects SQL into inputs Database theft
    Clickjacking Tricks the user into clicking Unintended actions
    MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) Intercepts communication Credential theft

    💉 XSS: Cross-Site Scripting¶

    Happens when an attacker injects JavaScript into your site, executing in other users' browsers.

    <!-- Vulnerable: input is rendered unescaped -->
<div>Hola, <?php echo $_GET["nombre"]; ?></div>

<!-- Attack: ?nombre=<script>alert("XSS")</script> -->

    How to Prevent It¶

    // ❌ Bad: innerHTML with user data
elemento.innerHTML = input;

// ✅ Good: textContent escapes HTML
elemento.textContent = input;

    // ✅ If you need to render HTML, sanitize it with DOMPurify
import DOMPurify from "dompurify";
elemento.innerHTML = DOMPurify.sanitize(input);

    Always sanitize

    Any data coming from the user (input, URL, cookies) must be treated as potentially malicious. Sanitize before rendering.

    🎭 CSRF: Cross-Site Request Forgery¶

    Happens when an attacker makes an authenticated user's browser perform an unwanted action on your site.

    How to Prevent It¶

    <form method="POST" action="/cambiar-password">
  <input type="hidden" name="csrf_token" value="token-único">
  <!-- ... -->
</form>

    // On the server: validate that the token matches
if (req.body.csrf_token !== req.session.csrf_token) {
  return res.status(403).json({ error: "CSRF token inválido" });
}
    • ✅ Use SameSite=Strict on cookies.
    • ✅ Validate the Origin and Referer headers.
    • ✅ Use CSRF tokens on forms.
    • ✅ Verify the HTTP method (POST, PUT, DELETE for mutations).

    🔐 HTTPS¶

    HTTPS encrypts communication between browser and server. Without HTTPS, anyone on the same network can read credentials.

    HTTP:  browser → plain text → server      (❌ insecure)
HTTPS: browser → TLS encryption → server (✅ secure)
    • ✅ Use Let's Encrypt (free).
    • ✅ Redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS.
    • ✅ Enable HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security).

    🌐 CORS¶

    CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a security mechanism that allows or blocks requests across different origins.

    // Server
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  res.setHeader("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", "[https://miapp.com](https://miapp.com)");
  res.setHeader("Access-Control-Allow-Methods", "GET, POST, PUT, DELETE");
  res.setHeader("Access-Control-Allow-Headers", "Content-Type, Authorization");
  next();
});

    Don't use * in production

    Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * lets any site make requests to your API. In production, use specific origins.

    🛡 Content Security Policy (CSP)¶

    CSP is an HTTP header that restricts which resources a page can load: scripts, styles, images, fonts… It is a strong defense against XSS.

    app.use((req, res, next) => {
  res.setHeader("Content-Security-Policy", [
    "default-src 'self'",
    "script-src 'self' [https://trusted.cdn.com](https://trusted.cdn.com)",
    "style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'",
    "img-src 'self' data: https:"
  ].join("; "));
  next();
});

    Start in report-only mode

    Use Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only at first to see what breaks without blocking anything. Once clean, switch to Content-Security-Policy.

    🔑 Secure Authentication¶

    • ✅ Hash passwords with bcrypt, argon2, or scrypt. Never store plain text.
    • ✅ Use short-lived JWTs (15 min) + refresh token.
    • ✅ Rotate tokens when changing passwords.
    • ✅ Rate limit login endpoints (5 attempts/min).
    • ✅ 2FA (two-factor authentication) for sensitive accounts.
    • ✅ HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookies.
    • ❌ Don't store tokens in localStorage if you can use HttpOnly cookies.

    Tool What it does
    OWASP ZAP Web vulnerability scanner
    Lighthouse Basic security audit
    Snyk Dependency vulnerabilities
    npm audit npm package vulnerabilities
    Security Headers Analyzes security headers 
    npm audit
