    27 — WebAssembly¶

    What you will learn

    • What WebAssembly is and why it exists.
    • When to use it and when not to.
    • Compiling Rust to Wasm.
    • Integrating it with JavaScript.
    • Real-world use cases.

    🧩 What is WebAssembly?¶

    WebAssembly (Wasm) is a binary format that lets you run code from other languages (Rust, C, C++, Go…) in the browser at near-native speed. It does not replace JavaScript—it complements it.

    JavaScript  → fast, but less so for heavy computation
WebAssembly → near-native speed for heavy computation

    Wasm doesn't replace JS

    WebAssembly isn't going to replace JavaScript. It coexists with it: JS for app logic, Wasm for the parts that need maximum performance.

    🎯 When to Use WebAssembly?¶

    Use Case Wasm?
    Real-time video and audio ✅
    3D games and simulations ✅
    Cryptography and compression ✅
    Browser image editing ✅
    AI and machine learning ✅
    Web app CRUD ❌
    Forms and validations ❌
    Basic animations ❌

    🦀 Compiling Rust to WebAssembly¶

    # Install wasm-pack
curl [https://rustwasm.github.io/wasm-pack/installer/init.sh](https://rustwasm.github.io/wasm-pack/installer/init.sh) -sSf | sh

# Create project
cargo new --lib mi-wasm
cd mi-wasm

    # Cargo.toml
[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib"]

[dependencies]
wasm-bindgen = "0.2"

    // src/lib.rs
use wasm_bindgen::prelude::*;

#[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn sumar(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 {
    a + b
}

#[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn fibonacci(n: u32) -> u64 {
    if n <= 1 { return n as u64; }
    let mut a = 0;
    let mut b = 1;
    for _ in 2..=n {
        let temp = a + b;
        a = b;
        b = temp;
    }
    b
}

    wasm-pack build --target web

    This generates a pkg/ folder with the .wasm binary and JavaScript bindings.

    🔗 Integrating with JavaScript¶

    <script type="module">
  import init, { sumar, fibonacci } from "./pkg/mi_wasm.js";

  await init();
  console.log(sumar(2, 3));      // 5
  console.log(fibonacci(40));    // 102334155 (fast)
</script>

    async init

    The init() function loads and compiles the .wasm binary. It returns a promise, so you must await it.

    ⚡ WebAssembly in the Browser (Native API)¶

    const respuesta = await fetch("modulo.wasm");
const bytes = await respuesta.arrayBuffer();
const { instance } = await WebAssembly.instantiate(bytes);

console.log(instance.exports.sumar(2, 3));

    The native API is more verbose. wasm-bindgen (Rust) or Emscripten (C/C++) generate the bindings automatically.

    🏆 Real-World Use Cases¶

    Company Wasm Usage
    Figma Vector graphics rendering and editing
    Google Earth 3D planet visualization
    AutoCAD Web Browser-based CAD design
    Photoshop Web Image editing
    Zoom Video and audio processing
    Unity 3D browser games
    Pyodide Full Python in the browser

    ⚡ Performance: Wasm vs. JS¶

    Task JavaScript WebAssembly Speedup
    Fibonacci(40) ~2 s ~0.4 s 5x
    gzip compression ~1.5 s ~0.3 s 5x
    3D rendering ~16 ms/frame ~4 ms/frame 4x
    Matrix math ~800 ms ~100 ms 8x

    Numbers vary

    These figures are approximate. They depend on browser, hardware, and task type. For small operations, .wasm loading overhead may outweigh any benefit.

    🛠 Tools¶

    Tool Language Purpose
    wasm-pack Rust Package Rust into Wasm
    wasm-bindgen Rust JS ↔ Rust bindings
    Emscripten C/C++ Compile C/C++ to Wasm
    AssemblyScript TypeScript-like Write Wasm with JS-like syntax
    TinyGo Go Compile Go to Wasm
    Blazor C# .NET in the browser
    Pyodide Python Python in the browser 
    # AssemblyScript (easiest if coming from JS)
npm install -g assemblyscript
npx asc modulo.ts -o modulo.wasm

    ✅ Best Practices¶

    • ✅ Use Wasm only when performance matters: for CRUD, JS is enough.
    • ✅ Load .wasm on demand: don't load it on first visit if unneeded.
    • ✅ Measure before and after: don't assume Wasm will be faster.
    • ✅ Use wasm-bindgen (Rust) instead of writing bindings by hand.
    • ✅ Cache .wasm with a Service Worker if it's large.
    • ❌ Don't rewrite your whole app in Rust: integrate only critical parts.

    🦀 Rust → WebAssembly with wasm-pack¶

    Rust is the most popular language for writing WebAssembly. Its type system and memory management without GC make it ideal for high-performance code.

    Installation¶

    # Install wasm-pack
curl https://rustwasm.github.io/wasm-pack/installer/init.sh -sSf | sh

# Create project
cargo new --lib mi-wasm
cd mi-wasm

    Configure Cargo.toml¶

    [package]
name = "mi-wasm"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"]

[dependencies]
wasm-bindgen = "0.2"

    Write the Function in Rust¶

    use wasm_bindgen::prelude::*;

#[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn sumar(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 {
    a + b
}

#[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn fib(n: u32) -> u64 {
    if n < 2 { n as u64 } else { fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2) }
}

    Compile¶

    wasm-pack build --target web

    Generates pkg/ with: - mi_wasm_bg.wasm — the binary - mi_wasm.js — the "glue" to call it from JS - mi_wasm.d.ts — TypeScript types

    Use from JavaScript¶

    import init, { sumar, fib } from "./pkg/mi_wasm.js";

await init();

console.log(sumar(2, 3));   // 5
console.log(fib(30));       // 832040

    init() is required

    The first time you must call init() to load the .wasm. It is asynchronous because it downloads and compiles the binary. Afterward, the functions are synchronous.

    🖥 WASI: WebAssembly Outside the Browser¶

    WASI (WebAssembly System Interface) lets you run Wasm outside the browser, with controlled access to files, network, clock, etc. It is the foundation of "Wasm containers".

    Example with Wasmtime (WASI runtime)¶

    # Install wasmtime
curl https://wasmtime.dev/install.sh -sSf | bash

# Run a .wasm with WASI
wasmtime mi-programa.wasm

    Compile Rust to WASI¶

    rustup target add wasm32-wasi
cargo build --target wasm32-wasi --release

    Why WASI Matters¶

    Benefit Detail
    Portability The same .wasm runs on any OS with a WASI runtime
    Security Code is sandboxed by default (no system access unless requested)
    Fast startup Milliseconds, compared to seconds for a Docker container
    Size A .wasm can be a few KB vs. MB for a Docker image

    WASI vs. Docker

    WASI does not replace Docker in every case. It's ideal for small functions, plugins, and edge computing. For complex apps with system dependencies, Docker is still better.

    🎯 Real-World Use Cases¶

    WebAssembly isn't just a future promise—it's already used in production.

    Company Use
    Figma Vector rendering and real-time collaborative editing
    Photoshop (web) Browser-based image processing
    Google Earth 3D planet visualization
    AutoCAD (web) CAD rendering in the browser
    Unity / Unreal 3D games exported to WebAssembly
    Cloudflare Workers Runs Wasm at the edge
    1Password Cryptography and password generation
    Zoom (web) Audio and video processing

    When is Wasm worth it?

    When you need near-native performance or to reuse C/C++/Rust code on the web. For everything else, JavaScript remains the best choice.

    🔗 Integrating with JavaScript¶

    WebAssembly is not a replacement for JavaScript: they complement each other. Integration is bidirectional.

    Passing Strings (Shared Memory)¶

    Strings are the trickiest part: Wasm doesn't understand UTF-8, only bytes.

    use wasm_bindgen::prelude::*;

#[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn saludar(nombre: &str) -> String {
    format!("Hola, {}!", nombre)
}

    import init, { saludar } from "./pkg/mi_wasm.js";
await init();

console.log(saludar("Urukais"));  // "Hola, Urukais!"

    wasm-bindgen handles the conversion automatically. Without it, you'd have to manage memory manually.

    Passing Arrays¶

    #[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn sumar_array(numeros: &[i32]) -> i32 {
    numeros.iter().sum()
}

    const numeros = new Int32Array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);
console.log(sumar_array(numeros));  // 15

    Calling JavaScript from Rust¶

    use wasm_bindgen::prelude::*;

#[wasm_bindgen]
extern "C" {
    fn alert(s: &str);
    #[wasm_bindgen(js_name = consoleLog)]
    fn console_log(s: &str);
}

#[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn saludar_usuario() {
    alert("¡Hola desde Rust!");
}

    ⚡ Performance: When Wasm Wins (and When It Doesn't)¶

    Wasm isn't always faster than JavaScript. It depends on the task type.

    Task Winner Why
    Heavy numeric loops ⚡ Wasm No GC, no dynamic types
    Cryptography ⚡ Wasm Large integer operations
    Image processing ⚡ Wasm SIMD, per-pixel operations
    DOM manipulation 🟡 JavaScript Direct access to browser APIs
    Simple business logic 🟡 JavaScript Avoids JS↔Wasm bridge overhead
    String operations 🟡 JavaScript No memory conversion

    The Cost of the JS ↔ Wasm Bridge¶

    Every call from JS to Wasm (and back) has a cost. If you make thousands of tiny calls, the overhead exceeds the gain.

    // ❌ Bad: 10,000 bridge calls
for (let i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {
    sumar(1, 1);  // each call crosses the bridge
}

// ✅ Good: single call, loop inside Wasm
sumar_muchas_veces(10000);

    Measure before optimizing

    Don't assume Wasm is faster. Benchmark your specific case. Sometimes well-written JavaScript is just as fast and much simpler.

    🧪 Hands-On Exercise¶

    Fibonacci in Rust + WebAssembly

    Create a function in Rust that computes the nth Fibonacci number, compile it to Wasm, and call it from JavaScript.

    • Rust: recursive fib(n: u32) -> u64 function.
    • JavaScript: call fib(30) and measure elapsed time.
    • Compare with the same function in plain JavaScript.
    Solution 
    // Rust
use wasm_bindgen::prelude::*;

#[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn fib(n: u32) -> u64 {
    if n < 2 { n as u64 } else { fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2) }
}

    // JavaScript
import init, { fib } from "./pkg/mi_wasm.js";
await init();

console.time("wasm");
console.log(fib(30));  // 832040
console.timeEnd("wasm");

function fibJS(n) {
    return n < 2 ? n : fibJS(n - 1) + fibJS(n - 2);
}
console.time("js");
console.log(fibJS(30));
console.timeEnd("js");

    Typical result: Wasm is 2-5x faster in this type of numeric loop.

    🧠 Review Quiz¶

    Check what you learned

    1. What is the difference between WebAssembly and JavaScript?

    WebAssembly is a low-level binary format that runs in the browser VM. JavaScript is a high-level language. Wasm is designed for performance and code reuse (C/C++/Rust); JS for logic and the DOM.

    2. What is wasm-bindgen for?

    To generate the "glue" between Rust and JavaScript: it converts strings, arrays, and complex structures automatically. Without it, you'd have to manage linear memory by hand.

    3. What is WASI?

    The WebAssembly System Interface. It lets you run Wasm outside the browser (servers, CLIs, edge) with controlled access to files, network, etc. It is the foundation of "Wasm containers".

    4. When is Wasm NOT worth using?

    When the task is DOM manipulation, simple logic, or strings. The JS↔Wasm bridge overhead outweighs the gain. Also when the team lacks C/C++/Rust experience.

    5. Which real-world use case uses WebAssembly in production?

    Figma (vector rendering), Photoshop web, Google Earth, AutoCAD web, Unity/Unreal, Cloudflare Workers, 1Password, Zoom web. All use Wasm for performance or code reuse.

    28 — AI in the Frontend¶

    What you will learn

    • How to use AI in the browser with TensorFlow.js.
    • Pretrained models.
    • Browser AI APIs.
    • Integrating with external AI APIs (OpenAI, etc.).

    🤖 AI in the Frontend?¶

    AI in the frontend lets you run machine learning models directly in the browser, without sending data to a server. This improves privacy, lowers latency, and works offline.

    Before: browser → server → model → response
Now:    browser → model → response (all local)

    AI is no longer backend-only

    Libraries and runtimes like TensorFlow.js, ONNX Runtime Web, and Transformers.js make running AI in the browser practical with solid performance.

    🧠 TensorFlow.js¶

    TensorFlow.js is Google's library for running ML models in the browser and in Node.js.

    npm install @tensorflow/tfjs

    import * as tf from "@tensorflow/tfjs";

// Create a tensor
const tensor = tf.tensor([1, 2, 3, 4]);
tensor.print();

// Operations
const doble = tensor.mul(2);
doble.print();

    📦 Pretrained Models¶

    import * as cocoSsd from "@tensorflow-models/coco-ssd";

const modelo = await cocoSsd.load();
const predicciones = await modelo.detect(imagen);

predicciones.forEach((p) => {
  console.log(p.class, p.score, p.bbox);
});
    Model What it does
    COCO-SSD Object detection
    MobileNet Image classification
    PoseNet Pose estimation
    FaceMesh Facial landmark mesh
    HandPose Hand tracking
    Speech Commands Voice recognition
    Toxicity Text toxicity detection

    🌐 Browser AI APIs¶

    Web Speech API¶

    const recognition = new webkitSpeechRecognition();
recognition.lang = "es-ES";
recognition.onresult = (event) => {
  console.log(event.results[0][0].transcript);
};
recognition.start();

    WebGPU¶

    const adapter = await navigator.gpu.requestAdapter();
const device = await adapter.requestDevice();
// Use device for GPU compute

    🔌 External AI APIs¶

    If a model is too large for the browser, use an API:

    const res = await fetch("[https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions](https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions)", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "Authorization": "Bearer " + apiKey
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    model: "gpt-4",
    messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Hola" }]
  })
});

const data = await res.json();
console.log(data.choices[0].message.content);

    Never expose your API key

    API keys must never live in the frontend. Use a backend proxy that attaches the key and enforces rate limiting.

    🤗 Transformers.js¶

    Transformers.js lets you run Hugging Face models directly in the browser, with no server.

    npm install @xenova/transformers

    import { pipeline } from "@xenova/transformers";

// Sentiment analysis
const clasificador = await pipeline("sentiment-analysis");
const resultado = await clasificador("Me encanta este libro");
console.log(resultado);
// [{ label: "POSITIVE", score: 0.9998 }]

    // Translation
const traductor = await pipeline("translation", "Xenova/opus-mt-es-en");
const salida = await traductor("Hola, mundo");
console.log(salida[0].translation_text);
// "Hello, world"
    Task Model
    Text classification sentiment-analysis
    Translation translation
    Summarization summarization
    Text generation text-generation
    Speech recognition automatic-speech-recognition
    Image generation text-to-image (experimental)

    Models in the browser

    Transformers.js downloads models on first use and caches them. The initial load can take a while; subsequent loads are instant.

    🎯 Real-World Use Cases¶

    Use Case Technology
    Object detection in photos TensorFlow.js (COCO-SSD)
    Real-time camera filters MediaPipe (FaceMesh)
    Automatic captions Web Speech API
    Text translation Transformers.js
    Serverless chatbot Transformers.js + IndexedDB
    Semantic search Embeddings + cosine similarity
    Content moderation Toxicity models

    ✅ Best Practices¶

    • ✅ Load models on demand: don't download them on the first visit.
    • ✅ Cache models using Service Worker or IndexedDB.
    • ✅ Use small models (MobileNet, DistilBERT) when performance matters.
    • ✅ Show progress feedback while the model loads ("Loading AI...").
    • ✅ Never expose API keys in the frontend.
    • ✅ Respect privacy: when models run locally, user data stays in the browser.
    • ❌ Don't run huge models on low-end mobile devices.

    29 — WebXR¶

    What you will learn

    • What WebXR is and what it is used for.
    • Virtual Reality (VR) in the browser.
    • Augmented Reality (AR) in the browser.
    • Three.js and A-Frame.
    • Use cases and limitations.

    🥽 What is WebXR?¶

    WebXR is a browser API that lets you build Virtual Reality (VR) and Augmented Reality (AR) experiences directly on the web, without installing native apps.

    WebXR = VR + AR + Mixed Reality (MR) in the browser

    The immersive web is already here

    Meta Quest, Apple Vision Pro, and other devices already support WebXR. You can create immersive experiences with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

    🎮 Virtual Reality (VR)¶

    Virtual Reality immerses the user in a fully digital environment. It requires a headset (Meta Quest, HTC Vive, PSVR…) or a Cardboard viewer.

    // Check VR support
if (navigator.xr) {
  const soportado = await navigator.xr.isSessionSupported("immersive-vr");
  if (soportado) {
    const sesion = await navigator.xr.requestSession("immersive-vr");
  }
}
    Device WebXR Support
    Meta Quest 2/3/Pro ✅
    Apple Vision Pro ✅
    HTC Vive ✅
    PSVR2 ⚠ Limited
    Cardboard ✅

    📱 Augmented Reality (AR)¶

    Augmented Reality overlays digital elements onto the real world using the device's camera.

    // Check AR support
if (navigator.xr) {
  const soportado = await navigator.xr.isSessionSupported("immersive-ar");
  if (soportado) {
    const sesion = await navigator.xr.requestSession("immersive-ar", {
      requiredFeatures: ["hit-test"]
    });
  }
}
    Device AR Support
    Android (Chrome) ✅
    iPhone (Safari) ✅ (iOS 17+)
    Meta Quest ✅
    Apple Vision Pro ✅

    🎨 Three.js¶

    Three.js is the most popular 3D library for JavaScript. It works with WebXR.

    npm install three

    import * as THREE from "three";

const escena = new THREE.Scene();
const camara = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(75, innerWidth / innerHeight, 0.1, 1000);
const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: true });

renderer.setSize(innerWidth, innerHeight);
renderer.xr.enabled = true;
document.body.appendChild(renderer.domElement);

// A cube
const geometria = new THREE.BoxGeometry();
const material = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: 0x6a5acd });
const cubo = new THREE.Mesh(geometria, material);
escena.add(cubo);

camara.position.z = 5;

function animar() {
  cubo.rotation.x += 0.01;
  cubo.rotation.y += 0.01;
  renderer.render(escena, camara);
}

renderer.setAnimationLoop(animar);

    🖼 A-Frame¶

    A-Frame is a framework for building VR/AR experiences using declarative HTML. Great for rapid prototyping.

    <script src="[https://aframe.io/releases/1.5.0/aframe.min.js](https://aframe.io/releases/1.5.0/aframe.min.js)"></script>

<a-scene>
  <a-box position="-1 0.5 -3" rotation="0 45 0" color="#6a5acd"></a-box>
  <a-sphere position="0 1.25 -5" radius="1.25" color="#00bcd4"></a-sphere>
  <a-cylinder position="1 0.75 -3" radius="0.5" height="1.5" color="#ffc65d"></a-cylinder>
  <a-plane position="0 0 -4" rotation="-90 0 0" width="4" height="4" color="#7bc8a4"></a-plane>
  <a-sky color="#1a1726"></a-sky>
</a-scene>

    A-Frame vs. Three.js

    A-Frame is easier to start with (declarative HTML). Three.js is more powerful and flexible for large projects. Both work with WebXR.

    🎯 Real-World Use Cases¶

    Use Case Technology
    Virtual apartment tours WebXR + Three.js
    Trying furniture in AR WebXR + ARCore
    Virtual museums A-Frame
    Immersive education WebXR + Three.js
    Industrial VR training WebXR
    Virtual try-on stores WebXR + AR
    Browser games Three.js + WebXR
    3D data visualization Three.js

    ⚠ Limitations¶

    • Performance: phones and headsets have constrained GPUs.
    • Compatibility: not every device supports WebXR.
    • Permissions: users must approve entering VR/AR.
    • Battery: VR/AR drains battery quickly.
    • Learning curve: 3D is complex (geometry, materials, lights, camera).
    • Motion sickness: some experiences make users dizzy.

    Test on real devices

    Chrome's WebXR simulator is useful during development, but nothing replaces testing on a real headset or supported phone.

    ✅ Best Practices¶

    • ✅ Start simple: a spinning cube is already a milestone.
    • ✅ Use A-Frame for rapid prototypes.
    • ✅ Use Three.js for large projects.
    • ✅ Optimize 3D models (glTF, Draco compression).
    • ✅ Limit polygon count and textures.
    • ✅ Test on low-end devices.
    • ✅ Provide a fallback for devices without WebXR.
    • ❌ Don't assume everyone owns a headset.

    🥽 WebXR vs. WebVR vs. AR.js¶

    WebVR (legacy) Virtual reality in the browser ❌ Deprecated
    WebXR (modern) VR and AR in the browser ✅ Current standard

    WebXR is the W3C standard API for immersive experiences in the browser. It replaced WebVR in 2019 and added AR support.

    Chrome (Android) ✅ ✅

    🚀 Your First VR Scene with Three.js¶

    Three.js is the most widely used 3D library for WebXR. It abstracts the API and lets you create complex scenes with minimal code.

    Installation¶

    npm install three

    Minimal VR Scene¶

    import * as THREE from "three";
import { VRButton } from "three/addons/webxr/VRButton.js";

// 1. Scene, camera, and renderer
const escena = new THREE.Scene();
const camara = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(75, innerWidth / innerHeight, 0.1, 100);
const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: true });

renderer.setSize(innerWidth, innerHeight);
renderer.xr.enabled = true; // enable WebXR
document.body.appendChild(renderer.domElement);

// 2. "Enter VR" button
document.body.appendChild(VRButton.createButton(renderer));

// 3. A spinning cube
const geometria = new THREE.BoxGeometry(1, 1, 1);
const material = new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x6a5acd });
const cubo = new THREE.Mesh(geometria, material);
escena.add(cubo);

// 4. Light
escena.add(new THREE.AmbientLight(0xffffff, 1));

// 5. Camera
camara.position.z = 3;

// 6. Render loop
renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => {
    cubo.rotation.x += 0.01;
    cubo.rotation.y += 0.01;
    renderer.render(escena, camara);
});

    setAnimationLoop instead of requestAnimationFrame

    With WebXR, renderer.setAnimationLoop() is mandatory. requestAnimationFrame does not work in VR mode because the browser controls the headset's refresh rate.

    📱 AR in the Browser with WebXR¶

    Browser augmented reality works on supported mobile devices (Android with ARCore, iOS with ARKit via Safari).

    Minimal AR Scene¶

    import * as THREE from "three";
import { ARButton } from "three/addons/webxr/ARButton.js";

const escena = new THREE.Scene();
const camara = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera();
const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: true });
renderer.xr.enabled = true;
renderer.setSize(innerWidth, innerHeight);
document.body.appendChild(renderer.domElement);

// "View in AR" button
const boton = ARButton.createButton(renderer, { requiredFeatures: ["hit-test"] });
document.body.appendChild(boton);

// A floating cube
const cubo = new THREE.Mesh(
    new THREE.BoxGeometry(0.2, 0.2, 0.2),
    new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x00bcd4 })
);
cubo.position.set(0, 0, -1);
escena.add(cubo);

escena.add(new THREE.AmbientLight(0xffffff, 1));
camara.position.set(0, 0, 0);

renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => {
    cubo.rotation.y += 0.01;
    renderer.render(escena, camara);
});

    HTTPS is mandatory

    WebXR only works over HTTPS (or localhost). Over http://, the browser blocks camera access and AR APIs.

    🎮 Real-World Use Cases¶

    Use Case Example Maturity
    AR E-commerce Preview furniture in your living room before buying 🟢 Production
    Education 3D anatomy, virtual museums 🟢 Production
    Tourism AR guides in museums and cities 🟡 Growing
    Industrial training Machinery simulations in VR 🟢 Production
    Real estate Virtual apartment tours 🟢 Production
    Gaming Immersive browser experiences 🟡 Growing
    Events VR concerts and exhibitions 🟡 Growing

    Real Examples¶

    • IKEA Place — preview furniture in AR
    • Google Arts & Culture — museums in VR
    • Sketchfab — 3D models in AR
    • Amazon View in Your Room — AR in e-commerce

    ⚡ VR Performance¶

    VR is much more demanding than a standard webpage: steady 90 fps, stereoscopy (two renders per frame), and head tracking.

    Requirement VR Standard Web
    FPS 90+ (72 on Quest) 30-60
    Renders per frame 2 (one per eye) 1
    Latency less than 20 ms (motion sickness) less than 100 ms
    Triangles less than 100k per eye Millions possible

    Key Optimizations¶

    // 1. Cap pixel ratio (don't render at 4K)
renderer.setPixelRatio(Math.min(devicePixelRatio, 2));

// 2. Disable shadows or keep them simple
renderer.shadowMap.enabled = false; // or THREE.PCFSoftShadowMap

// 3. Geometries with LOD
const lod = new THREE.LOD();
lod.addLevel(meshDetallado, 0);
lod.addLevel(meshSimple, 50);

// 4. Frustum culling (Three.js enables this by default)
// 5. InstancedMesh for many identical objects
const instancias = new THREE.InstancedMesh(geometria, material, 1000);

    Motion sickness is real

    When latency exceeds 20 ms, users experience motion sickness (dizziness, nausea). That's why VR isn't for everyone. Always prioritize FPS over visual fidelity.

    🧪 Hands-On Exercise¶

    VR Scene with an Interactive Cube

    Create a Three.js VR scene that:

    • Has a spinning cube in the center.
    • Changes color when clicked (with a VR controller).
    • Has an "Enter VR" button that hides on unsupported mobile devices.
    Solution 
    import * as THREE from "three";
import { VRButton } from "three/addons/webxr/VRButton.js";

const escena = new THREE.Scene();
const camara = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(75, innerWidth / innerHeight, 0.1, 100);
const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: true });
renderer.setSize(innerWidth, innerHeight);
renderer.xr.enabled = true;
document.body.appendChild(renderer.domElement);
document.body.appendChild(VRButton.createButton(renderer));

const cubo = new THREE.Mesh(
    new THREE.BoxGeometry(1, 1, 1),
    new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x6a5acd })
);
escena.add(cubo);
escena.add(new THREE.AmbientLight(0xffffff, 1));
camara.position.z = 3;

// Change color on click (with VR controller)
cubo.addEventListener("select", () => {
    cubo.material.color.setHex(Math.random() * 0xffffff);
});

renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => {
    cubo.rotation.y += 0.01;
    renderer.render(escena, camara);
});

    🧠 Review Quiz¶

    Check what you learned

    1. What is the difference between WebVR and WebXR?

    WebVR was the legacy API (VR only). WebXR is the modern API supporting VR and AR in the browser. It replaced WebVR in 2019.

    2. Why is renderer.setAnimationLoop mandatory in VR?

    Because the browser controls the headset refresh rate (90 Hz). requestAnimationFrame does not work in VR mode: the browser needs to decide when to render each eye.

    3. How many FPS does VR need?

    90 FPS (72 on Meta Quest). That is double a typical webpage, because the human brain detects motion with high precision and low FPS causes motion sickness.

    4. What is motion sickness in VR?

    The dizziness caused by VR when latency exceeds 20 ms or FPS drops. The brain expects visual motion to match body movement, and when it doesn't, motion sickness occurs.

    5. Which real-world use case uses WebXR in production?

    IKEA Place (furniture in AR), Amazon View in Your Room (AR e-commerce), Google Arts & Culture (VR museums), Sketchfab (3D models in AR), industrial VR training.

    30 — Web3¶

    What you will learn

    • What Web3 is (and what it is not).
    • Blockchain as the underlying technology.
    • Smart contracts and their role in DApps.
    • The typical stack: Ethereum, Solidity, ethers.js, IPFS.
    • Real-world use cases, limitations, and criticisms.

    🌐 What is Web3?¶

    Web3 (or Web 3.0) is a set of technologies aiming for a decentralized web, where data and logic do not depend on a central company, but on a network of nodes that validate one another.

    The public ledger analogy

    Imagine an account ledger kept not by a bank, but by thousands of people at once. Every time someone records a transaction, everyone else verifies and copies it. If someone tries to alter a past line, the others detect it because it doesn't match their copies. That is, in essence, a blockchain.

    graph LR
    U1[User] --> W[Wallet]
    W --> SC[Smart Contract]
    SC --> BC[(Blockchain)]
    BC --> N1[Node 1]
    BC --> N2[Node 2]
    BC --> N3[Node 3]

    🔗 Blockchain as the Foundation¶

    A blockchain is a distributed, append-only (only added to, never deleted) database validated by consensus. Each block contains:

    Field What It Stores
    Transactions The operations (transfers, contract calls)
    Previous block hash Links to the prior block (hence "chain")
    Own hash Identifies the block
    Timestamp When it was mined/validated
    Nonce Proof of work (in Proof of Work)

    Practical immutability

    Once a block has enough confirmations (6 in Bitcoin, 12-64 in Ethereum depending on the context), altering it would require rewriting the entire chain from that point on. That is why it is called practically immutable.

    🏛 Smart Contracts¶

    A smart contract is code that runs on the blockchain. Once deployed, nobody can modify it (unless the contract itself includes upgrade functions).

    // SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

contract Contador {
    uint256 public total;

    function incrementar() public {
        total += 1;
    }
}
    • public total → state variable, readable by anyone.
    • incrementar() → function that modifies state. Costs gas (fee).
    • Deploying it costs gas. Calling it also does.

    Code is law

    A bug in a smart contract can cost millions. There is no "rollback" or "customer support". That's why they are audited and thoroughly tested before deployment. The DAO hack (2016, ~$60M) is the classic example.

    🧰 The Typical Web3 Stack¶

    Layer Technology Purpose
    Blockchain Ethereum, Polygon, Solana, Arbitrum Execute contracts
    Contract language Solidity, Vyper, Rust (Solana) Write smart contracts
    JS client ethers.js, viem, web3.js Talk to the blockchain from the frontend
    Wallet MetaMask, Rainbow, WalletConnect Sign transactions
    Storage IPFS, Arweave, Filecoin Store decentralized files
    Indexing The Graph Query on-chain data efficiently
    RPC node Alchemy, Infura, QuickNode Network access without running a node

    Ethereum isn't the only one

    Ethereum is the most widely used, but Polygon (an Ethereum sidechain) is cheaper to get started with. Solana is faster with a different model. Arbitrum/Optimism are L2s (Layer 2) that inherit Ethereum's security with lower fees.

    📝 Your First DApp in 4 Steps¶

    A DApp (decentralized application) is a web frontend that talks to smart contracts.

    1. Connect the Wallet¶

    import { BrowserProvider } from "ethers";

async function conectar() {
    if (!window.ethereum) {
        alert("Instala MetaMask");
        return;
    }
    const provider = new BrowserProvider(window.ethereum);
    const signer = await provider.getSigner();
    const address = await signer.getAddress();
    console.log("Conectado como", address);
}

    2. Read Contract State¶

    import { Contract } from "ethers";

const ABI = ["function total() view returns (uint256)"];
const DIRECCION = "0x...";

async function leerTotal(provider) {
    const contrato = new Contract(DIRECCION, ABI, provider);
    const total = await contrato.total();
    console.log("Total:", total.toString());
}

    3. Write (Transaction)¶

    async function incrementar(signer) {
    const contrato = new Contract(DIRECCION, ABI, signer);
    const tx = await contrato.incrementar();
    await tx.wait();
    console.log("Hecho:", tx.hash);
}

    4. Listen to Events¶

    contrato.on("Incrementado", (nuevoTotal) => {
    console.log("Nuevo total:", nuevoTotal.toString());
});

    Gas and fees

    Every write to the blockchain costs gas. On Ethereum L1 it can be expensive (dollars per transaction). On L2s (Arbitrum, Polygon) it's cents. Always check gasEstimate before sending.

    🎯 Real-World Use Cases¶

    Use Case Example Maturity
    DeFi (finance) Uniswap, Aave, Compound 🟢 Production
    NFTs OpenSea, Foundation 🟢 Production
    DAOs Snapshot, Aragon 🟡 Growing
    Identity ENS, Worldcoin 🟡 Growing
    Gaming Axie Infinity, Gods Unchained 🟡 Growing
    Supply chain IBM Food Trust, VeChain 🟠 Niche
    Voting (experimental) 🔴 Low maturity
    Social networks Farcaster, Lens 🟠 Niche

    ⚠ Limitations and Criticisms¶

    Limitation Detail
    Scalability Ethereum L1 does ~15 TPS; Visa does ~24,000
    Cost A swap on L1 can cost €5-€50
    UX Managing wallets and gas is complex for non-technical users
    Security Contract bugs = total loss; wallet phishing is very common
    Regulation Varies by country; affects tokens and DeFi
    De facto centralization Many RPC nodes run on Alchemy/Infura; many NFTs sit on central servers
    Inflated claims "Decentralizing everything" isn't always viable or desirable

    Web3 isn't the answer to everything

    For an internal management app, a Postgres database is still better. Web3 shines when trust between parties is the problem—not when the problem is speed or convenience.

    🏗 DApp Architecture¶

    graph TD
    U[User] --> F[Frontend React/Next]
    F --> W[MetaMask]
    W --> SC[Smart Contract]
    SC --> BC[(Blockchain)]
    F --> IPFS[IPFS: metadata]
    F --> G[The Graph: queries]
    G --> BC
    • The frontend can be a static Next.js app.
    • The wallet signs transactions.
    • The contract executes logic.
    • IPFS stores files (images, NFT metadata).
    • The Graph indexes events for fast queries (avoids scanning the entire chain).

    🧪 Hands-On Exercise¶

    Read the total of a deployed counter

    You have a Contador contract deployed on Sepolia (testnet) at address 0x1234... with the total() function.

    Write an ethers.js script that:

    • Connects to Sepolia using a public RPC (https://rpc.sepolia.org).
    • Reads total() from the contract.
    • Logs it to the console.
    Solution 
    import { JsonRpcProvider, Contract } from "ethers";

const RPC = "https://rpc.sepolia.org";
const DIRECCION = "0x1234...";
const ABI = ["function total() view returns (uint256)"];

async function main() {
    const provider = new JsonRpcProvider(RPC);
    const contrato = new Contract(DIRECCION, ABI, provider);
    const total = await contrato.total();
    console.log("Total on-chain:", total.toString());
}

main().catch(console.error);

    Note: reading doesn't require a wallet or gas, only an RPC. Writing does.

    🧠 Quiz¶

    Check what you learned

    1. What is the difference between a blockchain and a traditional database?

    A blockchain is distributed, append-only, consensus-validated, and practically immutable. A traditional database is centralized, mutable, and managed by an entity.

    2. What is a smart contract?

    Code that runs on the blockchain. Once deployed, it is immutable (barring explicit upgrade functions).

    3. Why does writing to Ethereum cost gas while reading does not?

    Reading (view) doesn't modify state or require consensus; writing does, and miners/validators charge for execution and storage.

    4. What is a DApp?

    A decentralized application: a web frontend that interacts with smart contracts through a wallet (MetaMask, etc.).

    5. When does using Web3 NOT make sense?

    When trust between parties isn't the problem (e.g., internal apps, CRUDs, dashboards). A traditional database is faster, cheaper, and simpler.

    ⚡ Nivel 7 — Sistemas, Edge y Producción

    31 — E2E Testing¶

    What you will learn

    • What an End-to-End test is and how it differs from unit and integration tests.
    • Main tools: Playwright, Cypress, Selenium.
    • How to write your first E2E test.
    • Patterns: Page Object Model, fixtures, waits.
    • When to use E2E and when NOT to.

    🎯 What is an E2E Test?¶

    An End-to-End (E2E) test simulates a real user interacting with your application: it opens the browser, clicks, types, navigates, and verifies that the outcome matches expectations.

    The test driver analogy

    A unit test is like inspecting every car part in isolation. An E2E test is like putting a test driver behind the wheel for a full road lap: it verifies everything works together under real conditions.

    graph LR
    A[E2E Test] --> B[Opens browser]
    B --> C[Navigates to app]
    C --> D[Interacts: click, keyboard, scroll]
    D --> E[Verifies results]
    E --> F[✅ Passes / ❌ Fails]

    🏛 E2E vs. Unit vs. Integration¶

    Type What It Tests Speed Cost Example
    Unit A single function or isolated component ⚡ Very fast (ms) Low sum(2,2) === 4
    Integration Multiple modules working together 🚀 Fast (100ms) Medium API + DB + service
    E2E The full app from the browser 🐢 Slow (seconds) High Login → cart → checkout

    The testing pyramid

    Many unit tests, some integration tests, few E2E tests. E2E tests are slow and fragile; reserve them for critical flows: login, checkout, signup, payment.

    🛠 Main Tools¶

    Tool Language Speed Cross-Browser Notes
    Playwright JS/TS, Python, C#, Java ⚡ Very fast ✅ Chromium, Firefox, WebKit Microsoft, very active
    Cypress JS/TS 🚀 Fast ⚠ Chromium only (Firefox experimental) Great DX, popular
    Selenium Multiple 🐢 Slow ✅ All The classic, more verbose
    Puppeteer JS/TS 🚀 Fast ⚠ Chromium only Chrome/Edge only
    WebdriverIO JS/TS 🐢 Medium ✅ All Built on WebDriver

    2026 Recommendation

    Playwright if you need cross-browser support or fast CI runs. Cypress if you prioritize DX and only care about Chromium. Selenium only for legacy systems or very old browsers.

    📝 Your First Test with Playwright¶

    Installation¶

    npm init playwright@latest

    Choose TypeScript, tests/ folder, and GitHub Actions if you want CI.

    Basic Test¶

    // tests/login.spec.js
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("login con credenciales válidas", async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto("https://mi-app.com/login");
    await page.fill('input[name="email"]', "user@example.com");
    await page.fill('input[name="password"]', "secreto123");
    await page.click('button[type="submit"]');
    await expect(page).toHaveURL("https://mi-app.com/dashboard");
    await expect(page.locator("h1")).toHaveText("Bienvenido");
});

    Running Tests¶

    npx playwright test
npx playwright test --headed        # show the browser
npx playwright test --ui             # interactive mode
npx playwright show-report           # view HTML report

    🧩 Key Patterns¶

    1. Page Object Model (POM)¶

    Encapsulates interactions with a page inside a class. Avoids duplicating selectors across tests.

    // pages/LoginPage.js
export class LoginPage {
    constructor(page) {
        this.page = page;
        this.email = 'input[name="email"]';
        this.password = 'input[name="password"]';
        this.submit = 'button[type="submit"]';
    }

    async goto() {
        await this.page.goto("/login");
    }

    async login(email, pass) {
        await this.page.fill(this.email, email);
        await this.page.fill(this.password, pass);
        await this.page.click(this.submit);
    }
}

    // tests/login.spec.js
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";
import { LoginPage } from "../pages/LoginPage";

test("login válido", async ({ page }) => {
    const login = new LoginPage(page);
    await login.goto();
    await login.login("user@example.com", "secreto123");
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/dashboard/);
});

    2. Fixtures¶

    Playwright injects page, context, and browser automatically. You can define custom fixtures:

    // fixtures.js
import { test as base } from "@playwright/test";
import { LoginPage } from "./pages/LoginPage";

export const test = base.extend({
    loginPage: async ({ page }, use) => {
        const login = new LoginPage(page);
        await login.goto();
        await use(login);
    },
});

    import { test, expect } from "./fixtures";

test("login", async ({ loginPage, page }) => {
    await loginPage.login("user@example.com", "secreto123");
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/dashboard/);
});

    3. Auto-Waits¶

    Playwright automatically waits for elements to be visible, enabled, and actionable. Never use sleep().

    // ✅ Playwright waits on its own
await page.click('button[type="submit"]');

// ❌ Don't do this
await page.waitForTimeout(2000);

    4. Recommended Selectors¶

    Selector When to Use It
    getByRole('button', { name: 'Enviar' }) ✅ Recommended (accessible and resilient)
    getByLabel('Email') Form inputs with a label
    getByText('Bienvenido') Visible text
    getByTestId('login-btn') When there's no clear role/label
    locator('css=.btn-primary') CSS (more brittle)

    Use getByRole first

    Selectors based on accessible role (getByRole) are the most resilient: they survive class, ID, or markup changes, while also checking accessibility.

    🏗 Example: Checkout Flow¶

    import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("checkout completo", async ({ page }) => {
    // 1. Login
    await page.goto("/login");
    await page.getByLabel("Email").fill("user@example.com");
    await page.getByLabel("Contraseña").fill("secreto123");
    await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Entrar" }).click();

    // 2. Add to cart
    await page.goto("/productos");
    await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Añadir al carrito" }).first().click();

    // 3. Go to cart
    await page.getByRole("link", { name: "Carrito" }).click();
    await expect(page.getByText("Teclado mecánico")).toBeVisible();

    // 4. Checkout
    await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Pagar" }).click();
    await page.getByLabel("Tarjeta").fill("4242424242424242");
    await page.getByLabel("Caducidad").fill("12/30");
    await page.getByLabel("CVC").fill("123");
    await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Confirmar pago" }).click();

    // 5. Verify
    await expect(page.getByText("Pago exitoso")).toBeVisible();
});

    ⚠ When NOT to Use E2E¶

    Case Why
    Complex business logic Better covered by fast unit tests
    Form validations Validator unit tests
    Isolated components Storybook + component tests
    Performance Use Lighthouse or k6, not E2E
    Every commit E2E is slow; in CI run in parallel or on PRs only

    Fragile E2E = ignored E2E

    An E2E test that fails randomly (flaky) is worse than having no test: the team learns to ignore failures. Invest in stability: resilient selectors, auto-waits, isolated test data.

    🚀 E2E in CI¶

    # .github/workflows/e2e.yml
name: E2E
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps
      - run: npx playwright test
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: failure()
        with:
          name: playwright-report
          path: playwright-report/

    CI best practices: - Run in parallel (--workers=4). - Retry suspicious failures (--retries=2). - Upload the HTML report as an artifact on failure. - Cache Playwright dependencies.

    🧪 Hands-On Exercise¶

    Login test with 3 cases

    Write E2E tests for an app's login flow covering:

    • Case 1: valid credentials → redirects to /dashboard.
    • Case 2: wrong password → shows "Credenciales inválidas".
    • Case 3: empty email → button is disabled or shows an error.
    Solution 
    import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test.describe("Login", () => {
    test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
        await page.goto("/login");
    });

    test("credenciales válidas", async ({ page }) => {
        await page.getByLabel("Email").fill("user@example.com");
        await page.getByLabel("Contraseña").fill("secreto123");
        await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Entrar" }).click();
        await expect(page).toHaveURL(/dashboard/);
    });

    test("contraseña incorrecta", async ({ page }) => {
        await page.getByLabel("Email").fill("user@example.com");
        await page.getByLabel("Contraseña").fill("mal");
        await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Entrar" }).click();
        await expect(page.getByText("Credenciales inválidas")).toBeVisible();
    });

    test("email vacío deshabilita el botón", async ({ page }) => {
        await page.getByLabel("Contraseña").fill("secreto123");
        await expect(
            page.getByRole("button", { name: "Entrar" })
        ).toBeDisabled();
    });
});

    🧠 Quiz¶

    Check what you learned

    1. What is the difference between a unit test and an E2E test?

    Unit: tests an isolated function or component, milliseconds. E2E: tests the full app from the browser, seconds or minutes.

    2. What is the general recommendation (testing pyramid)?

    Many unit tests, some integration tests, few E2E tests. E2E only for critical flows.

    3. What is the Page Object Model?

    A pattern that encapsulates page interactions in a class, avoiding duplicate selectors and making maintenance easier.

    4. Why shouldn't you use sleep() or waitForTimeout() in Playwright?

    Because Playwright already waits automatically for elements to be ready. Fixed sleeps make tests slow and brittle.

    5. What is a "flaky" test?

    A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails with no code changes. Worse than no test, because it teaches the team to ignore failures.

    32 — Server Components¶

    What you will learn

    • What React Server Components (RSC) are and what problem they solve.
    • The difference between Server and Client Components.
    • How the hybrid rendering model works.
    • When to use each component type.
    • Common pitfalls and best practices.

    🌐 What Are Server Components?¶

    React Server Components (RSC) are components that run on the server and send a serialized React tree to the client, without including those components' JavaScript code in the browser bundle.

    The restaurant analogy

    A Client Component is like cooking at home: you have every ingredient and utensil (JavaScript) in your kitchen (browser), even if you don't use them all. A Server Component is like ordering delivery: the restaurant (server) cooks and sends you the finished dish (HTML/serialized React) without you having to lug the whole kitchen around.

    graph LR
    A[Source Code] --> B{Server or Client?}
    B -->|Server Component| C[Runs on server]
    B -->|Client Component| D[Runs in browser]
    C --> E[Serializes to RSC Payload]
    D --> F[Sends JS to bundle]
    E --> G[Renders in browser]
    F --> G

    🏛 Server vs. Client Components¶

    Feature Server Component Client Component
    Directive None (default in App Router) "use client" at top of file
    Runs on Server Browser (and server during SSR)
    Backend access ✅ Direct (database, FS, secrets) ❌ Via API only
    Hooks (useState, useEffect) ❌ No ✅ Yes
    Event handlers (onClick, etc.) ❌ No ✅ Yes
    Browser APIs (window, localStorage) ❌ No ✅ Yes
    Adds to JS bundle size ❌ No ✅ Yes
    Can import Client Components ✅ Yes ✅ Yes
    Can import Server Components ❌ No (but can receive as children) ❌ No

    Rule of thumb

    Server Component by default. Only add "use client" when you need interactivity (hooks, events, browser APIs).

    🔄 The Hybrid Model¶

    In Next.js App Router (and similar frameworks), components are Server by default. Communication flows like this:

    sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client (browser)
    participant S as Server
    participant DB as Database
    C->>S: Page request
    S->>DB: Direct query
    DB->>S: Data
    S->>S: Renders Server Components
    S->>C: RSC Payload + HTML + Client Component JS
    C->>C: Hydrates Client Components

    Flow: 1. The browser requests a route. 2. The server runs Server Components (including database queries). 3. The server serializes the result and sends: - Initial HTML (for fast first paint). - The RSC Payload (component structure for hydration). - Client Component JS (for interactivity). 4. The browser hydrates Client Components.

    🏷 The "use client" Directive¶

    It is a string literal at the top of a file (before any import) that marks the entry point into client code:

    "use client";

import { useState } from "react";

export default function Contador() {
    const [n, setN] = useState(0);
    return <button onClick={() => setN(n + 1)}>Clicks: {n}</button>;
}

    Not a magic directive

    "use client" does not mean "this only runs in the browser". The component also renders on the server (SSR), while its JS code is shipped to the browser for hydration. What changes is that it can use hooks and event handlers.

    Boundary rules: - A Client Component cannot import a Server Component. - However, it can receive one as children or as a prop (the "children pattern").

    // page.js (Server Component)
import ClientWrapper from "./client-wrapper";
import ServerChart from "./server-chart"; // is a Server Component

export default function Page() {
    return (
        <ClientWrapper>
            <ServerChart />
        </ClientWrapper>
    );
}

    // client-wrapper.js
"use client";
export default function ClientWrapper({ children }) {
    return <div onClick={() => console.log("click")}>{children}</div>;
}

    🎯 When to Use Each One¶

    Server Component (Default)¶

    • ✅ Data fetching (DB, external APIs, FS).
    • ✅ Accessing environment variables and secrets.
    • ✅ Rendering static or data-driven content.
    • ✅ Large non-interactive components (lists, layouts, pages).
    • ✅ Shrinking the client JS bundle.

    Client Component ("use client")¶

    • ✅ useState, useEffect, useReducer, useContext.
    • ✅ Event handlers (onClick, onChange, onSubmit).
    • ✅ Browser APIs (window, document, localStorage, IntersectionObserver).
    • ✅ DOM-dependent libraries (Chart.js, Mapbox, etc.).

    Isolate interactivity

    A strong pattern is pairing Server pages with Client islands: the page renders on the server, and only interactive parts (buttons, forms, modals) use "use client". That keeps the JS bundle small.

    📝 Complete Example: Dashboard¶

    // app/dashboard/page.js  (Server Component)
import { db } from "@/lib/db";
import BotonRefrescar from "./boton-refrescar";

export default async function Dashboard() {
    const ventas = await db.ventas.findMany(); // direct query
    const total = ventas.reduce((s, v) => s + v.monto, 0);

    return (
        <div>
            <h1>Ventas totales: {total} €</h1>
            <ul>
                {ventas.map((v) => (
                    <li key={v.id}>{v.producto}: {v.monto} €</li>
                ))}
            </ul>
            <BotonRefrescar />
        </div>
    );
}

    // app/dashboard/boton-refrescar.js  (Client Component)
"use client";

import { useRouter } from "next/navigation";

export default function BotonRefrescar() {
    const router = useRouter();
    return <button onClick={() => router.refresh()}>Refrescar</button>;
}

    What you get: - The DB query runs on the server (the client never sees credentials). - The browser JS bundle does not include dashboard code, only the button's. - The button itself is interactive (Client Component).

    ⚠ Common Mistakes¶

    Error What Happens Fix
    Using useState in a Server Component Build error Add "use client" to the file
    Importing fs or pg in a Client Component Build error (modules unavailable) Move logic to a Server Component
    Importing a Server Component inside a Client Component Build error Pass it as children or a prop
    Forgetting "use client" on a component with onClick Error: "Event handlers cannot be passed to Client Component props" Add "use client"
    Accessing window on initial render Hydration error Wrap in useEffect or check typeof window !== "undefined"

    Most common error

    Event handlers cannot be passed to Client Component props. Happens when trying to pass a function (such as onClick) from a Server Component to a Client Component. Props crossing from Server to Client must be serializable (numbers, strings, arrays, plain objects)—not functions.

    🏗 Recommended Architecture¶

    graph TD
    A[app/layout.js] -->|Server| B[app/page.js]
    B -->|Server| C[Product list]
    B -->|Server| D[Product detail]
    C -->|Client island| E[Add to cart button]
    D -->|Client island| F[Quantity selector]
    E --> G[Cart context]
    F --> G

    Rule: Server at the top, Client at the leaves (islands).

    🧪 Hands-On Exercise¶

    Turn an interactive component into a hybrid

    You have a component with a counter. Split it into:

    • A Server Component Producto that loads product data (simulated via fetch to an API).
    • A Client Component Contador with a button that increments by 1 on click.

    The Server Component should render the product name and the Client Component below it.

    Solution 
    // app/producto/page.js  (Server Component)
import Contador from "./contador";

async function getProducto() {
    return { id: 1, nombre: "Teclado mecánico", precio: 89 };
}

export default async function Producto() {
    const prod = await getProducto();
    return (
        <div>
            <h1>{prod.nombre}</h1>
            <p>Precio: {prod.precio} €</p>
            <Contador />
        </div>
    );
}

    // app/producto/contador.js  (Client Component)
"use client";
import { useState } from "react";

export default function Contador() {
    const [n, setN] = useState(0);
    return (
        <div>
            <p>Cantidad: {n}</p>
            <button onClick={() => setN(n + 1)}>Añadir uno</button>
        </div>
    );
}

    🧠 Quiz¶

    Check what you learned

    1. Are Server Components sent to the browser bundle?

    No. Only the RSC Payload (serialized representation) is sent. The component's JS code stays on the server.

    2. What is "use client" for?

    It marks the entry point into client code. It indicates that the component and its imports can use hooks, event handlers, and browser APIs, and includes its JS in the bundle.

    3. Can a Client Component import a Server Component?

    Not directly. However, it can receive one as children or as a prop from a parent Server Component.

    4. What kind of props can pass from Server to Client?

    Only serializable props: strings, numbers, booleans, arrays, plain objects, dates, null (and undefined is allowed). Not functions, classes, or symbols.

    5. What is the recommended architecture pattern?

    Server at the top, Client at the leaves: pages and layouts on the server, interactive islands (buttons, forms, modals) as Client Components.

    • Next.js — Client Components
    • RFC original de React Server Components
    • Patrones de composición Server/Client

    33 — Edge Computing¶

    What you will learn

    • What Edge Computing is and why it matters.
    • The difference between a traditional CDN and Edge Functions.
    • Popular platforms: Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Edge, Deno Deploy.
    • Real-world use cases: personalization, A/B testing, geolocation.
    • Limitations and when NOT to use edge.

    🌍 What is Edge Computing?¶

    Edge Computing is running code as close to the user as possible, instead of on a central server. Rather than routing every request to a single data center, requests are handled across a global network of nodes.

    The supermarket analogy

    A central server is like having one single store in Madrid for all of Spain: convenient for the owner, yet a customer in Barcelona takes 6 hours to get there. Edge Computing is like having a store in every city: same goods, much closer to the customer.

    graph LR
    U1[Madrid User] --> E1[Madrid Edge]
    U2[Tokyo User] --> E2[Tokyo Edge]
    U3[NY User] --> E3[NY Edge]
    E1 --> DB[(Central Database)]
    E2 --> DB
    E3 --> DB

    Each user reaches the nearest node, which responds in milliseconds.

    ⚡ CDN vs. Edge Functions¶

    Traditional CDN Edge Functions
    What it does Serves static files (HTML, CSS, JS, images) Runs code at the edge node
    Logic None (caching only) JavaScript, TypeScript, Rust, WASM
    Personalization Limited to headers Full (read cookies, geolocation, etc.)
    Latency Low for static assets Low for everything (including logic)
    Example Cloudflare CDN, Fastly Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Edge

    CDN = delivering files. Edge = delivering files and running code near the user.

    Rule of thumb

    Use a CDN for all static assets (images, fonts, client JS). Use Edge Functions for logic that benefits from proximity to the user: redirects, personalization, authentication, geolocation.

    🚀 Popular Platforms¶

    Platform Language Free Tier Ideal Use Cases
    Cloudflare Workers JS/TS, Rust, WASM 100,000 req/day Lightweight APIs, middleware, A/B testing
    Vercel Edge Functions JS/TS 100 GB-hours/month Next.js apps, personalization
    Deno Deploy JS/TS 100,000 req/day APIs, bots, webhooks
    Netlify Edge Functions JS/TS 1M invocations/month JAMstack middleware
    AWS Lambda@Edge Node.js, Python Pay per use CloudFront integration

    Not all edge platforms are equal

    Cloudflare Workers uses V8 Isolates (not containers), starting up in less than 5 ms. Traditional Lambdas take 100-500 ms on cold start. For edge, isolates are the standard.

    🧩 Real-World Use Cases¶

    1. Geolocation and Redirects¶

    // Cloudflare Worker: redirects based on country
export default {
    async fetch(request) {
        const country = request.cf.country;
        if (country === "ES") {
            return Response.redirect("https://es.mi-sitio.com", 302);
        }
        return fetch(request);
    },
};

    2. Backendless A/B Testing¶

    // Vercel Edge Function: assigns variant from cookie
export const config = { runtime: "edge" };

export default function handler(request) {
    const cookie = request.headers.get("cookie") || "";
    const variant = cookie.includes("variant=b") ? "b" : "a";
    return new Response(JSON.stringify({ variant }), {
        headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
    });
}

    3. HTML Personalization¶

    // Deno Deploy: injects user name into HTML
Deno.serve(async (req) => {
    const url = new URL(req.url);
    const user = url.searchParams.get("user") || "invitado";
    const res = await fetch("https://mi-sitio.com/index.html");
    const html = await res.text();
    const personalized = html.replace("{{user}}", user);
    return new Response(personalized, {
        headers: { "content-type": "text/html" },
    });
});

    4. Edge Authentication¶

    Validating a JWT at the edge avoids hitting the central server. Invalid tokens are rejected in milliseconds without consuming backend resources.

    Most common pattern

    Authentication middleware at the edge + business logic on the central server. The edge filters out 90% of malicious traffic; the server only processes legitimate requests.

    ⚠ Edge Limitations¶

    Limitation Why
    No persistent local state Each request may hit a different node
    No filesystem Only standard Web APIs (fetch, KV, D1, R2)
    Short timeouts Cloudflare Workers: 50 ms CPU per request (free)
    Memory limits Typically 128 MB
    Restricted APIs No fs, child_process, or native Node modules
    Cold starts (some) Vercel/Netlify can have slower startups

    When NOT to use edge

    • Heavy processing (images, video, ML).
    • Operations needing shared real-time state.
    • Logic relying on a high-latency traditional relational DB (unless using serverless D1/Turso/Neon).
    • Long-running tasks (greater than 30 s).

    🏗 Typical Edge Architecture¶

    graph TD
    U[User] --> C[Edge CDN]
    C -->|static| H[HTML/CSS/JS]
    C -->|dynamic| F[Edge Function]
    F -->|auth| A[Edge Auth]
    A -->|valid| B[Central Backend]
    A -->|invalid| R[401 Unauthorized]
    B --> DB[(Database)]

    Flow: 1. The user requests a page. 2. The CDN serves static files. 3. If logic is needed, the Edge Function runs it. 4. Only valid requests reach the central backend.

    🧪 Hands-On Exercise¶

    Authentication middleware at the edge

    Write an Edge Function (Cloudflare Workers) that:

    • Reads an Authorization: Bearer <token> header.
    • Lets the request pass through if the token is "secreto123".
    • Otherwise returns 401 Unauthorized with JSON { "error": "No autorizado" }.
    Solution 
    export default {
    async fetch(request) {
        const auth = request.headers.get("Authorization") || "";
        const token = auth.replace("Bearer ", "");

        if (token !== "secreto123") {
            return new Response(
                JSON.stringify({ error: "No autorizado" }),
                {
                    status: 401,
                    headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
                }
            );
        }

        return fetch(request);
    },
};

    🧠 Quiz¶

    Check what you learned

    1. What is the difference between a CDN and an Edge Function?

    A CDN only serves static files; an Edge Function executes code at the node closest to the user.

    2. Why is Cloudflare Workers faster than Lambda@Edge on cold start?

    Workers uses V8 Isolates (startup less than 5 ms) instead of containers (startup 100-500 ms).

    3. What should you NOT do at the edge?

    Heavy processing (images, video, ML), operations with shared real-time state, or tasks over 30 s.

    4. What is the most common edge pattern in production?

    Authentication middleware at the edge + business logic on the central server.

    5. Which APIs do Cloudflare Edge Functions use to run?

    Standard Web APIs (fetch, Request, Response, URL, crypto). They do not have access to fs, child_process, or native Node modules.

    34 — Docker for Frontend¶

    What you will learn

    • What Docker is and why to use it for frontend.
    • Images and containers.
    • Dockerfile for a frontend app.
    • Multi-stage builds.
    • Docker Compose.

    🐳 What is Docker?¶

    Docker packages your application with all its dependencies into a container. That container behaves the same way on your laptop, on your company's server, and in production.

    Without Docker: "it works on my machine" 🤷
With Docker:    "it works everywhere" ✅

    A container is a sealed box

    Inside it carries your app, Node.js, dependencies, and configuration. Outside, whatever operating system is running doesn't matter: it executes the same way.

    📦 Images and Containers¶

    Concept What It Is
    Image Read-only template containing the app and its dependencies
    Container Running instance of an image
    Dockerfile Recipe to build an image
    Registry Image repository (Docker Hub)
    Volume Persistent storage
    Network Virtual network between containers 
    docker pull nginx:alpine
docker run -p 8080:80 nginx:alpine
docker ps
docker stop <id>
docker rm <id>

    📝 Dockerfile for Frontend¶

    # Stage 1: build
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci

COPY . .
RUN npm run build

# Stage 2: serve with Nginx
FROM nginx:alpine
COPY --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf

EXPOSE 80
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]

    docker build -t mi-frontend .
docker run -p 8080:80 mi-frontend

    🏗 Multi-Stage Build¶

    The Dockerfile above uses two stages:

    1. build: installs dependencies and builds the app (large image).
    2. runtime: copies only static files into Nginx (small image).
    Image Size
    Single-stage ~1 GB
    Multi-stage ~25 MB

    Always use multi-stage

    The final image only contains Nginx and the static files. Node.js and dependencies stay in the build stage, which gets discarded.

    ⚙ nginx.conf¶

    server {
  listen 80;
  root /usr/share/nginx/html;
  index index.html;

  # SPA: redirect everything to index.html
  location / {
    try_files $uri$uri/ /index.html;
  }

  # Asset caching
  location ~* \.(js|css|png|jpg|svg|woff2)$ {
    expires 1y;
    add_header Cache-Control "public, immutable";
  }
}

    🐙 Docker Compose¶

    Docker Compose lets you define and run multiple containers at once (frontend + backend + database) with a single file.

    # docker-compose.yml
services:
  frontend:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
    depends_on:
      - api

  api:
    build: ./api
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      - DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@db:5432/miapp
    depends_on:
      - db

  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: pass
      POSTGRES_DB: miapp
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  postgres_data:

    docker compose up -d
docker compose down
docker compose logs -f

    ✅ Best Practices¶

    • ✅ Multi-stage build: small final image.
    • ✅ npm ci instead of npm install in Docker (faster and reproducible).
    • ✅ .dockerignore so you don't copy node_modules, .git, etc.
    • ✅ Non-root user inside the container.
    • ✅ Layer caching: copy package.json before the rest.
    • ✅ Pin versions: node:20.11-alpine, not node:latest.
    • ✅ Healthchecks to verify the container is healthy.
    • ❌ Don't put secrets in the Dockerfile.
    # .dockerignore
node_modules
.git
.env
dist
*.log

    35 — GraphQL¶

    What you will learn

    • What GraphQL is and how it differs from REST.
    • Schema and types.
    • Queries, mutations, and subscriptions.
    • Apollo Client.
    • When to use GraphQL and when not to.

    🔷 What is GraphQL?¶

    GraphQL is a query language for APIs created by Facebook. Unlike REST, the client asks for the exact data it needs, nothing more and nothing less.

    REST:     GET /usuarios/1 → returns the ENTIRE user
GraphQL:  query { usuario(id: 1) { nombre } } → only the name

    Ask for what you need, nothing more

    With REST, you sometimes get 50 fields when you only need 2. With GraphQL, you ask for those exact 2. That saves bandwidth, especially on mobile.

    📜 Schema¶

    The schema defines the available types and operations. It is the contract between client and server.

    type Usuario {
  id: ID!
  nombre: String!
  email: String!
  posts: [Post!]!
}

type Post {
  id: ID!
  titulo: String!
  contenido: String!
  autor: Usuario!
}

type Query {
  usuarios: [Usuario!]!
  usuario(id: ID!): Usuario
  posts: [Post!]!
}

type Mutation {
  crearUsuario(nombre: String!, email: String!): Usuario!
  crearPost(titulo: String!, contenido: String!, autorId: ID!): Post!
}

    🔍 Queries¶

    # Get all users with their name
query {
  usuarios {
    id
    nombre
  }
}

# Get a user with their posts
query {
  usuario(id: "1") {
    nombre
    posts {
      titulo
    }
  }
}

# With variables
query GetUsuario($id: ID!) {
  usuario(id: $id) {
    nombre
    email
  }
}

    ✏ Mutations¶

    mutation {
  crearUsuario(nombre: "Ana", email: "ana@ejemplo.com") {
    id
    nombre
  }
}

    📡 Subscriptions¶

    Subscriptions let you receive real-time data (like WebSockets, but with GraphQL).

    subscription {
  nuevoPost {
    id
    titulo
    autor {
      nombre
    }
  }
}

    ⚛ Apollo Client¶

    Apollo Client is the most popular library for consuming GraphQL from React, Vue, Svelte, or vanilla JS.

    npm install @apollo/client graphql

    import { ApolloClient, InMemoryCache, gql, useQuery } from "@apollo/client";

const client = new ApolloClient({
  uri: "[https://api.ejemplo.com/graphql](https://api.ejemplo.com/graphql)",
  cache: new InMemoryCache()
});

const GET_USUARIOS = gql`
  query {
    usuarios {
      id
      nombre
    }
  }
`;

function Usuarios() {
  const { data, loading, error } = useQuery(GET_USUARIOS);
  if (loading) return <p>Cargando...</p>;
  if (error) return <p>Error: {error.message}</p>;

  return (
    <ul>
      {data.usuarios.map((u) => <li key={u.id}>{u.nombre}</li>)}
    </ul>
  );
}

    🖥 GraphQL Server with Node.js¶

    npm install @apollo/server graphql

    import { ApolloServer } from "@apollo/server";
import { startStandaloneServer } from "@apollo/server/standalone";

const typeDefs = `
  type Usuario {
    id: ID!
    nombre: String!
  }

  type Query {
    usuarios: [Usuario!]!
  }
`;

const resolvers = {
  Query: {
    usuarios: () => [
      { id: "1", nombre: "Ana" },
      { id: "2", nombre: "Luis" }
    ]
  }
};

const server = new ApolloServer({ typeDefs, resolvers });
const { url } = await startStandaloneServer(server, { listen: { port: 4000 } });
console.log("Servidor en " + url);

    ✅ GraphQL vs. REST¶

    Aspect REST GraphQL
    Requests Multiple endpoints Single endpoint
    Data Overfetching / underfetching Only what you ask for
    Versioning v1, v2... Schema evolution
    Learning curve Low Medium
    Caching HTTP caching More complex
    File uploads Native Requires multipart

    When to use GraphQL

    • Many related entities.
    • Mobile with limited bandwidth.
    • Multiple clients (web, iOS, Android).
    • Avoiding overfetching on large APIs.

    When NOT to use GraphQL

    • Simple APIs with few resources.
    • Small teams without prior experience.
    • When HTTP caching is critical.

    36 — Micro-frontends¶

    What you will learn

    • What micro-frontends are and when to use them.
    • Module Federation with Vite.
    • Runtime composition.
    • Communication between micro-frontends.
    • Pros and cons.

    🧩 What Are Micro-Frontends?¶

    Micro-frontends split a large frontend application into smaller, independent applications that can be built, deployed, and scaled separately. They are the frontend equivalent of microservices.

    Frontend monolith:  1 giant app, 1 team, 1 deployment
Micro-frontends:    N small apps, N teams, N deployments

    Divide and conquer (on the frontend too)

    When 50 developers work in the same repository, conflicts are constant. Micro-frontends let each team own its slice.

    🎯 When to Use Micro-Frontends?¶

    Scenario Micro-Frontends?
    Large teams (10+ devs) ✅
    Multiple independent teams ✅
    Incremental migration from Angular to React ✅
    Multiple products inside one platform ✅
    Small project (1-3 devs) ❌
    MVP or prototype ❌
    App with heavy cross-slice interaction ❌

    ⚡ Module Federation¶

    Module Federation (Webpack 5, Vite 5+) lets one app load code from another at runtime, without duplicating dependencies.

    Host (Container)¶

    // host vite.config.js
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import federation from "@originjs/vite-plugin-federation";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    federation({
      name: "host",
      remotes: {
        productos: "http://localhost:5001/assets/remoteEntry.js",
        carrito: "http://localhost:5002/assets/remoteEntry.js"
      },
      shared: ["react", "react-dom"]
    })
  ]
});

    import Productos from "productos/Productos";
import Carrito from "carrito/Carrito";

function App() {
  return (
    <div>
      <Productos/>
      <Carrito/>
    </div>
  );
}

    Remote¶

    // remote vite.config.js
export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    federation({
      name: "productos",
      filename: "remoteEntry.js",
      exposes: {
        "./Productos": "./src/Productos.jsx"
      },
      shared: ["react", "react-dom"]
    })
  ]
});

    🔗 Runtime Composition¶

    Strategy When It Composes
    Build time When building the app (npm packages)
    Run time When loading the app (Module Federation)
    Iframes Full isolation (but limited)
    Web Components Native composition

    Start simple

    If you've never built micro-frontends, start with Web Components or iframes. Module Federation is powerful, but complex.

    📡 Communication Between Micro-Frontends¶

    Micro-frontends should communicate without tight coupling. Options:

    Strategy When to Use It
    Custom Events Simple communication between apps
    Shared global state Small state (user, theme)
    URL / query params Navigation between apps
    Web Components Shared native components
    Event bus Complex communication (EventEmitter) 
    // App A dispatches an event
window.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("carrito:add", {
  detail: { productoId: 42 }
}));

// App B listens to it
window.addEventListener("carrito:add", (e) => {
  console.log("Añadido:", e.detail.productoId);
});

    Watch out for coupling

    If two micro-frontends talk to each other constantly, they probably shouldn't be separate micro-frontends. Excessive communication is a sign of poor domain boundaries.

    ⚖ Pros and Cons¶

    Pros¶

    • ✅ Independent teams: each team deploys on its own schedule.
    • ✅ Organizational scalability: add teams without stepping on toes.
    • ✅ Fault isolation: if one micro-frontend goes down, the others keep running.
    • ✅ Incremental migration: migrate one piece without rewriting everything.
    • ✅ Different tech stacks: one team can use React, another Vue.

    Cons¶

    • ❌ Complexity: more repos, more pipelines, more deployments.
    • ❌ Duplication: each app loads its own dependencies.
    • ❌ Visual consistency: you must share a design system.
    • ❌ Performance: more requests, more JS.
    • ❌ Debugging: harder to trace a flow across apps.
    • ❌ E2E testing: harder to automate.

    1. What are micro-frontends?

    2. Which tool lets you share code at runtime?

    3. When should you NOT use micro-frontends?

    37 — Introduction to Generative AI¶

    What you will learn

    • What generative AI is and how it works.
    • LLMs: GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama.
    • Integrating AI into a web app.
    • Prompt engineering.
    • Risks and best practices.

    🤖 What is Generative AI?¶

    Generative AI is a type of artificial intelligence that creates new content: text, images, code, audio, or video. LLMs (Large Language Models) are models that generate text.

    Prompt  →  Model  →  Generated response

    AI isn't magic, it's statistics

    An LLM predicts the next most probable word. It does it well enough to look like it "understands", yet it doesn't reason like a human.

    🧠 Popular LLMs¶

    Model Company Strength
    GPT-4 OpenAI Widely used, huge ecosystem
    Claude Anthropic Long context, strong with documents
    Gemini Google Multimodal (text, image, audio)
    Llama Meta Open source, runnable locally
    Mistral Mistral AI Open source, efficient
    DeepSeek DeepSeek Very competitive in code

    🔌 Integrating AI into a Web App¶

    // Call to the OpenAI API
async function preguntar(prompt) {
  const res = await fetch("[https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions](https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions)", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "Authorization": "Bearer " + process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      model: "gpt-4",
      messages: [
        { role: "system", content: "Eres un experto en desarrollo web." },
        { role: "user", content: prompt }
      ],
      temperature: 0.7
    })
  });

  const data = await res.json();
  return data.choices[0].message.content;
}

    Never expose the API key in the frontend

    The code above belongs in the backend. In the frontend, send a request to your own backend, which attaches the key and enforces rate limiting.

    🎯 Prompt Engineering¶

    The difference between a good response and a bad one lies in the prompt.

    ❌ Bad:  "Make me a website"
✅ Good: "Create a landing page for a personal finance app,
   with hero, features, and CTA. Use React, Tailwind, and a minimalist
   design with blue tones. Include full code."
    Technique Example
    Role "You are a senior developer..."
    Context "I'm using React 18 and TypeScript..."
    Examples "Here is an example of what I want..."
    Format "Respond in JSON with the fields..."
    Step by step "Think step by step before answering"
    Constraints "Do not use external libraries"

    📚 RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)¶

    RAG combines an LLM with your own knowledge base. The model retrieves relevant information and uses it to answer.

    Question → Search your database → LLM with context → Accurate answer
    Step Tool
    Embeddings OpenAI, Cohere, Hugging Face
    Vector database Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, pgvector
    LLM GPT-4, Claude, Llama 
    // 1. Turn the question into an embedding
const embedding = await openai.embeddings.create({
  model: "text-embedding-3-small",
  input: pregunta
});

// 2. Search similar documents
const docs = await db.query(
  "SELECT * FROM documentos ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 5",
  [embedding.data[0].embedding]
);

// 3. Pass docs to the LLM as context
const respuesta = await openai.chat.completions.create({
  model: "gpt-4",
  messages: [
    { role: "system", content: "Responde usando solo este contexto: " + docs.join("\n") },
    { role: "user", content: pregunta }
  ]
});

    ⚠ Risks and Limitations¶

    Risk Description
    Hallucinations The model invents plausible-sounding facts
    Bias Reflects biases present in training data
    Privacy Never send sensitive data to external APIs
    Cost APIs charge per token
    Latency Responses can take seconds
    Dependency If the API goes down, your app stops working
    Security Prompt injection, jailbreaks

    Never trust blindly

    An LLM can invent a non-existent function, a non-existent package, or a fake citation. Always verify what it generates before using it.

    ✅ Best Practices¶

    • ✅ Validate and verify model outputs.
    • ✅ Don't send sensitive data to external APIs.
    • ✅ Use RAG to supply domain-specific context.
    • ✅ Rate-limit and cap costs.
    • ✅ Provide a fallback if AI fails.
    • ✅ Let the user know they are interacting with AI.
    • ✅ Log interactions to improve the system.
    • ❌ Don't use AI for critical decisions without human oversight.
