      💼 Interview Questions¶

      Get ready for your next opportunity

      A collection of common frontend technical interview questions with detailed answers and code examples, organized by level so you can practice at your pace.

      🎯 How to use this page¶

      1. Read the question and try to answer it yourself before opening the solution.
      2. Click the question to expand the detailed answer.
      3. Practice the example code in your editor.
      4. Do not memorize: understand the underlying concept.

      Interview tip

      In a technical interview, how you think matters just as much as the right answer. If you do not know something, say so and explain how you would look it up. Honesty beats pretending.

      🟢 Beginner Level¶

      What is the difference between let, const, and var?

      var: Function-scoped and hoisted. Can be redeclared. Avoid it in modern code.

      let: Block-scoped. Cannot be redeclared in the same scope, but can be reassigned.

      const: Block-scoped. Cannot be redeclared or reassigned. Requires initialization.

      var x = 1;
let y = 2;
const z = 3;
      What is the DOM and what is it used for?

      The DOM (Document Object Model) is a tree-like representation of the HTML document built in memory by the browser. It lets JavaScript access and manipulate elements on the page.

      const title = document.querySelector('h1');
title.textContent = 'New title';
      What is an event and how do you handle it in JavaScript?

      An event is an action that happens in the browser—a click, a keypress, a form submit, scrolling, page load… JavaScript can listen for these events and run code when they occur.

      const button = document.querySelector('button');
button.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  console.log('Clicked', event.target);
});
      What is the difference between == and ===?
      • == compares values after type coercion.
      • === compares both value and type (strict equality).
      5 == '5';   // true
5 === '5';  // false
null == undefined;   // true
null === undefined;  // false

      Always use === unless you have a clear, justified reason not to.

      What is hoisting?

      It is JavaScript behavior that hoists variable and function declarations to the top of their scope. Function declarations can be called before their definition; var variables are hoisted with a value of undefined until assignment.

      console.log(name); // undefined (no error)
var name = 'Ana';

greet(); // 'Hello' (works)
function greet() { console.log('Hello'); }
      What is a closure and what is it used for?

      A closure is a function that "remembers" the environment in which it was created, even after that outer scope has finished executing. It is commonly used to encapsulate private state.

      function createCounter() {
  let count = 0;
  return function () {
    count++;
    return count;
  };
}

const counter = createCounter();
console.log(counter()); // 1
console.log(counter()); // 2
console.log(counter()); // 3

      🟡 Intermediate Level¶

      What is the event loop in JavaScript?

      The event loop is the mechanism that allows JavaScript (which runs on a single thread) to coordinate asynchronous operations. It works with:

      1. Call stack: stack of synchronous function calls.
      2. Task queue: queue of tasks (macrotasks) such as setTimeout.
      3. Microtask queue: queue of microtasks such as resolved/rejected promises.

      The event loop drains the call stack, then runs microtasks, then takes macrotasks one by one.

      console.log('1');
setTimeout(() => console.log('2'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3'));
console.log('4');
// Output: 1, 4, 3, 2
      What is the difference between a promise and async/await?

      Both are the same thing under the hood: async/await is syntactic sugar over promises. The difference is in readability and structure:

      // With promises
fetch('/api/user')
  .then(res => res.json())
  .then(data => console.log(data))
  .catch(err => console.error(err));

// With async/await
async function load() {
  try {
    const res = await fetch('/api/user');
    const data = await res.json();
    console.log(data);
  } catch (err) {
    console.error(err);
  }
}

      async/await is often easier to read, especially with sequential steps and try/catch error handling.

      What is event delegation and why is it useful?

      It is a technique where you attach a single event listener to a parent element instead of attaching one to every child element. It relies on event bubbling.

      document.querySelector('ul').addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  if (e.target.matches('li')) {
    console.log('Clicked li:', e.target.textContent);
  }
});

      Benefits: fewer listeners (better memory/performance), works for dynamically added children, and cleaner code.

      What is the difference between localStorage, sessionStorage, and cookies?
      Feature localStorage sessionStorage Cookies
      Persistence Persistent Session only Configurable
      Capacity ~5 MB ~5 MB ~4 KB
      Sent to server No No Yes (with matching requests)
      Accessible from JS Yes Yes Yes (unless HttpOnly)
      Typical uses Preferences, achievements Temporary form state Auth tokens, tracking 
      localStorage.setItem('theme', 'dark');
sessionStorage.setItem('cart', JSON.stringify(items));
document.cookie = 'user=ana; max-age=3600; path=/';
      What is event propagation (bubbling and capturing)?

      When an event happens on an element, it travels through three phases:

      1. Capturing: from the document root down to the target element.
      2. Target: the event reaches the target element.
      3. Bubbling: from the target element back up to the root.
      // Bubbling (default)
child.addEventListener('click', () => console.log('child'));
parent.addEventListener('click', () => console.log('parent'));
// Click on child → 'child', 'parent'

// Capturing
parent.addEventListener('click', () => console.log('parent'), true);
// Click on child → 'parent', 'child'
      How does this work in JavaScript?

      this depends on how a function is called, not where it is defined. Four common rules:

      // 1. Object method → the object
const obj = { name: 'Ana', greet() { console.log(this.name); } };
obj.greet(); // 'Ana'

// 2. Standalone function → window (or undefined in strict mode)
function globalFn() { console.log(this); }
globalFn(); // window / undefined

// 3. Arrow function → lexical this from surrounding scope
const obj2 = {
  name: 'Ana',
  greet: () => console.log(this.name)
};

// 4. call/apply/bind → explicitly passed object
function sayName() { console.log(this.name); }
sayName.call({ name: 'Luis' }); // 'Luis'
      What is the module pattern?

      It is a pattern for encapsulating code and exposing only what is needed, using closures or ES6 modules.

      // With closure
const counter = (() => {
  let value = 0;
  return {
    increment: () => ++value,
    get: () => value,
  };
})();

counter.increment();
console.log(counter.get()); // 1

// With ES6 modules
export const PI = 3.14;
export function add(a, b) { return a + b; }

      🟠 Advanced Level¶

      What is the Virtual DOM?

      It is an in-memory representation of the real DOM, used by libraries/frameworks like React to batch and minimize direct DOM mutations. When state changes, a new Virtual DOM tree is created, diffed against the previous one, and only the necessary updates are applied to the real DOM.

      What are debounce and throttle?

      Debounce: delays running a function until a specified quiet period has passed without new events. Great for search inputs.

      function debounce(fn, ms = 300) {
  let timer;
  return (...args) => {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), ms);
  };
}

      Throttle: runs a function at most once every X ms. Useful for scroll or resize handlers.

      function throttle(fn, ms = 200) {
  let last = 0;
  return (...args) => {
    const now = Date.now();
    if (now - last >= ms) { last = now; fn(...args); }
  };
}
      What is conditional rendering in React?

      Showing or hiding parts of the UI based on state or props.

      function Greeting({ user }) {
  return user ? <p>Hello, {user.name}</p> : <p>Hello, guest</p>;
}
      What is the React Context API?

      A way to share data across the component tree without passing props manually through every intermediate level.

      const ThemeContext = React.createContext('light');
      What are hooks and which ones are most common?

      Hooks are functions in React that let you hook into state and lifecycle/other features inside function components.

      Hook Purpose
      useState Local component state
      useEffect Side effects
      useContext Consume context
      useRef Mutable reference across renders
      useMemo Memoize computed values
      useCallback Memoize function references
      What is frontend performance optimization?

      Improving how fast and smooth a web app feels. Techniques include lazy loading, code splitting, memoization, list virtualization, modern image formats (WebP/AVIF), HTTP caching, and service workers.

      What is web accessibility?

      Designing websites so anyone can use them. Key practices include semantic HTML, descriptive alt text, WCAG AA contrast, keyboard navigation, aria-label, and visible focus styles.

      🔴 Professional Level¶

      What is Server-Side Rendering (SSR)?

      SSR renders HTML on the server before sending it to the browser. Benefits: better SEO and faster initial content visibility. Trade-offs: higher server load and extra architectural complexity.

      What is a micro-frontend?

      An architecture that splits a large frontend into smaller, independent applications that teams can build, test, and deploy separately.

      What is hydration in SSR?

      The process where server-rendered HTML becomes interactive in the client browser by attaching event listeners and hydrating client state.

      How does HTTP caching work?
      Header Role
      Cache-Control Caching directives
      ETag Version identifier for validation
      Last-Modified Last modification timestamp

      Common strategies: hashed static assets → long max-age; HTML → no-cache; dynamic API responses → private or short max-age.

      What is CORS and why does it cause errors?

      CORS is a browser security mechanism that controls cross-origin requests. The server must include Access-Control-Allow-Origin (and matching headers) to allow the origin.

      Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://libro.urukais.com
      What is a Content Security Policy (CSP)?

      An HTTP response header that restricts which resources (scripts, styles, images, frames) the browser is allowed to load or execute—a key defense against XSS.

      How would you improve the performance of a slow website?
      1. Measure with Lighthouse and Core Web Vitals
      2. Optimize images (WebP/AVIF, proper sizing, lazy loading)
      3. Minify CSS/JS and apply code splitting
      4. Use font-display: swap for web fonts
      5. Configure HTTP caching and service workers
      6. Serve static assets through a CDN
      7. Use SSR or SSG when SEO and initial HTML matter
      8. Inline critical CSS

      ❓ Frequently Asked Questions¶

      Quick Answers

      Here you'll find answers to the most common questions about the Web Developer's Book (Libro del Desarrollador Web). If you don't find what you're looking for, open an issue on GitHub or reach out.

      🏠 About the Project¶

      What is the Web Developer's Book exactly?

      It is a free, open-source educational resource that teaches web development from scratch to an advanced level. It is structured into 7 levels and 38 chapters, including theory, runnable examples, solved exercises, interactive quizzes, and an achievement system.

      It's not a paid course or a subscription platform: it's an open book you can read, copy, and reuse freely.

      Who is behind the project?

      The project is maintained by Manuel Casimiro Carrasco (Urukais), web developer and technical writer. You can learn more on the About the Author page.

      Why is it free?

      When I started learning, there wasn't enough open material without paywalls or awkward machine translations. I wanted anyone—regardless of financial situation—to be able to learn how to code. The book has no ads, no affiliates, and no paywalls. If you want to support the project, you're welcome to, but it's never required.

      How is it funded?

      With the author's free time and community support. Infrastructure (GitHub Pages, GitHub Actions) is free. Any support via Substack or support goes back into the project or a thank-you coffee.

      How long has it been published?

      The project launched publicly in October 2026. Since then, it has been updated regularly with new chapters, design improvements, and extra resources.

      Does it have an end date?

      No. The project is a marathon, not a sprint. Chapters are published when they're ready, not on a forced rush. I'd rather have one well-crafted chapter a month than a rushed one every week.

      📚 About the Content¶

      Who is this book for?

      Mainly for three profiles:

      • Complete beginners: people who have never written a line of code.
      • Students and self-taught learners: looking for structured reference material.
      • Developers in transition: who already code and want to go deeper or modernize their skills.

      It's not a narrow reference for specialists; while higher levels cover advanced topics, the approach is pedagogical and progressive.

      In what order should I read the chapters?

      In order, especially if you're just starting out. Each chapter builds on the previous one. If you already have experience, you can jump straight to the right level using the 🗂 Explore menu at the top.

      How is it different from other books or courses?

      Three main things:

      1. Written from scratch with clear explanations, not machine-translated filler.
      2. Free and open source, with no ads or subscriptions.
      3. Interactive learning tools (quizzes, live editors, achievement system) that static books don't offer.
      Can I use the content to teach classes?

      Yes, as long as you keep attribution and don't sell it as your own. The MIT license lets you use, copy, and modify the content. Feel free to message me to share how you use it—I'd love to hear.

      Is the content kept up to date?

      Yes. The book is reviewed periodically as the web ecosystem evolves. You can check updates in the Changelog. If you spot outdated info, open an issue.

      Does it cover frameworks like React, Vue, or Angular?

      It covers the fundamentals (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) and the core concepts behind frameworks. It doesn't dive deep into any single framework because frameworks come and go, while fundamentals remain.

      In the Advanced Level there are chapters on modules, bundlers, and architecture that prepare you to pick up any framework afterward.

      Does it include backend?

      Yes. The Professional Level covers Full-stack with Node.js and DevOps for frontend. It's not frontend-only.

      Does it include exercises and projects?

      Yes. Each chapter includes:

      • Runnable examples
      • Practice exercises
      • An interactive quiz
      • In some cases, a guided project

      You also have the Solved Exercises section with over 30 annotated solutions.

      🛠 About the Tech Stack¶

      Can I follow the book without installing anything?

      Yes, the early chapters can be followed right in your browser using the live editors on each page. Only when you reach Node.js or backend topics will you need to install tools on your machine.

      Which code editor do you recommend?

      VS Code is the most popular and the one I use in examples. You can also try Zed, Sublime Text, or Neovim if you prefer something faster or more customizable.

      Does it work on Windows, macOS, and Linux?

      Yes. The book is a website, so it works on any OS. Terminal commands focus on Linux/macOS (most common in web dev), while on Windows you can use WSL or PowerShell with minor adjustments.

      Do I need a powerful computer?

      No. For 90% of the book, almost any computer from the last 10 years works fine. Only for Docker and certain backend tools will you want at least 8 GB of RAM.

      Can I use a phone or tablet?

      Yes, the site is responsive and works on any device. For coding, though, a physical keyboard is strongly recommended.

      Which browser do I need?

      Any modern browser: up-to-date Chrome, Firefox, Edge, or Safari. It won't target Internet Explorer.

      🎓 About Learning¶

      How long does it take to finish the book?

      It depends on your pace and prior experience. As a rough guide:

      • Full-time (4–6 h/day): 3–4 months
      • Steady pace (1–2 h/day): 8–12 months
      • Light pace (2–3 h/week): 2–3 years

      Speed matters less than consistency.

      Do I need strong math skills?

      No, for 95% of the book you only need basic arithmetic. Math only shows up in specific advanced areas (WebGL, cryptography, WebAssembly), where it's explained from scratch.

      Do I need to know English?

      Not strictly required to start, though strongly recommended. Most technical docs, articles, and Stack Overflow answers are in English. Key terms are explained as they come up, and as you advance you'll benefit from reading English documentation.

      "English is the lingua franca of programming. You don't need to speak it fluently on day one, but you do need to read it."

      Can I learn to code with this book alone?

      Yes, with a caveat. The book gives you theory, examples, and exercises. Learning to program takes practice: building your own projects, making mistakes, debugging, reading other people's code. The book is a map, not a shortcut.

      How can I tell if I'm making progress?
      • Achievement system: completing a chapter unlocks a badge.
      • Quizzes: at the end of each chapter, you test what you've learned.
      • Solved exercises: compare your solution against the reference one.
      • Personal projects: the clearest sign is building something on your own without following a step-by-step tutorial.
      What should I do when I get stuck?
      1. Re-read the chapter calmly.
      2. Search the error on Google or Stack Overflow.
      3. Ask the community on GitHub Discussions.
      4. Take a break: stepping away for 10 minutes often clears things up.

      Tip

      When stuck, try explaining the problem out loud (or in writing). Rubber duck debugging works because walking through the problem often reveals the solution.

      How can I practice more?
      • Do the exercises in each chapter.
      • Tackle the weekly challenges.
      • Build personal projects (a portfolio, a to-do app, a blog…).
      • Contribute to open-source projects (including this one).
      • Read other developers' code on GitHub.

      🏆 About Achievements & Certificate¶

      How does the achievement system work?

      When you finish a chapter, you check the box at the bottom of the page. A badge unlocks and is saved in your browser via localStorage. You can view your progress on the My Achievements page.

      Are achievements stored on a server?

      No. Everything is stored in your browser. Nothing is sent to a server. Clearing your browser storage resets your achievements.

      Can I sync achievements across devices?

      Not yet. It's on the Roadmap, but requires an authentication system that isn't implemented yet.

      Is the certificate officially accredited?

      No. The certificate is a symbolic recognition that you completed the book. It has no official academic or professional accreditation, though you can add it to your portfolio or LinkedIn as proof of self-directed study.

      How do I get the certificate?

      Once you complete all chapters in the book, you'll unlock the option to generate your certificate on the Certificate page, downloadable as a PDF with your name and completion date.

      🤝 About Contributing¶

      Can I contribute if I don't know how to code?

      Yes. There are plenty of ways to contribute without writing code: reporting typos, suggesting improvements, sharing the book, translating sections. Everything helps. See the Contribute page for details.

      How do I report a bug?

      Open an issue on GitHub with:

      • What you expected to happen
      • What actually happened
      • Steps to reproduce it
      • Your environment (browser, operating system)
      Can I translate the book into another language?

      Yes, we're actively working on English localization with mkdocs-static-i18n. If you'd like to help, open an issue with the i18n label and let us know which language interests you.

      Do I get paid to contribute?

      No. This is a volunteer open-source project. What you gain is experience, visibility, and the satisfaction of helping others learn. Contributors are recognized on the Acknowledgements page.

      📜 About Licensing¶

      What license is the book under?

      Under the MIT License, one of the most permissive open-source licenses. You can use, copy, modify, and distribute the content freely as long as you keep the attribution.

      Can I sell the content?

      Not directly. The MIT license lets you use the content, not sell it as your own. You may incorporate parts into a paid course if you add substantial value and preserve attribution, but you can't simply copy and resell it as-is.

      Can I use the code examples in my projects?

      Yes, without restriction. The code examples are there for you to use, modify, and adapt to your projects.

      Can I use the logo on my website?

      You can use the logo to mention the project in articles, reviews, or resource lists. Don't use it in a way that implies official endorsement or affiliation. If unsure, contact me.

      🌐 About the Website¶

      Why does the site sometimes take a moment to load?

      The first visit may take a couple of seconds to load fonts, styles, and scripts. After that, navigation feels instant thanks to Material's instant loading/prefetching.

      Does it work offline?

      Partially. The book is configured as a PWA (Progressive Web App), so once visited, some pages are cached for offline reading. Not every interactive feature works offline.

      Can I read the book on a Kindle or e-reader?

      Yes, using the printable version you can generate a PDF or EPUB to send to your e-reader. Keep in mind interactive quizzes and live editors won't run inside an e-reader.

      Is there a PDF version?

      Yes. You can generate the printable view from the Printable version link, which combines chapters onto a single page that you can save as PDF from your browser.

      How do I report a website issue?

      If something looks off (a broken link, layout glitch, console error), open an issue on GitHub with:

      • The page URL
      • A screenshot
      • Your browser and operating system

      ❓ Frequently asked questions¶

      Where is my progress saved?

      In your browser, in localStorage, under the uru-* keys. Nothing is sent to any server. If you clear your browser data, you will lose your progress.

      Can I sync across devices?

      Not for now—it is stored locally. If you want, you can back it up manually by exporting localStorage (F12 → Application → Local Storage).

      Do achievements expire?

      No. They stay saved indefinitely until you delete them.

      How is the percentage calculated?

      Based on the number of unlocked achievements out of the total (23 achievements). The circular ring updates automatically.

      🎓 Certificate of Completion¶

      Your effort deserves recognition

      Completing all 38 chapters of the book is no small feat. That is why, once you finish, you can generate a personalized PDF certificate with your name and completion date.

      🎯 What is this certificate?¶

      It is a symbolic recognition that you have completed the Web Developer Book. It carries no official academic or professional accreditation, but you can:

      • Include it in your portfolio as evidence of self-directed learning.
      • Add it to your LinkedIn profile under education/certifications.
      • Share it on social media to celebrate your milestone.
      • Print it and frame it on your wall (if that is your style).

      Not an official credential

      This certificate does not replace an official degree or qualification. It is a recognition from this project, not from an educational institution. If you need an officially recognized credential, look into accredited programs (such as freeCodeCamp, Meta, Google, or Microsoft).

      ✅ Requirements to unlock it¶

      To unlock the certificate, you need to:

      1. Complete all 38 chapters of the book.
      2. Mark each chapter as completed at the bottom of its page.
      3. Solve at least 30 exercises (optional, but recommended).
      4. Complete at least 3 weekly challenges (optional).

      Your progress is saved in your browser

      Completed chapters are stored via localStorage. Clearing your browser data will erase your progress. Switching devices does not sync progress (yet).

      ❓ Frequently asked questions¶

      Do I have to pay for the certificate?

      No. The certificate is 100% free, just like the rest of the book. There is no "premium" tier or hidden fee.

      Can I get the certificate without finishing the book?

      No. The certificate only unlocks once you have completed all 38 chapters. This keeps the milestone meaningful. If you try to generate it earlier, the button stays disabled.

      Is the certificate stored on any server?

      No. The PDF is generated in your browser using JavaScript. Nothing is sent to any server. Your name and date stay on your device.

      Can I use a handle or nickname instead of my real name?

      Yes. You can enter whatever name you prefer. It is your certificate after all.

      Can I customize the certificate design?

      Yes. The certificate code lives in docs/assets/js/certificado.js and docs/assets/css/certificado.css. Feel free to customize colors, typography, or copy—it is open source.

      How can someone verify a certificate is authentic?

      It cannot be verified. Without a central server, there is no way to verify authenticity. It is a symbolic recognition, not an official credential. Anyone verifying it will have to take your word for it.

      Can I still get the certificate if I cleared my browser data?

      If you cleared your browser data, your progress was wiped. You will need to mark the chapters as completed again to unlock the certificate.

      🚀 Haven't finished the book yet?¶

      If you are reading this and have not finished all 38 chapters yet, do not worry. Go at your own pace. The certificate will be waiting when you are done.

      Behind the scenes

      🚀 October 18, 2026 — The Day the Book Came to Life¶

      My workspace, after weeks of coffee and code.

      Today is a special day. After weeks of work, the book is no longer just an idea. It has 36 chapters, interactive diagrams, solved exercises, and even an achievements system so you learn by playing.

      The idea grew out of my own notes. I realized there was a missing resource in Spanish that wasn't afraid to talk about architecture, performance, and security. I wanted to build something I wish I'd had when I started out.

      🛠 The Stack Behind the Book¶

      For the curious, this book is built with:

      Technology Purpose
      MkDocs Markdown-based static site generator
      Material for MkDocs The best theme out there, hands down
      GitHub Pages Free hosting with a custom domain
      GitHub Actions Automated deployment on every push to master
      Giscus Comments powered by GitHub Discussions
      Mermaid Architecture and flow diagrams in Markdown

      🧠 October 15, 2026 — When I Decided to Add Quizzes¶

      At first, the book was plain text. And I realized that reading without practicing gets you nowhere. So I set out to figure out how to add interactive quizzes without breaking the site.

      ❌ What I Tried That Didn't Work¶

      1. Embedded Google Forms: ugly, slow, with Google branding.
      2. NPM quiz libraries: bloated, with dependencies that broke Material.
      3. External iframes: didn't adapt to dark mode.

      ✅ What Actually Worked¶

      A bit of plain JavaScript and CSS. Each quiz is an HTML block with data-answer and data-opt, and a global script validates it:

      <div class="quiz" data-quiz="capitulo-1">
  <div class="quiz-question" data-answer="b">
    <p>What are the three pillars of web development?</p>
    <button class="quiz-option" data-opt="a">A) Python, Java, and C++</button>
    <button class="quiz-option" data-opt="b">B) HTML, CSS, and JavaScript</button>
    <button class="quiz-option" data-opt="c">C) React, Vue, and Angular</button>
  </div>
</div>
<script>document.querySelectorAll('.quiz-question').forEach(function (q) {
  var answer = q.dataset.answer;
  q.querySelectorAll('.quiz-option').forEach(function (btn) {
    btn.addEventListener('click', function () {
      if (q.dataset.done) return;
      if (btn.dataset.opt === answer) {
        btn.classList.add('is-correct');
        q.dataset.done = '1';
      } else {
        btn.classList.add('is-wrong');
      }
    });
  });
});</script>

      🎵 Music for Coding¶

      The developer soundtrack

      Coding with music is a common habit. Some prefer total silence, while many of us find the right focus zone in certain genres to get into a flow state.

      🔍 Search music (30s preview)¶

      Type a song or artist name and click ▶ Listen to play a 30-second preview.

      Not playing Search for a track to get started
      0:00 0:00

      🎯 What music to pick by task¶

      Task Recommended genre
      Writing new code Lo-fi hip hop, jazz
      Refactoring Synthwave, electronic
      Debugging errors Silence or white noise
      Reading documentation Classical, ambient
      Designing Video game soundtracks
      Studying Lo-fi, soft piano

      The flow trick

      Music with lyrics can be distracting while reading or writing code. For tasks that demand deep focus, go for instrumental music.

      🎧 Community playlists¶

      Have a playlist that works well for you? Share it in Community Challenges or open an issue on GitHub.

      📚 Resources¶

      • Music for Programming (web)
      • Focus at Will (focus science)
      • Lofi Girl (YouTube)
      • Synthwave Radio (YouTube)

      🧠 Quiz¶

      Check what you learned

      1. What kind of music works best for focus?

      Instrumental music (no lyrics). Lyrics compete for attention when you are reading or writing code.

      2. Why are video game soundtracks great for coding?

      Because they are designed not to distract the player, who needs to stay focused on the main task. That makes them ideal for cognitive work.

      3. What genre is most popular for coding?

      Lo-fi hip hop. Steady rhythm, no vocals, and hours upon hours of tracks available.

      🤝 How to Contribute¶

      This book belongs to everyone

      The Web Developer's Book is an open-source project. That means you can be part of it too, even if you don't know how to code yet. There are many ways to help, and every single one counts.

      🌟 Why Contribute?¶

      Contributing to an open-source project comes with plenty of benefits:

      Benefit Why It Matters
      Learn by doing Reading other people's code and proposing improvements is one of the best ways to grow as a developer.
      Add experience to your résumé Open-source contributions are publicly visible and highly valued in interviews.
      Meet people This project's community is made up of people who share your interests.
      Improve the book Every fix, suggestion, or translation helps thousands of readers.
      Get credited in acknowledgments Everyone who contributes is listed on the Acknowledgments page.

      You don't need to be an expert

      Many of the most valuable contributions come from people who are actively learning. A beginner spots clarity gaps that an expert easily overlooks.

      🎯 Ways to Contribute¶

      1. Report a Bug 🐛¶

      If you spot a broken link, a typo, code that doesn't work, or a confusing explanation:

      1. Search first to see if an issue is already open: Project Issues
      2. If not, open a new one: New Issue
      3. Fill out the template with:
      4. Expected behavior
      5. Actual behavior
      6. Steps to reproduce (screenshot, URL, code…)
      7. Your environment (browser, operating system…)

      ❤️ Apoya el Proyecto¶

      El libro es gratis. Siempre lo será.

      Este proyecto no tiene publicidad, ni suscripciones, ni muros de pago. Todo el contenido es accesible para cualquiera, independientemente de su situación económica. Pero mantenerlo lleva tiempo y esfuerzo. Si te resulta útil, aquí tienes formas de apoyarlo.

      🎯 ¿Por qué apoyar el proyecto?¶

      Este libro nació de una frustración: la falta de material de calidad en español para aprender desarrollo web. Lo que empezó como apuntes personales se ha convertido en un recurso que leen miles de personas cada mes.

      Mantenerlo requiere:

      • Tiempo: escribir, revisar y actualizar capítulos.
      • Infraestructura: aunque GitHub Pages es gratis, hay servicios externos (dominio, analíticas, etc.).
      • Herramientas: editores, tipografías, servicios de email.
      • Café: mucho café. ☕

      El apoyo es opcional

      Nada de lo que hay en esta página es obligatorio. El libro seguirá siendo gratis y completo, tanto si apoyas como si no. Si no puedes o no quieres aportar nada económico, no pasa nada. Hay muchas otras formas de ayudar (las tienes más abajo).

      📝 Descripción corta (para medios)¶

      Versión de una línea (para redes sociales)¶

      "Un libro gratuito y open source que lleva a cualquier persona desde su primera etiqueta HTML hasta las arquitecturas más avanzadas del desarrollo web moderno."

      Versión de un párrafo (para notas de prensa)¶

      Libro del Desarrollador Web es un proyecto educativo de código abierto, escrito íntegramente en español, que ofrece un recorrido estructurado por el desarrollo web moderno. Dividido en 7 niveles y 38 capítulos, cubre desde los fundamentos de HTML, CSS y JavaScript hasta temas avanzados como TypeScript, Web Components, PWA, WebAssembly, IA generativa y Edge Computing. El proyecto es gratuito, sin anuncios ni suscripciones, y todo su contenido está disponible en GitHub bajo licencia MIT. Incluye ejercicios resueltos, quizzes interactivos, editores de código en vivo y un sistema de logros para fomentar el aprendizaje práctico.

      Versión larga (para artículos o entrevistas)¶

      Libro del Desarrollador Web nace de una frustración común: la falta de material estructurado y de calidad en español para aprender desarrollo web desde cero. Su autor, Manuel Casimiro Carrasco (Urukais), decidió convertir sus apuntes personales en un recurso abierto para cualquiera que quiera iniciarse en la programación.

      El libro está organizado en 7 niveles progresivos que van desde los fundamentos (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) hasta la vanguardia tecnológica (Server Components, Edge Computing, IA generativa, Web3). Cada capítulo incluye teoría, ejemplos ejecutables, ejercicios resueltos y un quiz interactivo para validar lo aprendido.

      Técnicamente, el sitio está construido con MkDocs y Material for MkDocs, se aloja en GitHub Pages y se despliega automáticamente con GitHub Actions. Todo el código es público y cualquier persona puede contribuir, reportar errores o proponer mejoras.

      El proyecto es 100% gratuito, sin publicidad, sin muros de pago y sin afiliados. Se financia con el tiempo libre del autor y el apoyo de la comunidad.

      👤 Biografía del autor¶

      Versión corta (para bio de redes sociales)¶

      Manuel Casimiro Carrasco (Urukais) es desarrollador web y creador del Libro del Desarrollador Web, un proyecto educativo open source en español. Escribe sobre HTML, CSS, JavaScript y arquitectura frontend.

      Versión media (para bio de blog o conferencia)¶

      Manuel Casimiro Carrasco, conocido en la comunidad como Urukais, es desarrollador web y divulgador técnico. Es el autor del Libro del Desarrollador Web, un recurso gratuito y open source que enseña desarrollo web desde cero a miles de personas en español. Su trabajo se centra en la enseñanza de los fundamentos de la web, la accesibilidad y las buenas prácticas de ingeniería frontend.

      Versión larga (para notas de prensa)¶

      Manuel Casimiro Carrasco (Urukais) es desarrollador web, divulgador y autor del Libro del Desarrollador Web. Empezó programando por curiosidad y acabó convirtiendo sus apuntes personales en un recurso educativo que hoy usan lectores de todo el mundo hispanohablante.

      Su enfoque pedagógico se basa en tres ideas: aprender haciendo, no depender de modas pasajeras y explicar las cosas en español con claridad. Defiende el software libre como herramienta de democratización del conocimiento y mantiene el libro como un proyecto abierto, sin publicidad ni muros de pago.

      Cuando no está escribiendo capítulos o revisando pull requests, suele estar leyendo documentación, probando nuevas herramientas o dando largos paseos con música de fondo.

      • 🎨 Octubre 2026 — Rediseño premium: mega-menú de navegación, footer de 5 columnas y header de una sola línea.
      • 📱 Octubre 2026 — Optimización completa para móvil y modo oscuro.
      • 🌍 Próximamente — Traducción al inglés (i18n en investigación).

      📰 Notas de prensa¶

      Nota de prensa — Lanzamiento (Octubre 2026)¶

      Titular: Nace el Libro del Desarrollador Web, un recurso gratuito y open source para aprender programación en español

      Subtítulo: 38 capítulos, 7 niveles y un sistema de logros interactivo. Todo el contenido es accesible desde cualquier navegador, sin registro ni pago.

      Cuerpo:

      Manuel Casimiro Carrasco (Urukais) ha lanzado el Libro del Desarrollador Web, un proyecto educativo de código abierto que ofrece un recorrido completo por el desarrollo web moderno, desde HTML y CSS hasta las arquitecturas más avanzadas del sector.

      El libro se estructura en 7 niveles progresivos y 38 capítulos, e incluye ejercicios resueltos, quizzes interactivos, editores de código en vivo y un sistema de logros para fomentar el aprendizaje práctico.

      Todo el contenido está disponible en libro.urukais.com de forma gratuita. El código fuente está publicado en GitHub bajo licencia MIT.

      "Quería crear el recurso que me hubiera gustado encontrar cuando empecé. En español, sin anuncios, sin muros de pago y sin promesas de aprender en 24 horas", explica el autor.

      Contacto de prensa: contacto@urukais.com

      ✉ Contact¶

      Let's talk

      Have a question, a suggestion, a collaboration idea, or just want to say hello? Here are all the ways to reach me. Pick whichever fits best.

      📬 Contact form¶

      Fill out the fields below and your email app or client will open with a message ready to send to urukaisk@gmail.com.

      Mail client not opening?

      If you do not have a mail client configured or prefer to write directly from webmail, send your message to urukaisk@gmail.com.

      📮 Direct channels¶

      If you prefer reaching out through another channel, here are all available options:

      Channel Best for Link
      📧 Email General inquiries, press, and collaborations urukaisk@gmail.com
      🐛 GitHub Issues Bugs, typos, and technical suggestions Open an issue
      💬 GitHub Discussions Questions, discussions, and ideas Go to Discussions
      🐦 Twitter / X Public mentions and sharing links @urukaisk
      💼 LinkedIn Professional outreach Manuel Casimiro Carrasco
      📰 Substack Newsletter and updates urukaisklick.substack.com
      🐙 GitHub Code and contributions @urukaisk-maker

      🎯 What can you write to me about?¶

      ✅ Yes, write to me if…¶

      • You have a question about the book's content.
      • You found a bug, typo, or broken link.
      • You want to suggest an improvement or a new topic.
      • You want to propose a collaboration (translation, guest chapter, etc.).
      • You are press or media and want to cover the project.
      • You want me to give a talk or workshop.
      • You built something using the book and want to share it.
      • You simply want to say hi or thank someone.

      ❌ No, please do not write to me if…¶

      • It is a personal tech support issue (my time is limited; Stack Overflow is the place for that).
      • It is a sales pitch (services, products, SEO, marketing…).
      • It is spam or automated messages.
      • You are asking me to do your homework (I do not do homework, though I can point you in the right direction).

      ⏱ Response times¶

      I am one person, not a company. Here are approximate response times:

      Channel Typical response time
      GitHub Issues 24–72 h (business days)
      GitHub Discussions 24–72 h (business days)
      Email 2–5 business days
      Form 2–5 business days
      Twitter / X Variable (I do not check it daily)
      LinkedIn 3–7 business days

      Fast replies are not guaranteed

      This book is a personal project I maintain in my free time. If I take longer than expected to reply, it does not mean I do not care—it just means I am busy with work, life, or the book itself.

      ❓ Before writing: is your question in the FAQ?¶

      Many common questions are already answered on the FAQ page. Before sending a message, take a quick look:

      • Is it free? How is it funded?
      • Who is the book for?
      • How can I contribute?
      • How do I get the certificate?

      If your question is not in the FAQ, go ahead and write.

      🤝 Collaborations¶

      If you want to collaborate on the project (translation, guest chapter, sponsorship, talk…), mention it in the form subject or by email. Tell me:

      • Who you are and what you do.
      • What you are proposing specifically.
      • Why you think it fits the project.
      • What you would need from me.

      Collaboration replies

      If your proposal aligns with the project's values (open source, free, and ad-free), I will gladly reply. If it does not fit, I will tell you honestly too.

      🗺 Where I'm based¶

      I am based in Spain 🇪🇸 and collaborate with people around the world. Keep that in mind if you write from a different time zone.

      🔐 Privacy¶

      Your details are only used to reply to you. They are never sold, shared with third parties, or used for spam. If you want me to delete your message after replying, just ask.

      For more details, see the privacy policy.

      💬 Final thought¶

      "A well-written email saves 10 messages."

      If you write to me, help me help you: be specific, tell me what you need, and if it is a technical issue, include screenshots, logs, or the failing code. With that context I can answer much faster and better.

      🙏 Acknowledgments¶

      None of this is mine alone

      This book wouldn't be possible without the work of thousands of people who share their knowledge freely on the internet. Behind every line of code is a community that has spent decades building the open web. To all of them, thank you.

      🌍 To the Web Community¶

      To everyone who writes, reviews, and maintains the resources that made this book possible:

      Resource Why It Is Essential
      MDN Web Docs The most complete and reliable web development reference. If it ever disappeared, the web would grind to a halt.
      CSS Tricks For decades, the best place to learn CSS. Its Almanac is pure gold.
      javascript.info The clearest JavaScript tutorial out there.
      Smashing Magazine Deep-dive articles on design and development, with zero fluff.
      web.dev Performance, accessibility, and best-practice guides from Google.
      Can I Use Every time I wondered "can I use this in production?", it was right there.
      Stack Overflow Not always the right answer, but always a starting point.

      If you're learning

      If you don't know these sites yet, check them out before paying for any course. 90% of what you need is already there, free and well explained.

      🛠 To Open-Source Tools¶

      This book is built from start to finish with free and open-source software. Without these tools, it wouldn't exist:

      • MkDocs — the static site generator that turns Markdown into HTML.
      • Material for MkDocs — the theme that makes this book feel premium.
      • Python — the engine powering everything.
      • Git — version control that makes sure nothing is lost.
      • GitHub and GitHub Actions — hosting and automated deployment.
      • Mermaid — architecture and flow diagrams.
      • Giscus — comments backed by GitHub Discussions.
      • FullCalendar — the calendar on the schedule page.
      • Inter and JetBrains Mono — the typefaces you're reading right now.

      And a special thanks to

      Martin Donath (squidfunk), creator of Material for MkDocs, who built the best documentation theme out there and maintains it as open source. Without his work, this book wouldn't look half as good.

      📚 To Inspiring Authors¶

      There are books that change how you think. These are the ones that have most shaped how I teach and write:

      Author Book Why It Stuck With Me
      Jon Duckett HTML and CSS: Design and Build Websites The most visual and approachable book to get started. I lent it out so many times I had to buy another copy.
      Marijn Haverbeke Eloquent JavaScript Taught me that JavaScript can be elegant, not just functional.
      Kyle Simpson You Don't Know JS (series) Forced me to look under the hood. Changed how I understand the language.
      Eric A. Meyer CSS: The Definitive Guide The CSS bible. Still a reference 20 years later.
      Martin Fowler Refactoring Taught me that clean code isn't a luxury, it's a necessity.
      Robert C. Martin Clean Code Controversial, yet essential for understanding good practices.
      Dan Abramov Just JavaScript (course) Helped me grasp the mental model of modern JavaScript.

      Reading other people's code

      Learning to program is also learning to read code written by others. These authors don't just teach concepts: they teach how to think.

      🎓 To Mentors and Role Models¶

      Even though I don't know them personally, their work has shaped me as a developer:

      • Evan You (creator of Vue.js) — for proving a framework can be both simple and powerful.
      • Dan Abramov (React) — for clear explanations of React's mental model.
      • Sarah Drasner (SVG and animations) — for making web animations look effortless.
      • Rachel Andrew (CSS Grid) — for explaining CSS Grid better than anyone else.
      • Josh Comeau (CSS and React) — for interactive articles that transform how people learn.
      • Kent C. Dodds (testing) — for his "testing trophy" philosophy over the "testing pyramid".
      • Cassie Evans (web animation) — for making GSAP approachable.

      And to all the anonymous developers who answer questions in forums, write on personal blogs, and post examples on CodePen. Your work is invisible yet indispensable.

      👥 To Contributors¶

      Anyone who opens an issue, proposes a PR, points out a typo, or suggests an improvement will be mentioned here.

      👤
      Your name here
      First contribution
      🌟
      Be next
      Open an issue or PR

      Want to appear here?

      There are many ways to contribute without writing code: reporting bugs, suggesting improvements, sharing the book, starring the repo on GitHub. Find every option on the Contribute page.

      💜 To the Spanish-Speaking Community¶

      To everyone building quality content in Spanish:

      • YouTube channels that teach without hype: MiduDev, Fazt, HolaMundo, MoureDev.
      • Discord and Telegram communities that answer questions generously.
      • Personal blogs that push back against short-video trends and keep publishing deep-dive articles.
      • Translators who make technical documentation accessible in Spanish.

      Truly in Spanish

      This book exists because for years I couldn't find a Spanish resource that wasn't a machine translation or a paid course. If you're thinking about writing your own material: do it. There's still so much to build.

      ❤ To You¶

      Yes, you. For taking the time to read this. For wanting to learn. For not settling for 5-minute tutorials.

      Learning to program isn't easy. There are days when nothing works, when a single ; has you staring at the screen for an hour, when you feel like you're not moving forward. Yet you're still here.

      That's the only thing that matters.

      Thank you for being here

      This book is my way of giving back everything the community has given me. If it helps you, it was already worth it. Now it's your turn: learn, practice, and someday teach someone else.

      📜 License and Attribution¶

      This book is released under the MIT license. You can copy, modify, and share it freely. I only ask one thing: keep attribution to the original authors and the tools that make it possible.

      If you build something with this material, I'd love to know. Nothing would make me happier than seeing what you're able to create.
